P1 · Probability Basics and Counting


                  
                  Why this matters for the term final 
                  
                

No past term final asks a pure “define sample space” question, but every probability question you will meet (Bayes in 2019-20 Q7(a), 2022-23 Q1, 2023-24 Q1; joint distributions in 2023-24 Q2(b); hypergeometric in 2021-22 Q6(c)) is built on the ideas in this note: events, the addition rule, complements and combinations. In particular, ==combinations (^nC_r)== are used every time you pick balls, pens or cars “at random without replacement”. Learn this note well and the later notes become easy.



1. What probability measures
Probability is a number between 0 and 1 that tells us how likely an outcome is. A probability of 0 means the event cannot happen, and a probability of 1 means it will certainly happen. Every other event lies somewhere in between. We use probability when we cannot predict the exact result of an experiment, but we do know the list of results that are possible. For example, when we toss a fair coin we cannot say whether a head or a tail will appear, but we know the only possibilities are H and T, and each has probability 0.5.
2. Random experiment, sample space and events
A random experiment is an experiment that satisfies three conditions. First, all the possible outcomes are known in advance. Second, on any single performance we cannot say exactly which outcome will occur. Third, the experiment can be repeated under identical conditions. Tossing a coin, rolling a die and drawing a card from a deck are all random experiments.


                  
                  Memorize: Sample space and event 
                  
                

The sample space S is the set of all possible outcomes of a random experiment. An event is any subset of the sample space, that is, a collection of some of the outcomes. An event “occurs” if the outcome of the experiment is one of its elements.


For a single die, S=\{1,2,3,4,5,6\}. The event “an even number appears” is A=\{2,4,6\}. For two tosses of a coin, S=\{HH, HT, TH, TT\}, and the event “at least one head” is \{HH, HT, TH\}. When a pair of dice is thrown, the sample space has 6\times 6=36 equally likely ordered pairs, which is something you should remember because dice problems appear often in lectures.
The complement of an event A, written A^c or \bar A, is the set of outcomes in S that are not in A. The union A\cup B is the event that A or B (or both) occurs. The intersection A\cap B is the event that both A and B occur.
Types of events
Two events are mutually exclusive (or disjoint) when they cannot happen together, which means A\cap B=\emptyset. Getting a 1 and getting a 6 on one roll of a die are mutually exclusive, because a single roll cannot show both faces.
A collection of events is exhaustive when together they cover the whole sample space, so at least one of them must happen. For a die, the events \{1,2\}, \{3,4\} and \{5,6\} are exhaustive (and also mutually exclusive). Events that are both mutually exclusive and exhaustive form a partition of the sample space; this idea is the backbone of the total probability rule and Bayes’ theorem in P2 Conditional Probability Independence and Bayes.
Events are equally likely when they have the same chance of happening. Head and tail of a fair coin are equally likely; the six faces of a fair die are equally likely.


                  
                  Common mistake 
                  
                

Do not confuse mutually exclusive with independent. Mutually exclusive means “cannot happen together” (P(A\cap B)=0). Independent means “one does not change the chance of the other” (P(A\cap B)=P(A)P(B)). These are completely different ideas, and in fact two events with non-zero probabilities can never be both. This exact point was asked in 2023-24 Q1(a), and it is explained fully in P2 Conditional Probability Independence and Bayes.


De Morgan’s laws
De Morgan’s laws connect complements, unions and intersections. In words, the complement of a union is the intersection of the complements, and the complement of an intersection is the union of the complements.
(A\cup B)^c = A^c\cap B^c \qquad\qquad (A\cap B)^c = A^c\cup B^c
These are very useful for “neither” and “at least one” questions. “Neither A nor B happens” is A^c\cap B^c=(A\cup B)^c, so P(\text{neither}) = 1-P(A\cup B).
For example, let S=\{a,b,c,d,e\}, A=\{a,b,c\} and B=\{b,d\}. Then A\cap B=\{b\}, so (A\cap B)^c=\{a,c,d,e\}. Checking with De Morgan, A^c=\{d,e\} and B^c=\{a,c,e\}, whose union is \{a,c,d,e\}. Both sides agree.

3. Definitions of probability
Classical (a priori) definition
If an experiment has n(S) equally likely, mutually exclusive outcomes, and n(A) of them are favourable to event A, then
P(A)=\frac{n(A)}{n(S)}=\frac{\text{number of favourable outcomes}}{\text{total number of outcomes}} .
This definition only works when the outcomes are equally likely and finite in number. For example, the probability of an even number on a fair die is 3/6=0.5, and the probability of choosing a girl from a class of 12 girls and 18 boys is 12/30=0.4.
Axiomatic definition
The modern definition says a probability is any rule P that assigns a number to each event and obeys three axioms.


                  
                  Memorize: The three axioms of probability 
                  
                

First, P(A)\ge 0 for every event A. Second, P(S)=1. Third, if A_1, A_2, \dots are mutually exclusive events, then P(A_1\cup A_2\cup\cdots)=P(A_1)+P(A_2)+\cdots.


From these axioms we can prove everything else, for example that P(\emptyset)=0, that 0\le P(A)\le 1, and the complement rule
P(A^c)=1-P(A).
The complement rule is one of the most useful tricks in the whole course. Whenever a question says “at least one”, it is almost always easier to compute 1-P(\text{none}).
Relative frequency (empirical) definition
If an experiment is repeated n times and event A occurs f times, then the relative frequency f/n approaches P(A) as n becomes very large. This is how probabilities such as “1 in every 1000 glass items has a bubble” (2019-20 Q8(a)) are obtained in practice.

4. The addition rule


                  
                  Memorize: Addition rule 
                  
                

For any two events,
P(A\cup B)=P(A)+P(B)-P(A\cap B).
If A and B are mutually exclusive, P(A\cap B)=0 and the rule becomes P(A\cup B)=P(A)+P(B).
For three events,
P(A\cup B\cup C)=P(A)+P(B)+P(C)-P(A\cap B)-P(A\cap C)-P(B\cap C)+P(A\cap B\cap C).


The reason we subtract P(A\cap B) is that the outcomes in both A and B were counted twice, once inside P(A) and once inside P(B). If you picture two overlapping circles inside a rectangle (a Venn diagram), the union is “A only” plus “overlap” plus “B only”, and simply adding the two circles counts the overlap twice, so we remove it once.
Worked example (lecture style). In an office of 100 employees, 75 read an English daily, 50 read a Bangla daily and 40 read both. What is the probability that a randomly selected employee reads at least one of the two papers, and what is the probability that the employee reads neither?
Let E be “reads English” and B be “reads Bangla”. Then P(E)=0.75, P(B)=0.50 and P(E\cap B)=0.40. By the addition rule,
P(E\cup B)=0.75+0.50-0.40=0.85 .
By De Morgan, “reads neither” is the complement of “reads at least one”, so P(\text{neither})=1-0.85=0.15. So 85% read at least one paper and 15% read neither.

5. Counting: permutations and combinations
When the outcomes are equally likely we need to count them, and counting is done with the multiplication principle, permutations and combinations.
The multiplication principle says that if one job can be done in m ways and, after it, a second job can be done in n ways, then the two jobs together can be done in m\times n ways. This is why two dice give 6\times 6=36 outcomes.


                  
                  Memorize: Permutation and combination 
                  
                

A permutation is an arrangement where order matters. The number of ways to arrange r objects chosen from n distinct objects is
^nP_r=\frac{n!}{(n-r)!}.
A combination is a selection where order does not matter. The number of ways to choose r objects from n is
^nC_r=\binom{n}{r}=\frac{n!}{r!\,(n-r)!}.


The way to decide which to use is to ask yourself, “If I swap two of the chosen objects, do I get a different result?” Electing a president, vice-president and secretary from 5 members is a permutation, because swapping the president and the secretary gives a different committee: ^5P_3 = 5!/2! = 60 ways. Choosing a team of 3 from 5 members is a combination, because the same three people form the same team in any order: ^5C_3=10 ways.


                  
                  Exam trick: "drawn at random" from a bag 
                  
                

In almost every bag problem (balls, pens, cars, markers), the items are drawn together or without replacement and their order is irrelevant, so you use combinations. The probability of getting exactly x items of type 1 and y items of type 2 is
P=\frac{\binom{\text{type-1 total}}{x}\binom{\text{type-2 total}}{y}\binom{\text{others}}{\text{rest}}}{\binom{\text{all items}}{\text{sample size}}} .
This one formula is behind 2021-22 Q6(c) (hypergeometric), 2023-24 Q2(b) (joint distribution of pens) and many lecture problems.


Worked example. A bag contains 10 balls of which 4 are black and 6 are white. Three balls are drawn at random without replacement. Find the probability that exactly 2 are black.
The total number of ways to choose 3 balls from 10 is \binom{10}{3}=120. To get exactly 2 black balls we must choose 2 of the 4 black balls and 1 of the 6 white balls, which can be done in \binom{4}{2}\binom{6}{1}=6\times 6=36 ways. Hence
P(\text{exactly 2 black})=\frac{36}{120}=0.3 .
Worked example. Two cards are drawn from a standard deck of 52 without replacement. Find the probability that both are aces. There are \binom{4}{2}=6 ways to pick two aces and \binom{52}{2}=1326 ways to pick any two cards, so the probability is 6/1326=1/221\approx 0.0045. You can also get the same answer with the multiplication law, \frac{4}{52}\times\frac{3}{51}=\frac{1}{221}, which is a nice check.

6. Odds
Odds compare the chance that an event happens with the chance that it does not happen. They are a ratio, not a probability.


                  
                  Memorize: Odds and probability 
                  
                

If P(A)=p, then the odds in favour of A are \dfrac{p}{1-p} and the odds against A are \dfrac{1-p}{p}. Odds in favour and odds against are reciprocals of each other.
If the odds in favour of A are a:b, then
P(A)=\frac{a}{a+b}, \qquad P(A^c)=\frac{b}{a+b}.


If the odds in favour of red balls are 3:7, then out of every 3+7=10 balls, 3 are red, so P(\text{red})=0.3 and P(\text{blue})=0.7. If the probability of an athlete winning is 0.2, the odds against winning are 0.8/0.2=4, written 4:1, which means for every one chance of winning there are four chances of losing.
Worked example (lecture Problem 1). The odds against student X solving a problem are 8:6, and the odds in favour of student Y solving it are 14:16. They work independently. Find the probability that at least one solves the problem.
From “odds against X are 8:6”, we get P(\bar X)=\frac{8}{14}=\frac47 and P(X)=\frac{6}{14}=\frac37. From “odds in favour of Y are 14:16”, we get P(Y)=\frac{14}{30}=\frac{7}{15} and P(\bar Y)=\frac{8}{15}. Since they work independently, the probability that neither solves it is P(\bar X)P(\bar Y)=\frac47\cdot\frac{8}{15}=\frac{32}{105}. Therefore
P(\text{at least one solves})=1-\frac{32}{105}=\frac{73}{105}\approx 0.695 .
The probability that both solve is \frac37\cdot\frac{7}{15}=\frac{1}{5}, and the probability that exactly one solves is \frac{73}{105}-\frac{21}{105}=\frac{52}{105}.

7. Joint probability tables
When we classify people by two characteristics, it is very helpful to arrange the probabilities in a two-way table. The inside cells are joint probabilities like P(A\cap B), and the row and column totals are the single (marginal) probabilities. This is exactly the structure that becomes a joint probability distribution in P4 Joint Marginal and Conditional Distributions.
Worked example (lecture Problem 3). A class contains 10 men and 20 women. Half of the men and half of the women have brown eyes. Find the probability that a person chosen at random is a man or has brown eyes.
There are 30 people, 10 men, and 5+10=15 brown-eyed people, of whom 5 are men. So P(M)=\frac{10}{30}, P(Br)=\frac{15}{30} and P(M\cap Br)=\frac{5}{30}. Then
P(M\cup Br)=\frac{10}{30}+\frac{15}{30}-\frac{5}{30}=\frac{20}{30}=\frac23 .



                  
                  Self-check 
                  
                

1. A die is rolled. Are “even” and “greater than 3” mutually exclusive? No: they share 4 and 6.
2. P(A)=0.5, P(B)=0.4, P(A\cup B)=0.7. Find P(A\cap B). 0.5+0.4-0.7=0.2.
3. How many ways can 2 pens be chosen from 8? \binom82=28.
4. Odds in favour of an event are 5:3. What is its probability? 5/8.
5. Why use 1-P(\text{none}) for “at least one”? Because “none” is a single simple case, while “at least one” splits into many cases.

P2 · Conditional Probability, Independence and Bayes’ Rule


                  
                  Why this matters for the term final 
                  
                

This is the single most reliable topic in Section A. It appeared in 2019-20 Q7(a) (truth serum, Bayes), 2022-23 Q1(a) (transfer a ball from bag 1 to bag 2) and Q1(b) (three machines, Bayes), and 2023-24 Q1(a) (can events be mutually exclusive and independent?), Q1(b) (define the multiplication law, then a ball-transfer problem) and Q1(c) (opinion poll, Bayes). Expect at least one full question of 30–35 marks from this note. The 2022-23 and 2023-24 versions are solved in TF 2022-23 Solutions and TF 2023-24 Solutions; here you learn the method and practise on similar problems.



1. Conditional probability
Very often we learn some information before we compute a probability. The conditional probability of A given B, written P(A\mid B), is the probability that A occurs when we already know that B has occurred. Knowing that B happened shrinks the sample space down to B, and inside this smaller space we look at the part where A also happens, which is A\cap B.


                  
                  Memorize: Conditional probability 
                  
                

P(A\mid B)=\frac{P(A\cap B)}{P(B)}, \qquad P(B)\neq 0 .
Read P(A\mid B) as “the probability of A given B“. In general P(A\mid B)\neq P(B\mid A) and P(A\mid B)\ne P(A).


Worked example (lecture Problem 01). A pair of dice is thrown. Find the probability that the sum is 10 or more, given that a 5 appears on the first die.
Let A be “sum is 10 or more” and B be “first die shows 5”. The event B contains 6 outcomes, (5,1),\dots,(5,6), so P(B)=6/36. Among these, only (5,5) and (5,6) have a sum of 10 or more, so P(A\cap B)=2/36. Therefore
P(A\mid B)=\frac{2/36}{6/36}=\frac13 .

2. The multiplication law (law of compound probability)
If we rearrange the definition of conditional probability, we get a rule for the probability that two events happen together.


                  
                  Memorize: Multiplication law — definition (asked in 2023-24 Q1(b)) 
                  
                

For two events A and B, the probability of their simultaneous occurrence equals the unconditional probability of one of them multiplied by the conditional probability of the other, given that the first has occurred. Symbolically,
P(A\cap B)=P(A)\,P(B\mid A)=P(B)\,P(A\mid B).
For three events, P(A_1\cap A_2\cap A_3)=P(A_1)\,P(A_2\mid A_1)\,P(A_3\mid A_1\cap A_2), and the pattern continues for k events.
If A and B are independent, the law simplifies to P(A\cap B)=P(A)P(B).


When a question says “define the multiplication law”, write the statement in words, write the formula, mention the independent special case, and give a one-line example such as drawing two cards without replacement: P(\text{both aces})=\frac{4}{52}\cdot\frac{3}{51}.
Worked example (lecture Problem 02). The probability that a married man watches a certain TV show is 0.4, the probability that his wife watches it is 0.5, and the probability that the man watches it given that his wife does is 0.7. Find the probability that both watch, the probability that the wife watches given that the husband does, and the probability that at least one watches.
Let H be “husband watches” and W be “wife watches”. By the multiplication law, P(W\cap H)=P(W)P(H\mid W)=0.5\times 0.7=0.35. Then P(W\mid H)=\frac{P(W\cap H)}{P(H)}=\frac{0.35}{0.40}=0.875. Finally, by the addition rule, P(W\cup H)=0.5+0.4-0.35=0.55.

3. Independent events
Two events are independent if the occurrence of one does not change the probability of the other, that is P(A\mid B)=P(A). Substituting into the multiplication law gives the working test.


                  
                  Memorize: Independence 
                  
                

A and B are independent if and only if
P(A\cap B)=P(A)\,P(B).
If A and B are independent, then so are A and B^c, A^c and B, and A^c and B^c.


Tossing a coin and rolling a die are independent experiments, so P(H \text{ and } 6)=\frac12\cdot\frac16=\frac1{12}. Drawing two cards without replacement is a dependent situation, because the first card changes what is left in the deck.
Can two events be mutually exclusive and independent at the same time? (2023-24 Q1(a))


                  
                  Memorize: The answer and the justification 
                  
                

Suppose A and B are mutually exclusive, so A\cap B=\emptyset and P(A\cap B)=0. If they were also independent we would need P(A\cap B)=P(A)P(B), that is 0=P(A)P(B). This is only possible if P(A)=0 or P(B)=0.
So two events with non-zero probabilities can never be both mutually exclusive and independent. In fact, mutually exclusive events with positive probabilities are strongly dependent: if A happens, we know for certain that B did not happen, so P(B\mid A)=0\neq P(B). The only exception is the trivial case where at least one of the events has probability zero (for example an impossible event), which is independent of everything and also disjoint from everything.


A simple illustration helps in the exam. When a die is rolled, let A=\{1\} and B=\{2\}. They are mutually exclusive. But P(A)P(B)=\frac1{36}\ne 0=P(A\cap B), so they are not independent. Knowing that a 1 appeared tells us for sure that 2 did not appear.

4. The total probability rule
Many problems describe a process in two stages: first something happens that can go several ways (which machine, which party, which bag, which colour was transferred), and then the event of interest happens with a probability that depends on the first stage. The total probability rule adds up all the routes.


                  
                  Memorize: Theorem of total probability 
                  
                

If B_1,B_2,\dots,B_k form a partition of the sample space (mutually exclusive and exhaustive, each with P(B_i)>0), then for any event A,
P(A)=\sum_{i=1}^{k}P(B_i)\,P(A\mid B_i)=P(B_1)P(A\mid B_1)+\cdots+P(B_k)P(A\mid B_k).


The logic is simple. The event A can happen together with B_1, or together with B_2, and so on; these pieces do not overlap, so we add them, and each piece is computed with the multiplication law.
Ball-transfer problems
The classic exam form is: “One ball is transferred unseen from bag 1 to bag 2, then a ball is drawn from bag 2.” The first stage (the colour of the transferred ball) is the partition. The trick is to remember that after the transfer, bag 2 has one more ball than before, and one more of the transferred colour.
Fresh practice (similar to 2022-23 Q1(a) and 2023-24 Q1(b)). Bag I contains 6 red and 4 green balls. Bag II contains 3 red and 7 green balls. One ball is drawn from Bag I and placed unseen in Bag II. A ball is then drawn from Bag II. What is the probability that it is red?
Let R_1 be “the transferred ball is red” and G_1 be “the transferred ball is green”. These two events form a partition, with P(R_1)=\frac{6}{10} and P(G_1)=\frac{4}{10}. Let R_2 be “the ball drawn from Bag II is red”.
If a red ball was transferred, Bag II now has 3+1=4 red balls out of 10+1=11, so P(R_2\mid R_1)=\frac{4}{11}. If a green ball was transferred, Bag II still has 3 red balls out of 11, so P(R_2\mid G_1)=\frac{3}{11}. By the total probability rule,
P(R_2)=\frac{6}{10}\cdot\frac{4}{11}+\frac{4}{10}\cdot\frac{3}{11}=\frac{24+12}{110}=\frac{36}{110}=\frac{18}{55}\approx 0.3273 .
The same tree, drawn as a diagram, looks like this. Multiply along each branch and add the branches that end in the event you want.
flowchart LR
    S((Start)) -- "6/10" --> R1["Red transferred<br/>Bag II: 4R, 7G"]
    S -- "4/10" --> G1["Green transferred<br/>Bag II: 3R, 8G"]
    R1 -- "4/11" --> A1["Red drawn: 24/110"]
    R1 -- "7/11" --> A2["Green drawn"]
    G1 -- "3/11" --> A3["Red drawn: 12/110"]
    G1 -- "8/11" --> A4["Green drawn"]



                  
                  Exam trick 
                  
                

Always write a sentence that defines your events before you write numbers (“Let W_1 be the event that a white ball is transferred…”). Examiners give marks for clear event definitions, and it stops you from mixing up P(A\mid B) and P(B\mid A).



5. Bayes’ rule
Bayes’ rule answers the reverse question. We observe the final result (the product is defective, the person did not vote, the serum says guilty) and want the probability that it came through a particular route B_r.


                  
                  Memorize: Bayes' theorem 
                  
                

If B_1,\dots,B_k form a partition of S with P(B_i)>0, and P(A)>0, then
P(B_r\mid A)=\frac{P(B_r)\,P(A\mid B_r)}{\sum_{i=1}^{k}P(B_i)\,P(A\mid B_i)}=\frac{P(B_r)\,P(A\mid B_r)}{P(A)} .
In words: ==posterior = (prior × likelihood of that route) ÷ (total probability of the observed result)==. The numerator is just one branch of the tree; the denominator is the sum of all branches that lead to A.




                  
                  A five-step routine for every Bayes question 
                  
                

Step 1, define the partition events B_1,\dots,B_k and write their prior probabilities, which must add to 1. Step 2, define the observed event A and write P(A\mid B_i) for each i. Be careful when the question gives the opposite event: if it says “65% of party A supporters voted” and the person did not vote, you need P(\text{not voted}\mid A)=0.35. Step 3, compute each product P(B_i)P(A\mid B_i). Step 4, add them to get P(A). Step 5, divide each product by P(A). As a final check, the posteriors must add to 1.


Past TF solved: 2019-20 Q7(a)


                  
                  Past TF 2019-20 Q7(a) (17 marks) — the truth serum 
                  
                

Setting up. Let G be the event that the suspect is guilty and I the event that the suspect is innocent. Only 5% of the group have ever committed a crime, so the priors are P(G)=0.05 and P(I)=0.95. Let J be the event that the serum judges the suspect guilty. The serum judges 90% of guilty suspects properly, so P(J\mid G)=0.90. Innocent suspects are misjudged (that is, judged guilty) 1% of the time, so P(J\mid I)=0.01.
Total probability that the serum says guilty.
P(J)=P(G)P(J\mid G)+P(I)P(J\mid I)=0.05(0.90)+0.95(0.01)=0.045+0.0095=0.0545 .
Bayes’ rule. We want the probability that he is innocent although the serum says guilty:
P(I\mid J)=\frac{P(I)P(J\mid I)}{P(J)}=\frac{0.0095}{0.0545}=0.1743 .
Comment. About 17.4% of the suspects whom the serum labels guilty are actually innocent. Although the serum is wrong only 1% of the time for an innocent person, innocent people are so much more common (95%) that they make up a noticeable share of the “guilty” verdicts.


Fresh practice in the style of 2022-23 Q1(b)
A factory buys a component from three suppliers S_1, S_2, S_3 in the proportions 50%, 30% and 20%. From past records, 1%, 4% and 5% of their components are defective. A component is picked at random and found to be defective. Find the probability that it came from each supplier.
The priors are P(S_1)=0.5, P(S_2)=0.3, P(S_3)=0.2, and the likelihoods are P(D\mid S_1)=0.01, P(D\mid S_2)=0.04, P(D\mid S_3)=0.05. The branch products are 0.5(0.01)=0.005, 0.3(0.04)=0.012 and 0.2(0.05)=0.010, so
P(D)=0.005+0.012+0.010=0.027 .
Then by Bayes’ rule,
P(S_1\mid D)=\frac{0.005}{0.027}=0.1852,\qquad P(S_2\mid D)=\frac{0.012}{0.027}=0.4444,\qquad P(S_3\mid D)=\frac{0.010}{0.027}=0.3704 .
These add to 1, as they must. Notice that supplier S_1 provides half the components but only about 18.5% of the defective ones, because its defect rate is low.
Fresh practice in the style of 2023-24 Q1(c) (the “complement” twist)
Using the same factory, suppose instead that the component is found to be not defective. Find the probability that it came from each supplier.
Now the observed event is D^c, so we need P(D^c\mid S_1)=0.99, P(D^c\mid S_2)=0.96, P(D^c\mid S_3)=0.95. The branch products are 0.495, 0.288 and 0.190, giving P(D^c)=0.973 (which also equals 1-0.027, a good check). Hence
P(S_1\mid D^c)=\frac{0.495}{0.973}=0.5087,\qquad P(S_2\mid D^c)=\frac{0.288}{0.973}=0.2960,\qquad P(S_3\mid D^c)=\frac{0.190}{0.973}=0.1953 .


                  
                  Common mistake 
                  
                

In questions like 2023-24 Q1(c), the data are given as “65% of A supporters turned up to vote”, but the person chosen did not vote. Students often plug in 0.65 instead of 1-0.65=0.35. Always ask yourself which event was actually observed, and use the probability of that event under each route.





                  
                  Self-check 
                  
                

1. State the multiplication law in words. The probability that two events occur together equals the probability of one times the conditional probability of the other given the first.
2. P(A)=0.3, P(B)=0.4, A and B independent. Find P(A\cup B). 0.3+0.4-0.12=0.58.
3. Can events with P(A)=0.2, P(B)=0.3 be both disjoint and independent? No, since 0\ne 0.06.
4. In Bayes’ rule, what is the denominator? The total probability of the observed event, the sum over all branches.
5. After transferring one ball into a bag of 11 balls, how many balls does it hold? 12.

P3 · Random Variables, PMF, PDF and CDF


                  
                  Why this matters for the term final 
                  
                

Almost every year has a “density function” question. In 2020-21 Q6(b) you had to find k for f(x)=k(3-x)^2 and compute probabilities; in 2021-22 Q6(c) you had to build a probability distribution and F(x) for a hypergeometric variable; in 2022-23 Q1(c) you had to find the CDF of an exponential density and use it; and in 2023-24 Q2(a) you were given a CDF and asked for a probability using both the CDF and the pdf. The 2022-23 and 2023-24 ones are solved in TF 2022-23 Solutions and TF 2023-24 Solutions. Master the three skills in this note: ==find the constant k, compute a probability as a sum or an area, and move between f(x) and F(x)==.



1. Random variables
A random variable is a rule (a function) that assigns a number to every outcome of a random experiment. We write random variables with capital letters such as X and their particular values with small letters such as x. For example, if a committee of 2 teachers is chosen from 4 men and 3 women, and Y is the number of men chosen, then Y can take the values 0, 1 or 2 depending on the outcome.


                  
                  Memorize: Discrete vs continuous random variables 
                  
                

A discrete random variable can take only a finite or countable list of separate values, such as 0,1,2,\dots (number of calls, number of defective items, number of heads). A continuous random variable can take any value in an interval (weight, waiting time, lifetime of a bulb, temperature).



2. Discrete distributions: the probability mass function
For a discrete random variable, the probability mass function (pmf) gives the probability of each value: f(x)=P(X=x).


                  
                  Memorize: Conditions for a valid pmf 
                  
                

f(x)\ge 0 \text{ for every } x, \qquad \sum_x f(x)=1, \qquad P(X=x)=f(x).


Worked example (lecture). A fair coin is tossed three times and X is the number of heads. The eight equally likely outcomes give P(X=0)=\frac18, P(X=1)=\frac38, P(X=2)=\frac38, P(X=3)=\frac18. These are all non-negative and add to 1, so this is a valid pmf.
Finding k in a pmf. If f(x)=kx for x=1,2,3,4, then k(1+2+3+4)=1, so 10k=1 and k=\frac1{10}. The method is always the same: add up all the probabilities, set the total equal to 1 and solve.

3. Continuous distributions: the probability density function
For a continuous random variable, the probability of any single exact value is zero, so we cannot list probabilities value by value. Instead we use a probability density function (pdf) f(x), and probabilities are areas under the curve.



                  
                  Memorize: Conditions for a valid pdf and how to use it 
                  
                

f(x)\ge 0, \qquad \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f(x)\,dx=1, \qquad P(a<X<b)=\int_a^b f(x)\,dx .
For a continuous variable, P(X=a)=0, so P(a<X<b)=P(a\le X\le b)=P(a\le X<b). The "<" or "\le" does not matter.


To find an unknown constant k in a pdf, integrate f(x) over the whole range where it is non-zero, set the answer equal to 1, and solve for k.

4. The cumulative distribution function (CDF)
The cumulative distribution function gives the probability that X is at most x:
F(x)=P(X\le x).


                  
                  Memorize: CDF formulas and properties 
                  
                

For a discrete variable, F(x)=\sum_{t\le x}f(t), which is a step function.
For a continuous variable,
F(x)=\int_{-\infty}^{x}f(t)\,dt, \qquad f(x)=\frac{dF(x)}{dx}, \qquad P(a<X\le b)=F(b)-F(a).
Every CDF starts at 0 (as x\to-\infty), ends at 1 (as x\to\infty), and never decreases.


These two relations are the key to questions like 2023-24 Q2(a). If you are given f, integrate to get F. If you are given F, differentiate to get f. Then you can compute the same probability in two ways, once as F(b)-F(a) and once as \int_a^b f(x)dx, and both must agree.


                  
                  Common mistake: units 
                  
                

In the 2023-24 radar question the variable is measured in hours but the question asks about 12 minutes. You must convert first: 12 minutes =12/60=0.2 hours. Always check the units of x before substituting.


Fresh practice: CDF from a pdf. Let f(x)=\frac{x}{2} for 0<x<2 and 0 elsewhere. Find F(x) and P(0.5<X<1.5).
First check validity: \int_0^2 \frac{x}{2}dx=\left[\frac{x^2}{4}\right]_0^2=1. For 0<x<2, F(x)=\int_0^x\frac t2dt=\frac{x^2}{4}. So
F(x)=\begin{cases}0, & x\le 0\\[2pt] \dfrac{x^2}{4}, & 0<x<2\\[4pt] 1, & x\ge 2\end{cases}
Using the CDF, P(0.5<X<1.5)=F(1.5)-F(0.5)=\frac{2.25}{4}-\frac{0.25}{4}=0.5. Using the pdf, \int_{0.5}^{1.5}\frac x2dx=\left[\frac{x^2}{4}\right]_{0.5}^{1.5}=0.5. The two methods agree.
Fresh practice: pdf from a CDF. The time (in hours) until a server receives a request has CDF F(x)=1-e^{-3x} for x\ge0 and 0 otherwise. Find the probability of waiting less than 20 minutes, using both the CDF and the pdf.
Twenty minutes is \frac{20}{60}=\frac13 hour. With the CDF, P(X<\frac13)=F(\frac13)=1-e^{-1}=0.6321. Differentiating, the pdf is f(x)=F'(x)=3e^{-3x} for x\ge 0. With the pdf,
P\left(X<\tfrac13\right)=\int_0^{1/3}3e^{-3x}\,dx=\left[-e^{-3x}\right]_0^{1/3}=1-e^{-1}=0.6321 .

5. Past TF questions solved


                  
                  Past TF 2020-21 Q6(b) (10 marks) — measurement error density 
                  
                

The density is f(x)=k(3-x)^2 for -1\le x\le 1 and 0 elsewhere.
(i) Finding k. The total area must be 1:
\int_{-1}^{1}k(3-x)^2\,dx=k\left[-\frac{(3-x)^3}{3}\right]_{-1}^{1}=k\left(\frac{4^3-2^3}{3}\right)=k\cdot\frac{64-8}{3}=\frac{56k}{3}=1 .
Hence k=\dfrac{3}{56}.
(ii) Error less than \frac12. The error must be between -1 and \frac12:
P\left(X<\tfrac12\right)=\frac{3}{56}\int_{-1}^{1/2}(3-x)^2dx=\frac{3}{56}\cdot\frac{4^3-(2.5)^3}{3}=\frac{64-15.625}{56}=\frac{48.375}{56}=0.8638 .
(iii) Magnitude of the error exceeds 0.8. “Magnitude exceeds 0.8” means |X|>0.8, which is the complement of -0.8\le X\le 0.8:
P(|X|\le 0.8)=\frac{3}{56}\cdot\frac{(3.8)^3-(2.2)^3}{3}=\frac{54.872-10.648}{56}=\frac{44.224}{56}=0.7897,
P(|X|>0.8)=1-0.7897=0.2103 .
Comment. There is about a 21% chance that the error is large enough to be undesirable.




                  
                  Past TF 2021-22 Q6(c) (15 marks) — cars with paint blemishes 
                  
                

A shipment of 5 cars contains 2 with paint blemishes. An agency receives 3 cars at random. Let X be the number of blemished cars received, so X can be 0, 1 or 2. The total number of ways to choose 3 cars from 5 is \binom53=10. Choosing x blemished cars from 2 and 3-x good cars from 3 gives
f(x)=P(X=x)=\frac{\binom{2}{x}\binom{3}{3-x}}{\binom{5}{3}},\qquad x=0,1,2 .
So f(0)=\frac{1\cdot1}{10}=\frac1{10}, f(1)=\frac{2\cdot 3}{10}=\frac35 and f(2)=\frac{1\cdot3}{10}=\frac3{10}. These add to 1.

















x012f(x)1/106/103/10
The cumulative distribution function adds the probabilities up to each point:
F(x)=\begin{cases}0, & x<0\\ 1/10, & 0\le x<1\\ 7/10, & 1\le x<2\\ 1, & x\ge 2\end{cases}
This is a step function that jumps by f(x) at each possible value. This distribution is the hypergeometric distribution, discussed in P6 Bernoulli Binomial Multinomial Hypergeometric Geometric.




                  
                  Exam trick 
                  
                

When you write a discrete CDF, use "\le" on the left and "<" on the right of each interval, as above, and always include the first line (F=0) and the last line (F=1). Missing these two lines is the most common way students lose marks here.





                  
                  Self-check 
                  
                

1. If f(x)=cx^2 on 0<x<3, find c. c\cdot 27/3=1, so c=1/9.
2. For a continuous X, what is P(X=2)? Zero.
3. How do you get f(x) from F(x)? Differentiate.
4. Write P(1<X\le 3) using the CDF. F(3)-F(1).
5. For a discrete CDF, what is the size of the jump at x? P(X=x).

1-Probability/P4-Joint-Marginal-and-Cond.content:
P4 · Joint, Marginal and Conditional Distributions


                  
                  Why this matters for the term final 
                  
                

Joint distributions have been asked in three of the last four years. In 2020-21 Q5(c) you had a joint density k(x^2+y^2) for tyre pressures; in 2022-23 Q2(a) a joint density 10xy^2 on the triangle 0<x<y<1 with marginals and a conditional density; and in 2023-24 Q2(b) (20 marks) a joint pmf built from drawing two pens from a bag, followed by P[(X,Y)\in A], the marginals, \mathrm{Var}(X) and \mathrm{Cov}(X,Y). The last two are solved in TF 2022-23 Solutions and TF 2023-24 Solutions. In this note you learn every one of these steps and practise on fresh examples of exactly the same shape.



1. Joint probability mass function (discrete case)
When two discrete random variables X and Y are observed on the same experiment, their joint pmf gives the probability of each pair of values:
f(x,y)=P(X=x,\;Y=y).


                  
                  Memorize: Properties of a joint pmf 
                  
                

f(x,y)\ge 0,\qquad \sum_x\sum_y f(x,y)=1,\qquad P[(X,Y)\in A]=\sum\sum_{(x,y)\in A} f(x,y).


The joint pmf is usually displayed in a two-way table with x values along one side and y values along the other. The row and column totals of this table are the marginal distributions described below.
2. Joint probability density function (continuous case)
For two continuous random variables, the joint pdf f(x,y) is a surface over the xy-plane, and probabilities are volumes under that surface.


                  
                  Memorize: Properties of a joint pdf 
                  
                

f(x,y)\ge 0,\qquad \int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f(x,y)\,dx\,dy=1,\qquad P[(X,Y)\in A]=\iint_A f(x,y)\,dx\,dy .


To find an unknown constant k, integrate over the whole region where f is non-zero and set the result equal to 1, exactly as for a single variable.
3. Marginal distributions
The marginal distribution of X alone is obtained by “adding up” (summing or integrating) the joint distribution over all values of Y, and vice versa.


                  
                  Memorize: Marginals 
                  
                

Discrete: \displaystyle g(x)=\sum_y f(x,y) and \displaystyle h(y)=\sum_x f(x,y) (the row and column totals of the table).
Continuous: \displaystyle g(x)=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f(x,y)\,dy and \displaystyle h(y)=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f(x,y)\,dx.


4. Conditional distributions
The conditional distribution of Y given X=x tells us how Y behaves when we already know the value of X. It is the joint divided by the marginal of the variable we condition on, which is the same idea as P(A\mid B)=P(A\cap B)/P(B).


                  
                  Memorize: Conditional distributions 
                  
                

f(y\mid x)=\frac{f(x,y)}{g(x)},\quad g(x)>0, \qquad\qquad f(x\mid y)=\frac{f(x,y)}{h(y)},\quad h(y)>0 .
Then P(a<Y<b\mid X=x)=\int_a^b f(y\mid x)\,dy (or a sum in the discrete case).


5. Independence


                  
                  Memorize: Independent random variables 
                  
                

X and Y are independent if and only if
f(x,y)=g(x)\,h(y) \quad\text{for every } (x,y).
To show they are not independent it is enough to find a single pair where this fails. A quick warning sign: if the region where f>0 is not a rectangle (for example a triangle like 0<x<y<1), then X and Y cannot be independent.



6. Regions that are not rectangles
When the support is a triangle such as 0<x<y<1, you must think about the limits of integration carefully. Draw the region first. For a fixed x, the variable y runs from the line y=x up to y=1. For a fixed y, the variable x runs from 0 up to y.



                  
                  Exam trick 
                  
                

Write the limits next to the region before integrating: “for marginal of X, integrate over y from x to 1; for marginal of Y, integrate over x from 0 to y.” Marginals of triangle-shaped densities always contain the variable in the limits, so g(x) usually looks like a polynomial in x with a factor such as (1-x^3).


Fresh practice (same shape as 2022-23 Q2(a)). Let f(x,y)=8xy for 0<y<x<1 and 0 elsewhere. Find the marginals, the conditional density of Y given X=x, and P(Y<\tfrac14\mid X=\tfrac12).
Here the triangle is below the diagonal, so for fixed x the variable y runs from 0 to x, and for fixed y the variable x runs from y to 1.
g(x)=\int_0^x 8xy\,dy=8x\cdot\frac{x^2}{2}=4x^3,\quad 0<x<1 .
h(y)=\int_y^1 8xy\,dx=8y\cdot\frac{1-y^2}{2}=4y(1-y^2),\quad 0<y<1 .
As a check, \int_0^1 4x^3dx=1. The conditional density is
f(y\mid x)=\frac{f(x,y)}{g(x)}=\frac{8xy}{4x^3}=\frac{2y}{x^2},\qquad 0<y<x .
With x=\tfrac12 this is f(y\mid \tfrac12)=8y for 0<y<\tfrac12, so
P\left(Y<\tfrac14\,\middle|\,X=\tfrac12\right)=\int_0^{1/4}8y\,dy=4\left(\tfrac14\right)^2=\tfrac14 .
Since g(x)h(y)=16x^3y(1-y^2)\ne 8xy, the variables are not independent, as expected for a triangular region.

7. Building a joint pmf from a “draw from a bag” experiment
This is the 2023-24 Q2(b) type. The idea is the combination formula from P1 Probability Basics and Counting: to get x items of colour 1 and y items of colour 2 in a sample of size n, we choose them separately and fill the rest of the sample with the third colour.
f(x,y)=\frac{\binom{N_1}{x}\binom{N_2}{y}\binom{N_3}{n-x-y}}{\binom{N}{n}}, \qquad x+y\le n .
Fresh practice. A box contains 4 red, 3 green and 2 white balls. Two balls are drawn at random. Let X be the number of red balls and Y the number of green balls in the sample. (i) Find the joint distribution and show it graphically. (ii) Find P[(X,Y)\in A] where A=\{(x,y): x+y\le 1\}. (iii) Find the marginal distributions. (iv) Find \mathrm{Var}(X). (v) Find \mathrm{Cov}(X,Y).
(i) Joint distribution. There are 9 balls, so the number of possible samples is \binom92=36. Since only 2 balls are drawn, the possible pairs are those with x+y\le 2. For example,
f(1,1)=\frac{\binom41\binom31\binom20}{36}=\frac{12}{36}=\frac13,\qquad f(0,0)=\frac{\binom40\binom30\binom22}{36}=\frac1{36}.
Doing this for every pair gives the table.








































f(x,y)y=0y=1y=2g(x)x=01/366/363/3610/36 = 5/18x=18/3612/36020/36 = 5/9x=26/36006/36 = 1/6h(y)15/36 = 5/1218/36 = 1/23/36 = 1/121
All entries add to 36/36=1. To “plot f(x,y) versus (x,y)”, draw the x and y axes on the floor, mark each of the six points (0,0),(0,1),(0,2),(1,0),(1,1),(2,0), and at each point draw a vertical stick whose height is f(x,y). The tallest stick is at (1,1) with height 1/3.
(ii) The pairs with x+y\le 1 are (0,0), (0,1) and (1,0), so
P[(X,Y)\in A]=\frac{1}{36}+\frac{6}{36}+\frac{8}{36}=\frac{15}{36}=\frac{5}{12}.
(iii) The marginals are the row and column totals of the table: g(0)=\frac5{18}, g(1)=\frac59, g(2)=\frac16; and h(0)=\frac5{12}, h(1)=\frac12, h(2)=\frac1{12}.
(iv) Variance of X. Using the marginal of X,
E(X)=0\cdot\tfrac{5}{18}+1\cdot\tfrac59+2\cdot\tfrac16=\tfrac89,\qquad E(X^2)=0+1\cdot\tfrac59+4\cdot\tfrac16=\tfrac{11}9,
\mathrm{Var}(X)=E(X^2)-[E(X)]^2=\tfrac{11}{9}-\tfrac{64}{81}=\tfrac{35}{81}\approx 0.4321 .
(v) Covariance. We need E(XY)=\sum\sum xy\,f(x,y). Every term with x=0 or y=0 vanishes, and the only remaining pair is (1,1), so E(XY)=1\cdot1\cdot\frac13=\frac13. Also E(Y)=1\cdot\frac12+2\cdot\frac1{12}=\frac23. Hence
\mathrm{Cov}(X,Y)=E(XY)-E(X)E(Y)=\frac13-\frac89\cdot\frac23=\frac{9}{27}-\frac{16}{27}=-\frac{7}{27}\approx -0.2593 .
The covariance is negative, which makes sense: with only two balls drawn, more red balls leaves less room for green balls. As a conditional example, P(X=1\mid Y=1)=\dfrac{f(1,1)}{h(1)}=\dfrac{1/3}{1/2}=\dfrac23.


                  
                  Common mistake 
                  
                

Students often forget the “third colour” factor \binom{N_3}{n-x-y}, or they include impossible cells like (1,2) when only 2 items are drawn. Always check that the table adds to exactly 1.



8. Past TF question solved


                  
                  Past TF 2020-21 Q5(c) (10 marks) — tyre pressures 
                  
                

The joint density is f(x,y)=k(x^2+y^2) for 30\le x<50,\ 30\le y<50, and 0 elsewhere. Here X is the right-tyre pressure and Y the left-tyre pressure, and each should be 40 psi.
(i) Finding k. The region is a square, so we integrate over y first and then over x. For fixed x,
\int_{30}^{50}(x^2+y^2)\,dy=20x^2+\frac{50^3-30^3}{3}=20x^2+\frac{98000}{3}.
Integrating this over x from 30 to 50,
\int_{30}^{50}\left(20x^2+\frac{98000}{3}\right)dx=20\cdot\frac{98000}{3}+20\cdot\frac{98000}{3}=\frac{3{,}920{,}000}{3}.
Setting k\cdot\frac{3{,}920{,}000}{3}=1 gives k=\dfrac{3}{3{,}920{,}000}\approx 7.653\times10^{-7}.
(ii) P(30\le X\le 40,\ 40\le Y<50). For fixed x, \int_{40}^{50}(x^2+y^2)dy=10x^2+\frac{50^3-40^3}{3}=10x^2+\frac{61000}{3}. Then
\int_{30}^{40}\left(10x^2+\frac{61000}{3}\right)dx=10\cdot\frac{40^3-30^3}{3}+10\cdot\frac{61000}{3}=\frac{370000+610000}{3}=\frac{980000}{3}.
So the probability is k\cdot\dfrac{980000}{3}=\dfrac{980000}{3{,}920{,}000}=0.25.
(iii) Both tyres underfilled, meaning both pressures are below 40: 30\le X<40,\ 30\le Y<40. By the same steps,
\int_{30}^{40}\!\!\int_{30}^{40}(x^2+y^2)\,dy\,dx=10\cdot\frac{37000}{3}+10\cdot\frac{37000}{3}=\frac{740000}{3},
so the probability is \dfrac{740000}{3{,}920{,}000}=\dfrac{37}{196}\approx 0.1888.




                  
                  Exam trick 
                  
                

For a square region and a function like x^2+y^2, the two halves of the integral are mirror images. Compute one carefully and double it, but show the line of working so the examiner sees where the factor 2 comes from.





                  
                  Self-check 
                  
                

1. How do you get h(y) from a joint pdf? Integrate f(x,y) over x.
2. What is the formula for f(y\mid x)? f(x,y)/g(x).
3. If the support is 0<x<y<1, can X and Y be independent? No, the region is not a rectangle.
4. In a joint pmf table, where are the marginals? In the row and column totals.
5. Formula for covariance? E(XY)-E(X)E(Y).

1-Probability/P5-Expectation-Variance-Co.content:
P5 · Expectation, Variance, Covariance and Chebyshev’s Theorem


                  
                  Why this matters for the term final 
                  
                

Expectation questions are short, quick marks. 2019-20 Q7(b) asked for E(e^{2X/3}); 2020-21 Q8(a) asked for the average hospital stay E(Y) where Y=X+4; 2022-23 Q2(b) asked for the mean and variance of Y=3X-2, and 2022-23 Q2(c) asked you to compute P(\mu-2\sigma<X<\mu+2\sigma) and compare with Chebyshev’s theorem; 2023-24 Q2(b) asked for a variance and a covariance, and 2023-24 Q3(a) asked you to state Chebyshev’s theorem and use it in a job-selection story. The 2022-23 and 2023-24 versions are solved in TF 2022-23 Solutions and TF 2023-24 Solutions; this note teaches the rules and gives fresh practice of the same type.



1. Expected value (mean) of a random variable
The expected value E(X), also called the mean \mu, is the long-run average value of X if the experiment is repeated many times. It is a weighted average of the possible values, with the probabilities as weights.


                  
                  Memorize: Expected value 
                  
                

\mu=E(X)=\sum_x x\,f(x)\ \ \text{(discrete)},\qquad \mu=E(X)=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}x\,f(x)\,dx\ \ \text{(continuous)}.
For any function g(X),
E[g(X)]=\sum_x g(x)f(x)\quad\text{or}\quad E[g(X)]=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}g(x)f(x)\,dx .


The second formula is very important: you do not need to find the distribution of g(X) first. You simply multiply g(x) by the original density and integrate.
Worked example. Let X have pmf f(0)=0.1,\ f(1)=0.3,\ f(2)=0.4,\ f(3)=0.2. Then E(X)=0(0.1)+1(0.3)+2(0.4)+3(0.2)=1.7, and E(X^2)=0+0.3+1.6+1.8=3.7.
2. Variance and standard deviation
The variance measures how spread out X is around its mean. It is the expected squared distance from the mean.


                  
                  Memorize: Variance 
                  
                

\sigma^2=\mathrm{Var}(X)=E\big[(X-\mu)^2\big]=E(X^2)-\mu^2 ,\qquad \sigma=\sqrt{\mathrm{Var}(X)} .
The shortcut E(X^2)-[E(X)]^2 is almost always easier.


In the example above, \mathrm{Var}(X)=3.7-1.7^2=3.7-2.89=0.81 and \sigma=0.9.
3. Rules for linear functions


                  
                  Memorize: Linear rules 
                  
                

For constants a and b,
E(aX+b)=aE(X)+b,\qquad \mathrm{Var}(aX+b)=a^2\,\mathrm{Var}(X).
Adding a constant shifts the mean but does not change the variance; multiplying by a multiplies the variance by a^2 (not by a). Also, E(X\pm Y)=E(X)\pm E(Y) always, and
\mathrm{Var}(aX+bY)=a^2\mathrm{Var}(X)+b^2\mathrm{Var}(Y)+2ab\,\mathrm{Cov}(X,Y).


These rules solve 2022-23 Q2(b) type questions instantly. For example, if E(X)=5 and \mathrm{Var}(X)=4, and Y=2X-3, then E(Y)=2(5)-3=7 and \mathrm{Var}(Y)=4\times4=16. A full exponential version is practised in P9 Uniform Exponential and Other Continuous Distributions.


                  
                  Common mistake 
                  
                

\mathrm{Var}(3X-2) is 9\,\mathrm{Var}(X), not 3\,\mathrm{Var}(X)-2 and not 9\,\mathrm{Var}(X)-2. The constant disappears and the multiplier is squared.


4. Covariance and correlation of two random variables
The covariance measures how two random variables move together. A positive covariance means large values of X tend to come with large values of Y; a negative covariance means large X tends to come with small Y.


                  
                  Memorize: Covariance 
                  
                

\sigma_{XY}=\mathrm{Cov}(X,Y)=E\big[(X-\mu_X)(Y-\mu_Y)\big]=E(XY)-\mu_X\mu_Y ,
where E(XY)=\sum_x\sum_y xy\,f(x,y) (discrete) or \iint xy\,f(x,y)\,dx\,dy (continuous). The correlation coefficient is \rho_{XY}=\dfrac{\sigma_{XY}}{\sigma_X\sigma_Y}, which always lies between -1 and 1.
If X and Y are independent, then E(XY)=E(X)E(Y) and so \mathrm{Cov}(X,Y)=0. The converse is not true: zero covariance does not prove independence.


A complete covariance calculation from a joint table is worked in P4 Joint Marginal and Conditional Distributions.

5. Chebyshev’s theorem
Sometimes we know only the mean and standard deviation of a variable, not its distribution. Chebyshev’s theorem still gives a guaranteed lower bound on how much probability lies near the mean.


                  
                  Memorize: Chebyshev's theorem — statement (asked in 2023-24 Q3(a)) 
                  
                

==The probability that any random variable X will assume a value within k standard deviations of the mean is at least 1-\dfrac{1}{k^2}.== That is, for any k>1,
P(\mu-k\sigma<X<\mu+k\sigma)\ \ge\ 1-\frac{1}{k^2},\qquad\text{equivalently}\qquad P(|X-\mu|\ge k\sigma)\ \le\ \frac1{k^2}.
With k=2 at least \frac34=75\% of the probability lies within 2\sigma; with k=3 at least \frac89\approx 88.9\% lies within 3\sigma. It holds for every distribution, which is why it is only a bound and is usually quite conservative.


Using Chebyshev in a “will I get the job?” story
Fresh practice (same logic as 2023-24 Q3(a)). Fifty jobs are available and 800 applicants take a test. The mean score is 70 and the standard deviation is 5. Assuming the score distribution is symmetric about the mean, can an applicant who scores 85 expect to get a job?
The score 85 is 85-70=15 points above the mean, which is k=15/5=3 standard deviations. By Chebyshev, P(|X-70|\ge 15)\le \frac1{9}. This bound covers both tails, below 55 and above 85. Because the distribution is symmetric, the upper tail has at most half of it:
P(X\ge 85)\le \frac{1}{2}\cdot\frac{1}{9}=\frac1{18}.
So at most 800\times\frac{1}{18}\approx 44.4, that is at most about 44 applicants, can score 85 or more. Since 50 jobs are available and at most 44 people can score as high or higher, a person scoring 85 should get a job.


                  
                  Exam trick 
                  
                

The three-line answer pattern is: compute k=\dfrac{\text{score}-\mu}{\sigma}; apply Chebyshev and halve because of symmetry; multiply by the number of applicants and compare with the number of jobs.


Comparing an exact probability with Chebyshev’s bound
Fresh practice (same logic as 2022-23 Q2(c)). Let f(x)=3x^2 for 0<x<1. Compute P(\mu-2\sigma<X<\mu+2\sigma) and compare with Chebyshev’s theorem.
First, \mu=\int_0^1x\cdot3x^2dx=\frac34 and E(X^2)=\int_0^1x^2\cdot3x^2dx=\frac35, so \sigma^2=\frac35-\frac9{16}=\frac{3}{80}=0.0375 and \sigma=0.1936. The interval is \mu\pm2\sigma=(0.3627,\ 1.1373). Because the density is zero above 1, the upper limit is effectively 1, so
P(0.3627<X<1)=\int_{0.3627}^{1}3x^2\,dx=1-(0.3627)^3=1-0.0477=0.9523 .
Chebyshev’s theorem with k=2 only guarantees at least 1-\frac14=0.75. The exact probability 0.9523 is larger, which agrees with the theorem: the bound is always satisfied, but it is not sharp for a particular distribution.

6. Past TF questions solved


                  
                  Past TF 2019-20 Q7(b) (18 marks) — expected value of g(X)=e^{2X/3}
                  
                

The density is f(x)=e^{-x} for x>0 and 0 otherwise. Using E[g(X)]=\int g(x)f(x)\,dx,
E\left(e^{2X/3}\right)=\int_0^{\infty}e^{2x/3}\,e^{-x}\,dx=\int_0^{\infty}e^{-x/3}\,dx=\Big[-3e^{-x/3}\Big]_0^{\infty}=0-(-3)=3 .
So the expected value of g(X) is 3. Notice that we did not need the distribution of g(X) at all.




                  
                  Past TF 2020-21 Q8(a) (10 marks) — average hospital stay 
                  
                

The hospital stay is Y=X+4 where f(x)=\dfrac{32}{(x+4)^3} for x>0. We want E(Y)=E(X+4). Directly,
E(X+4)=\int_0^{\infty}(x+4)\frac{32}{(x+4)^3}\,dx=32\int_0^{\infty}(x+4)^{-2}\,dx=32\left[-\frac{1}{x+4}\right]_0^{\infty}=32\cdot\frac14=8 .
Equivalently, E(X)=4 and E(Y)=E(X)+4=8. So a patient is hospitalized for 8 days on average.





                  
                  Self-check 
                  
                

1. E(X)=3, \mathrm{Var}(X)=2. Find E(4X+1) and \mathrm{Var}(4X+1). 13 and 32.
2. What does Chebyshev guarantee for k=3? At least 8/9 of the probability is within 3\sigma.
3. If \mathrm{Cov}(X,Y)=0, are X and Y independent? Not necessarily.
4. Shortcut formula for variance? E(X^2)-[E(X)]^2.
5. Why halve Chebyshev’s bound in the job problem? Symmetry puts at most half of the tail probability on the high side.

1-Probability/P6-Bernoulli-Binomial-Mult.content:
P6 · Bernoulli, Binomial, Multinomial, Hypergeometric and Geometric Distributions


                  
                  Why this matters for the term final 
                  
                

Discrete distributions are tested every single year. 2020-21 asked a geometric/negative binomial question (Q6(c), the “fifth prescription”) and a binomial question on diodes (Q7(a)); 2021-22 asked a binomial lottery question (Q6(a)), a multinomial question (Q6(b)) and a hypergeometric distribution (Q6(c)); 2022-23 Q3(c)(iii) used the binomial on top of a normal probability; and 2023-24 Q3(c) (12 marks) was a pure binomial question with “at least”, “from … to” and “exactly … die”. The 2022-23 and 2023-24 parts are solved in TF 2022-23 Solutions and TF 2023-24 Solutions. The key skill is recognising which distribution the story describes.




1. Bernoulli trials and the Bernoulli distribution
A Bernoulli trial is a single experiment with exactly two outcomes, called “success” and “failure”, with P(\text{success})=p and P(\text{failure})=q=1-p. A Bernoulli process is a sequence of such trials in which the trials are independent and p stays the same from trial to trial.
If X=1 for success and X=0 for failure, then X has the Bernoulli distribution f(x)=p^xq^{1-x} for x=0,1, with E(X)=p and \mathrm{Var}(X)=pq. The binomial distribution with n=1 is exactly the Bernoulli distribution.
2. The binomial distribution


                  
                  Memorize: Binomial distribution 
                  
                

If a Bernoulli trial with success probability p is repeated n times independently, the number of successes X has the binomial distribution
b(x;n,p)=\binom{n}{x}p^x q^{\,n-x},\qquad x=0,1,2,\dots,n,\quad q=1-p .
Its mean and variance are
\mu=np,\qquad \sigma^2=npq .
Use it when four conditions hold: a ==fixed number of trials n, two outcomes per trial, constant p, and independent trials==.


The reason for the formula is simple. A particular arrangement with x successes and n-x failures has probability p^xq^{n-x} by independence, and there are \binom nx ways to choose which x of the n trials are the successes.
Derivation of the mean and variance
Using x\binom nx=n\binom{n-1}{x-1},
E(X)=\sum_{x=0}^{n}x\binom nx p^xq^{n-x}=np\sum_{x=1}^{n}\binom{n-1}{x-1}p^{x-1}q^{n-x}=np\,(p+q)^{n-1}=np .
For the variance it is easiest to find E[X(X-1)] first, using x(x-1)\binom nx=n(n-1)\binom{n-2}{x-2}:
E[X(X-1)]=n(n-1)p^2\sum_{x=2}^{n}\binom{n-2}{x-2}p^{x-2}q^{n-x}=n(n-1)p^2 .
Then E(X^2)=E[X(X-1)]+E(X)=n(n-1)p^2+np, and
\mathrm{Var}(X)=n(n-1)p^2+np-n^2p^2=np-np^2=np(1-p)=npq .
A quicker argument: X is the sum of n independent Bernoulli variables, each with mean p and variance pq, so the means and variances add to give np and npq.


                  
                  Exam trick: translating words into x values
                  
                

“At least 10” means x\ge 10, which is 1-P(X\le 9). “From 3 to 8” means 3\le x\le 8, which is P(X\le8)-P(X\le2). “At most 2” means x\le 2. “Exactly 5 die” when X counts survivors among 15 means exactly 15-5=10 survive. Always state clearly what X counts, then translate the words.


Fresh practice (same shape as 2023-24 Q3(c)). The probability that a patient recovers from a certain illness is 0.3. If 12 people have the illness, find the probability that (i) at least 8 recover, (ii) from 2 to 5 recover, (iii) exactly 4 die.
Let X be the number who recover; then X\sim b(x;12,0.3). Using the binomial formula (or the cumulative binomial table),
P(X\ge 8)=\sum_{x=8}^{12}\binom{12}{x}(0.3)^x(0.7)^{12-x}=0.0095 ,
P(2\le X\le 5)=P(X\le5)-P(X\le1)=0.7971 .
Exactly 4 die means exactly 8 recover:
P(X=8)=\binom{12}{8}(0.3)^8(0.7)^4=495\times 0.00006561\times 0.2401=0.0078 .
Past TF questions solved


                  
                  Past TF 2021-22 Q6(a) (10 marks) — lottery tickets 
                  
                

Out of 500 tickets, 200 pay back at least their cost, so for each ticket p=\frac{200}{500}=0.4 and q=0.6. Buying 5 tickets gives n=5 (we treat the tickets as independent, since 5 is tiny compared with 500). Let X be the number of tickets that win back at least their cost. We need P(X\ge3):
P(X=3)=\binom53(0.4)^3(0.6)^2=10(0.064)(0.36)=0.2304,
P(X=4)=\binom54(0.4)^4(0.6)=5(0.0256)(0.6)=0.0768,\qquad P(X=5)=(0.4)^5=0.01024 .
P(X\ge3)=0.2304+0.0768+0.01024=0.3174 .




                  
                  Past TF 2020-21 Q7(a) (17 marks) — diode failures on a circuit board 
                  
                

Each of the n=200 diodes fails independently with p=0.03, so the number of failures X is binomial with n=200, p=0.03, q=0.97.
(i) Mean: \mu=np=200(0.03)=6 failures.
(ii) Variance: \sigma^2=npq=200(0.03)(0.97)=5.82, so \sigma=2.41.
(iii) The board works only if no diode fails:
P(X=0)=\binom{200}{0}(0.03)^0(0.97)^{200}=(0.97)^{200}=0.00226 .
Comment. The board will almost never work. As a check, the Poisson approximation with \lambda=np=6 gives e^{-6}=0.00248, which is close (see P7 Poisson Distribution and Poisson Process).



3. The multinomial distribution
The binomial distribution has two outcomes per trial. If each trial can end in one of k outcomes with probabilities p_1,\dots,p_k (adding to 1), the counts X_1,\dots,X_k in n independent trials follow the multinomial distribution.


                  
                  Memorize: Multinomial distribution 
                  
                

f(x_1,\dots,x_k;\,p_1,\dots,p_k,n)=\frac{n!}{x_1!\,x_2!\cdots x_k!}\;p_1^{x_1}p_2^{x_2}\cdots p_k^{x_k},\qquad \sum x_i=n,\ \ \sum p_i=1 .




                  
                  Past TF 2021-22 Q6(b) (10 marks) — how delegates arrived 
                  
                

The probabilities of arriving by air, bus, automobile and train are 0.4,\ 0.2,\ 0.3,\ 0.1. Among n=9 delegates we want 3 by air, 3 by bus, 1 by automobile and 2 by train (check: 3+3+1+2=9).
P=\frac{9!}{3!\,3!\,1!\,2!}(0.4)^3(0.2)^3(0.3)^1(0.1)^2=\frac{362880}{72}\times0.064\times0.008\times0.3\times0.01 .
The coefficient is 5040 and the product of the powers is 1.536\times10^{-6}, so
P=5040\times1.536\times10^{-6}=0.00774 .



4. The hypergeometric distribution
The binomial needs independent trials with constant p. When we sample without replacement from a small finite population, p changes after each draw, and we use the hypergeometric distribution instead.


                  
                  Memorize: Hypergeometric distribution 
                  
                

A population of N items contains k “successes”. A sample of n is drawn without replacement. The number of successes X in the sample has
h(x;N,n,k)=\frac{\binom{k}{x}\binom{N-k}{n-x}}{\binom{N}{n}},\qquad \mu=\frac{nk}{N},\qquad \sigma^2=\frac{N-n}{N-1}\cdot n\cdot\frac kN\left(1-\frac kN\right).


The 2021-22 Q6(c) cars problem (N=5, k=2, n=3) is solved step by step in P3 Random Variables PMF PDF CDF; its mean is \frac{3\times2}{5}=1.2, which matches 0(0.1)+1(0.6)+2(0.3)=1.2. When n is small compared with N (say n/N\le 0.05), the hypergeometric is well approximated by the binomial with p=k/N, which is why the lottery question above could use the binomial.

5. Geometric and negative binomial distributions
Sometimes the number of trials is not fixed; instead we keep going until we obtain a certain number of successes. Then the random variable is the trial number on which a success occurs.


                  
                  Memorize: Negative binomial and geometric 
                  
                

The probability that the k-th success occurs on the x-th trial is the negative binomial distribution
b^*(x;k,p)=\binom{x-1}{k-1}p^k q^{\,x-k},\qquad x=k,k+1,\dots
The reasoning: the x-th trial must be a success, and among the first x-1 trials there must be exactly k-1 successes.
The special case k=1 (the first success occurs on trial x) is the geometric distribution
g(x;p)=p\,q^{\,x-1},\qquad x=1,2,\dots,\qquad \mu=\frac1p,\qquad \sigma^2=\frac{q}{p^2}.




                  
                  Past TF 2020-21 Q6(c) (10 marks) — Valium prescriptions 
                  
                

Two-thirds of Valium users are women, so a prescription is “for a woman” (success) with p=\frac23 and q=\frac13. Prescriptions are treated as independent trials.
(i) The fifth prescription is the first one for a woman. The first four must be for men and the fifth for a woman, which is geometric with x=5:
g(5;\tfrac23)=\left(\tfrac23\right)\left(\tfrac13\right)^4=\frac{2}{243}=0.00823 .
(ii) The fifth prescription is the third one for a woman. This is negative binomial with k=3, x=5: among the first four there are exactly two for women, and the fifth is for a woman:
b^*(5;3,\tfrac23)=\binom{4}{2}\left(\tfrac23\right)^3\left(\tfrac13\right)^2=6\cdot\frac{8}{27}\cdot\frac19=\frac{48}{243}=0.1975 .




                  
                  Common mistake 
                  
                

Do not use \binom{5}{3} in part (ii). The last trial is forced to be a success, so only the first x-1=4 trials are free to be arranged, giving \binom{4}{2}.



6. How to recognise the distribution quickly
Read the story and ask a few questions in order. If there is a fixed number of independent trials with two outcomes and constant p, it is binomial. If each trial has more than two outcomes and you want counts of each, it is multinomial. If you draw without replacement from a small population that contains a known number of successes, it is hypergeometric. If you count trials until the first (or the k-th) success, it is geometric (or negative binomial). If you count events in an interval of time or space at an average rate, or n is huge and p is tiny, it is Poisson, covered in P7 Poisson Distribution and Poisson Process.



                  
                  Self-check 
                  
                

1. Mean and variance of b(x;20,0.25)? 5 and 3.75.
2. “At least 10 out of 15” in terms of the CDF? 1-P(X\le 9).
3. Probability the first head appears on the 4th toss of a fair coin? (1/2)^4=1/16.
4. When does hypergeometric become binomial? When the sample is small relative to the population.
5. Multinomial coefficient for counts 2, 1, 1 out of 4? 4!/(2!1!1!)=12.

1-Probability/P7-Poisson-Distribution-an.content:
P7 · Poisson Distribution and the Poisson Process


                  
                  Why this matters for the term final 
                  
                

The Poisson distribution is a favourite for both theory and calculation. 2019-20 Q8(a) used the Poisson approximation for glass bubbles; 2022-23 Q3(a) asked you to discuss the Bernoulli and Poisson processes and derive the Poisson distribution, and Q3(b) asked you to calculate the variance of a Poisson variable and then approximate a binomial; 2023-24 Q3(b) asked you to establish the relation between the binomial and Poisson distributions and then compute a call-arrival probability. These derivations are pure memory marks, so learn them line by line. The 2022-23 and 2023-24 numerical parts are solved in TF 2022-23 Solutions and TF 2023-24 Solutions.



1. Bernoulli process versus Poisson process


                  
                  Memorize: Bernoulli process 
                  
                

A Bernoulli process is a sequence of trials with three properties. First, each trial has only two outcomes, success or failure. Second, the probability of success p remains the same from trial to trial. Third, the trials are independent. The number of successes in n trials of a Bernoulli process is binomial, b(x;n,p).




                  
                  Memorize: Poisson process 
                  
                

A Poisson process describes events that occur randomly in continuous time (or space), such as calls arriving at a switchboard, accidents in a factory, or flaws along a cable. It has three properties. First, the numbers of events in non-overlapping intervals are independent (the process has no memory). Second, the probability of exactly one event in a very short interval is proportional to the length of the interval and does not depend on what happened outside it. Third, the probability of two or more events in a very short interval is negligible. The number of events X in an interval of length t then follows the Poisson distribution with mean \lambda t, where \lambda is the average rate per unit time.


You can think of the Poisson process as the limit of a Bernoulli process in which time is cut into a huge number of tiny pieces, each piece being a trial with a tiny chance of containing an event.
2. The Poisson distribution


                  
                  Memorize: Poisson distribution 
                  
                

p(x;\lambda t)=\frac{e^{-\lambda t}(\lambda t)^x}{x!},\qquad x=0,1,2,\dots
Writing \mu=\lambda t for the average number of events in the interval,
E(X)=\mu,\qquad \mathrm{Var}(X)=\mu .
The mean and the variance are equal; this is the signature of a Poisson variable.




                  
                  Common mistake: scaling the rate 
                  
                

The rate must match the interval in the question. If calls arrive at 0.5 per minute and the question is about a five-minute period, then \mu=0.5\times5=2.5. If accidents happen 3 times per month and the question is about a year, \mu=36.


Fresh practice (same shape as 2023-24 Q3(b)). Requests reach a server at an average rate of 2 per minute. Find the probability that exactly 4 requests arrive in a particular 3-minute period. Here \mu=2\times3=6, so
P(X=4)=\frac{e^{-6}6^4}{4!}=\frac{0.0024788\times1296}{24}=0.1339 .

3. Derivation: the Poisson distribution as the limit of the binomial
This is the derivation asked as “establish the relation between binomial and Poisson” (2023-24 Q3(b)) and “derive the Poisson distribution” (2022-23 Q3(a)).


                  
                  Memorize: Derivation 
                  
                

Let X\sim b(x;n,p), and let n\to\infty and p\to0 in such a way that np=\mu stays fixed. Put p=\mu/n. Then
b(x;n,p)=\frac{n!}{x!\,(n-x)!}\left(\frac{\mu}{n}\right)^x\left(1-\frac{\mu}{n}\right)^{n-x}.
Rearranging the factors,
b(x;n,p)=\frac{\mu^x}{x!}\cdot\frac{n(n-1)\cdots(n-x+1)}{n^x}\cdot\left(1-\frac{\mu}{n}\right)^{n}\cdot\left(1-\frac{\mu}{n}\right)^{-x}.
Now let n\to\infty with x and \mu fixed. The second factor is 1\cdot\left(1-\frac1n\right)\cdots\left(1-\frac{x-1}{n}\right)\to1. The third factor tends to e^{-\mu}, because \lim_{n\to\infty}\left(1-\frac{\mu}{n}\right)^n=e^{-\mu}. The last factor tends to 1. Therefore
\lim_{n\to\infty}b(x;n,p)=\frac{e^{-\mu}\mu^x}{x!}=p(x;\mu),\qquad x=0,1,2,\dots
This shows that ==the Poisson distribution is the limiting form of the binomial when n is large, p is small and np=\mu is moderate==.


Relation in words. Both distributions count successes. The binomial counts successes in a fixed number of trials; the Poisson counts events in a continuous interval. The binomial has mean np and variance npq; when p\to0, q\to1 and the variance npq\to np, which is why the Poisson has equal mean and variance. In practice, use the Poisson approximation when n is large (say n\ge20) and p is small (say p\le0.05), with \mu=np.
To show that the Poisson probabilities form a valid distribution, note that \sum_{x=0}^\infty \frac{e^{-\mu}\mu^x}{x!}=e^{-\mu}e^{\mu}=1, using the series e^\mu=\sum \mu^x/x!.

4. Derivation of the mean and variance


                  
                  Memorize: Mean of the Poisson 
                  
                

E(X)=\sum_{x=0}^{\infty}x\frac{e^{-\mu}\mu^x}{x!}=\mu e^{-\mu}\sum_{x=1}^{\infty}\frac{\mu^{x-1}}{(x-1)!}=\mu e^{-\mu}e^{\mu}=\mu .




                  
                  Memorize: Variance of the Poisson (asked in 2022-23 Q3(b)) 
                  
                

The trick, as the lecture note says, is to compute E[X(X-1)] first, because x(x-1) cancels nicely with x!:
E[X(X-1)]=\sum_{x=2}^{\infty}x(x-1)\frac{e^{-\mu}\mu^x}{x!}=\mu^2e^{-\mu}\sum_{x=2}^{\infty}\frac{\mu^{x-2}}{(x-2)!}=\mu^2 e^{-\mu}e^{\mu}=\mu^2 .
Then E(X^2)=E[X(X-1)]+E(X)=\mu^2+\mu, and
\mathrm{Var}(X)=E(X^2)-[E(X)]^2=\mu^2+\mu-\mu^2=\mu .



5. Poisson approximation to the binomial — worked problems
Fresh practice (same shape as 2022-23 Q3(b)). On average, 1 in every 1000 tickets printed by a machine is misprinted. If 5000 tickets are checked, find the probability that 3, 4 or 5 of them are misprinted.
The exact distribution is binomial with n=5000 and p=0.001, which is awkward to compute, but n is large and p small, so we use the Poisson with \mu=np=5:
p(3;5)=\frac{e^{-5}5^3}{3!}=0.1404,\quad p(4;5)=\frac{e^{-5}5^4}{4!}=0.1755,\quad p(5;5)=\frac{e^{-5}5^5}{5!}=0.1755 .
The required probability is 0.1404+0.1755+0.1755=0.4913.


                  
                  Past TF 2019-20 Q8(a) (10 marks) — glass bubbles 
                  
                

On average 1 in every 1000 items has bubbles, so p=0.001, and the sample has n=8000 items. Since n is large and p is small, the number of defective items X is approximately Poisson with
\mu=np=8000\times0.001=8 .
“Fewer than 7” means X\le6, so we add the Poisson probabilities from 0 to 6:

























x0123456e^{-8}8^x/x!0.00030.00270.01070.02860.05730.09160.1221
P(X<7)=\sum_{x=0}^{6}\frac{e^{-8}8^x}{x!}=0.3134 .
(From the cumulative Poisson table, P(X\le6;\mu=8)=0.3134.) So there is about a 31% chance that fewer than 7 of the 8000 items have bubbles.




                  
                  Exam trick 
                  
                

Compute successive Poisson terms with the recursion p(x)=p(x-1)\cdot\dfrac{\mu}{x}. Start from p(0)=e^{-\mu}, then multiply by \mu/1, \mu/2, \mu/3 and so on. It is much faster and less error-prone on a calculator than recomputing each factorial.





                  
                  Self-check 
                  
                

1. Mean and variance of a Poisson with \mu=4? Both 4.
2. Calls arrive at 3 per hour; what is \mu for 20 minutes? 1.
3. What limit is used in the derivation? (1-\mu/n)^n\to e^{-\mu}.
4. When do we approximate binomial by Poisson? n large, p small, \mu=np.
5. Why compute E[X(X-1)]? Because x(x-1) cancels with x!, giving \mu^2 directly.
