1-Probability/P8-Normal-Distribution.content:
P8 · The Normal Distribution


                  
                  Why this matters for the term final 
                  
                

The normal distribution is the most important continuous distribution in the course and it is used again in every hypothesis test. It appeared in 2020-21 Q7(b) (mice lifetimes), 2021-22 Q7(b) (ball bearings scrapped), 2022-23 Q3(c) (lawyer’s commute, including a percentile and a binomial on top) and Q4(a) (properties of the normal curve; mean, mode and standard deviation; standard normal), and 2023-24 Q4(a) (==show that the mode equals \mu==, then a light-bulb probability). The 2022-23 and 2023-24 ones are solved in TF 2022-23 Solutions and TF 2023-24 Solutions. You must be fast and accurate with the z-table.



1. The normal density


                  
                  Memorize: Normal pdf 
                  
                

A random variable X is normal with mean \mu and variance \sigma^2, written X\sim N(\mu,\sigma^2), if its density is
n(x;\mu,\sigma)=\frac{1}{\sigma\sqrt{2\pi}}\,e^{-\frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{x-\mu}{\sigma}\right)^2},\qquad -\infty<x<\infty .



2. Properties of the normal curve (asked in 2022-23 Q4(a))


                  
                  Memorize: Properties of the normal curve 
                  
                

The normal curve is ==bell-shaped and symmetric about the vertical line x=\mu. Because of this symmetry, the mean, median and mode are all equal to \mu==, and the highest point of the curve is at x=\mu, where the height is \frac{1}{\sigma\sqrt{2\pi}}. The curve has points of inflection at x=\mu\pm\sigma; it is concave downward between them and concave upward outside them. The curve approaches the horizontal axis asymptotically in both directions but never touches it, so X can in principle take any real value. The total area under the curve and above the axis is 1. About 68.27% of the area lies within \mu\pm\sigma, 95.45% within \mu\pm2\sigma and 99.73% within \mu\pm3\sigma (the empirical rule). The coefficient of skewness is 0 and \beta_2=3 (mesokurtic). Finally, the two parameters \mu and \sigma completely determine the curve: \mu fixes the centre and \sigma fixes the spread, so a larger \sigma gives a lower, wider curve.


3. Mean, mode and standard deviation of the normal distribution
The mode is \mu (2023-24 Q4(a))
The mode is the value of x at which the density is largest. Write f(x)=n(x;\mu,\sigma). Differentiating with the chain rule,
f'(x)=\frac{1}{\sigma\sqrt{2\pi}}e^{-\frac12\left(\frac{x-\mu}{\sigma}\right)^2}\cdot\left(-\frac{x-\mu}{\sigma^2}\right)=-\frac{x-\mu}{\sigma^2}\,f(x).
Since f(x)>0 for every x, setting f'(x)=0 gives x-\mu=0, so x=\mu. To confirm it is a maximum, differentiate again:
f''(x)=-\frac{1}{\sigma^2}f(x)+\frac{(x-\mu)^2}{\sigma^4}f(x)=\frac{f(x)}{\sigma^2}\left[\frac{(x-\mu)^2}{\sigma^2}-1\right].
At x=\mu this is -\dfrac{f(\mu)}{\sigma^2}<0, so f has a maximum at x=\mu. Hence ==the mode of the normal distribution is \mu==. As a bonus, f''(x)=0 when (x-\mu)^2=\sigma^2, that is at x=\mu\pm\sigma, which proves the points of inflection.
The mean is \mu
E(X)=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\frac{x}{\sigma\sqrt{2\pi}}e^{-\frac12\left(\frac{x-\mu}{\sigma}\right)^2}dx .
Substitute z=\dfrac{x-\mu}{\sigma}, so x=\mu+\sigma z and dx=\sigma\,dz:
E(X)=\mu\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}e^{-z^2/2}dz+\sigma\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\frac{z}{\sqrt{2\pi}}e^{-z^2/2}dz=\mu(1)+\sigma(0)=\mu .
The first integral is the total area under the standard normal curve, which is 1, and the second is zero because z\,e^{-z^2/2} is an odd function.
The standard deviation is \sigma
With the same substitution,
\mathrm{Var}(X)=E[(X-\mu)^2]=\sigma^2\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\frac{z^2}{\sqrt{2\pi}}e^{-z^2/2}dz .
Integrating by parts with u=z and dv=z\,e^{-z^2/2}dz (so v=-e^{-z^2/2}),
\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}z^2e^{-z^2/2}dz=\Big[-z\,e^{-z^2/2}\Big]_{-\infty}^{\infty}+\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}e^{-z^2/2}dz=0+\sqrt{2\pi}.
So \mathrm{Var}(X)=\sigma^2\cdot\dfrac{\sqrt{2\pi}}{\sqrt{2\pi}}=\sigma^2 and the standard deviation is \sigma. The median is also \mu, because the curve is symmetric about \mu and so exactly half the area lies on each side.
4. The standard normal distribution


                  
                  Memorize: Standardizing 
                  
                

If X\sim N(\mu,\sigma^2), then
Z=\frac{X-\mu}{\sigma}
has the standard normal distribution N(0,1), with mean 0 and variance 1, and density \phi(z)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}e^{-z^2/2}. This follows from the linear rules: E(Z)=\frac{E(X)-\mu}{\sigma}=0 and \mathrm{Var}(Z)=\frac{\mathrm{Var}(X)}{\sigma^2}=1. Every normal probability can therefore be read from one single table.


5. Using the standard normal table
The table attached to the exam paper gives \Phi(z)=P(Z\le z), the area to the left of z.



                  
                  Memorize: Table rules 
                  
                

P(Z\le z)=\Phi(z),\qquad P(Z>z)=1-\Phi(z),\qquad P(a<Z<b)=\Phi(b)-\Phi(a),\qquad \Phi(-z)=1-\Phi(z).


Round z to two decimals, find the row for the first decimal and the column for the second. For example \Phi(1.43) is in row 1.4, column 0.03, giving 0.9236. If your table only has positive z, use \Phi(-z)=1-\Phi(z).


                  
                  Exam trick: always draw the curve 
                  
                

Draw a small bell curve, mark \mu and the x values, shade the area you want, and write the z values under them. This takes ten seconds and prevents the most common error, which is taking the wrong side.


Reverse lookup: finding x for a given probability
If the question gives a probability and asks for a value (a percentile, a cut-off, “the slowest 15%”), you go backwards. Find z in the body of the table such that \Phi(z) equals the required left area, then convert back with
x=\mu+z\sigma .
Fresh practice. Exam scores are N(500,\,50^2). Find P(450<X<620) and the score that cuts off the top 10%.
For the probability, z_1=\frac{450-500}{50}=-1.00 and z_2=\frac{620-500}{50}=2.40. So P=\Phi(2.40)-\Phi(-1.00)=0.9918-0.1587=0.8331.
For the top 10%, the left area is 0.90. The table gives \Phi(1.28)\approx0.8997, so z=1.28 and x=500+1.28(50)=564. Students scoring above 564 are in the top 10%.

6. Normal approximation to the binomial (with continuity correction)
When n is large and p is not too close to 0 or 1 (a common rule is np\ge5 and nq\ge5), the binomial X is approximately normal with \mu=np and \sigma=\sqrt{npq}.


                  
                  Memorize: Continuity correction 
                  
                

The binomial is discrete and the normal is continuous, so each integer x is represented by the interval from x-0.5 to x+0.5. Therefore
P(X\le a)\approx P\!\left(Z\le\frac{a+0.5-np}{\sqrt{npq}}\right),\qquad P(X\ge a)\approx P\!\left(Z\ge\frac{a-0.5-np}{\sqrt{npq}}\right).


Fresh practice. A coin-type process has p=0.3 and n=100. Find P(X\le25). Here \mu=30 and \sigma=\sqrt{100(0.3)(0.7)}=\sqrt{21}=4.583. With the continuity correction,
P(X\le25)\approx P\!\left(Z\le\frac{25.5-30}{4.583}\right)=P(Z\le-0.98)=0.1635 .
The exact binomial answer is 0.1631, so the approximation is very good.

7. Past TF questions solved


                  
                  Past TF 2020-21 Q7(b) (18 marks) — mice lifetimes 
                  
                

Lifetimes are normal with \mu=40 months and \sigma=6.3 months.
(i) More than 32 months. z=\dfrac{32-40}{6.3}=-1.27. Then
P(X>32)=P(Z>-1.27)=1-\Phi(-1.27)=1-0.1020=0.8980 .
(ii) Between 37 and 49 months. z_1=\dfrac{37-40}{6.3}=-0.48 and z_2=\dfrac{49-40}{6.3}=1.43. Then
P(37<X<49)=\Phi(1.43)-\Phi(-0.48)=0.9236-0.3156=0.6080 .
(Without rounding z the answer is 0.6065; either is accepted when you show the table values.) So about 89.8% of mice live more than 32 months and about 61% live between 37 and 49 months.




                  
                  Past TF 2021-22 Q7(b) (15 marks) — ball bearings scrapped 
                  
                

The diameter is X\sim N(3.0,\ 0.005^2) and the specification is 3.0\pm0.01, so a bearing is accepted if 2.99\le X\le3.01 and scrapped otherwise. The z values of the limits are
z_1=\frac{2.99-3.0}{0.005}=-2.0,\qquad z_2=\frac{3.01-3.0}{0.005}=+2.0 .
P(\text{scrapped})=P(Z<-2)+P(Z>2)=2\,\Phi(-2.0)=2(0.0228)=0.0456 .
On average 4.56% of the ball bearings will be scrapped.




                  
                  Common mistake 
                  
                

In “between” questions do not subtract the z values; subtract the areas \Phi(z_2)-\Phi(z_1). And in “more than” questions remember to take 1-\Phi(z), because the table gives the left area.





                  
                  Self-check 
                  
                

1. Where is the mode of N(\mu,\sigma^2) and how do you prove it? At x=\mu; set f'(x)=0 and check f''(\mu)<0.
2. Mean and variance of Z? 0 and 1.
3. \Phi(-1.5) in terms of \Phi(1.5)? 1-\Phi(1.5).
4. What z gives the slowest 15% (upper tail)? z\approx1.04 since \Phi(1.04)\approx0.85.
5. Continuity-corrected form of P(X\ge 40)? P(Z\ge (39.5-np)/\sqrt{npq}).

1-Probability/P9-Uniform-Exponential-and.content:
P9 · Uniform, Exponential and Other Continuous Distributions


                  
                  Why this matters for the term final 
                  
                

The exponential distribution is examined almost every year, often hidden inside a “density function” question. 2019-20 Q8(b) (25 marks) was a five-part exponential question on fire-station calls including the memoryless property; 2022-23 Q1(c) gave the DVD-player lifetime density \frac{1}{2000}e^{-x/2000} and asked for the CDF and two probabilities; 2022-23 Q2(b) asked for the mean and variance of Y=3X-2 when X is exponential with mean 4; and 2023-24 Q2(a) used the exponential CDF 1-e^{-8x}. The 2022-23 and 2023-24 versions are solved in TF 2022-23 Solutions and TF 2023-24 Solutions. The chi-square, t and F distributions introduced briefly here are the tools of S8 Hypothesis Testing Concepts and z t Tests, S9 Chi-Square Tests and S10 ANOVA One-Way and Two-Way.



1. The continuous uniform distribution
The uniform distribution describes a variable that is equally likely to fall anywhere in an interval [A,B]. Its density is flat, like a rectangle.


                  
                  Memorize: Uniform distribution 
                  
                

f(x;A,B)=\frac{1}{B-A},\quad A\le x\le B,\qquad \mu=\frac{A+B}{2},\qquad \sigma^2=\frac{(B-A)^2}{12}.
Probabilities are simply proportional to length: P(c<X<d)=\dfrac{d-c}{B-A} for A\le c<d\le B.


Worked example (Walpole 6.1). A conference room can be reserved for at most 4 hours, and the length of a reservation X is uniform on [0,4]. The probability that a conference lasts at least 3 hours is P(X\ge3)=\frac{4-3}{4}=\frac14. The mean length is \frac{0+4}{2}=2 hours and the variance is \frac{16}{12}=\frac43.

2. The exponential distribution
The exponential distribution models waiting times and lifetimes: the time between calls, the time until a component fails, the time between speeders passing a radar.


                  
                  Memorize: Exponential distribution 
                  
                

X is exponential with mean \beta (equivalently rate \lambda=1/\beta) if
f(x)=\frac{1}{\beta}e^{-x/\beta}=\lambda e^{-\lambda x},\qquad x>0,
and 0 elsewhere. Its CDF and “survival” probability are
F(x)=P(X\le x)=1-e^{-x/\beta},\qquad P(X>x)=e^{-x/\beta}.
Its mean and variance are
\mu=\beta=\frac1\lambda,\qquad \sigma^2=\beta^2=\frac1{\lambda^2}.





                  
                  Exam trick: recognise the parameter 
                  
                

If the density is written \frac{1}{2000}e^{-x/2000}, the mean is \beta=2000. If it is written 8e^{-8x} (or the CDF is 1-e^{-8x}), the rate is \lambda=8 and the mean is \frac18. Always identify \beta first, then everything else follows from the boxed formulas.


Deriving the CDF, mean and variance
The CDF comes from integrating the pdf:
F(x)=\int_0^x\frac1\beta e^{-t/\beta}dt=\Big[-e^{-t/\beta}\Big]_0^x=1-e^{-x/\beta},\qquad x>0 .
For the mean, integrate by parts (or use \int_0^\infty x^{n}e^{-x/\beta}dx=n!\,\beta^{n+1}):
E(X)=\int_0^\infty x\cdot\frac1\beta e^{-x/\beta}dx=\frac1\beta\cdot1!\,\beta^2=\beta,\qquad E(X^2)=\frac1\beta\cdot2!\,\beta^3=2\beta^2 .
So \mathrm{Var}(X)=2\beta^2-\beta^2=\beta^2.
The memoryless property


                  
                  Memorize: Memoryless (lack of memory) property 
                  
                

For an exponential variable and any s,t>0,
P(X>s+t\mid X>s)=P(X>t).
In words, ==if you have already waited s units without the event happening, the chance of waiting a further t units is the same as if you had just started==. The past does not matter.


The proof uses the definition of conditional probability. The event \{X>s+t\} is contained in \{X>s\}, so
P(X>s+t\mid X>s)=\frac{P(X>s+t)}{P(X>s)}=\frac{e^{-(s+t)/\beta}}{e^{-s/\beta}}=e^{-t/\beta}=P(X>t).
Relation to the Poisson process
If events occur according to a Poisson process with rate \lambda per unit time (see P7 Poisson Distribution and Poisson Process), then the waiting time T until the next event is exponential with rate \lambda. The reason is that “the wait is longer than t” means “no events in an interval of length t”, and the Poisson probability of zero events is
P(T>t)=P(\text{0 events in } t)=\frac{e^{-\lambda t}(\lambda t)^0}{0!}=e^{-\lambda t}.
So the Poisson counts how many events happen, and the exponential measures how long we wait between them. This link is exactly what 2019-20 Q8(b) parts (iii) and (iv) test.
Linear functions of an exponential variable
Fresh practice (same shape as 2022-23 Q2(b)). The time to process an order, in minutes, is Y=2X+5, where X has density f(x)=\frac13e^{-x/3} for x>0. Find the mean and variance of Y, and P(Y>11).
Here X is exponential with \beta=3, so E(X)=3 and \mathrm{Var}(X)=9. By the linear rules in P5 Expectation Variance Covariance and Chebyshev,
E(Y)=2E(X)+5=2(3)+5=11,\qquad \mathrm{Var}(Y)=2^2\,\mathrm{Var}(X)=4(9)=36 .
For the probability, translate the event back to X: Y>11 means 2X+5>11, so X>3, and P(X>3)=e^{-3/3}=e^{-1}=0.3679.

3. Past TF question solved


                  
                  Past TF 2019-20 Q8(b) (25 marks) — calls to a fire station 
                  
                

The time between calls is exponential with rate \lambda=1.8 calls per day, so the mean time between calls is \frac{1}{1.8} day. Because the rate is per day, every time must be converted into days (or the rate into hours: 1.8/24=0.075 per hour).
(i) A call within the next 15 minutes after clocking on. Fifteen minutes is \frac{15}{1440}=\frac1{96} day.
P\left(T\le\tfrac{1}{96}\right)=1-e^{-1.8/96}=1-e^{-0.01875}=0.0186 .
(ii) No call so far, 15 minutes left in the shift. By the memoryless property, the time already waited does not matter, so the answer is the same as in (i): \mathbf{0.0186}.
(iii) No calls in a 10-hour shift. Ten hours is \frac{10}{24} day. “No calls” means the waiting time exceeds the shift, equivalently zero Poisson events with mean 1.8\times\frac{10}{24}=0.75:
P(\text{no call})=e^{-0.75}=0.4724 .
(iv) No calls in four successive shifts. The shifts do not overlap, so in a Poisson process they are independent:
P=(e^{-0.75})^4=e^{-3}=0.0498 .
(v) “In 10% of shifts there is a call in the first x hours.” We need P(T\le x)=0.1 with the rate 0.075 per hour:
1-e^{-0.075x}=0.1\ \Rightarrow\ e^{-0.075x}=0.9\ \Rightarrow\ x=\frac{-\ln 0.9}{0.075}=\frac{0.10536}{0.075}=1.40 .
So x\approx\mathbf{1.4} hours.




                  
                  Common mistake 
                  
                

Mixing units is the number-one error in exponential questions. Write the rate and the time in the same unit before substituting, and say so in your answer (“15 minutes = 1/96 day”).



4. Other continuous distributions you must recognise
These three distributions are mainly used as sampling distributions for test statistics. You do not need to memorize their density formulas, but you must know their shapes, their parameters (degrees of freedom) and when each is used.


                  
                  Memorize: Chi-square, t and F
                  
                

The chi-square distribution \chi^2_v with v degrees of freedom is the distribution of a sum of v squared independent standard normal variables. It takes only non-negative values, is skewed to the right, has mean v and variance 2v, and becomes more symmetric as v grows. It is used for goodness-of-fit and contingency-table tests and for the sample variance, since \frac{(n-1)S^2}{\sigma^2}\sim\chi^2_{n-1}.
The t distribution t_v is bell-shaped and symmetric about 0 like Z, but it has heavier tails, so its critical values are larger than those of Z. As v\to\infty it approaches the standard normal. It is used when \sigma is unknown and the sample is small: T=\frac{\bar X-\mu}{S/\sqrt n}\sim t_{n-1}.
The F distribution F_{v_1,v_2} is the ratio of two independent chi-square variables, each divided by its degrees of freedom. It takes only non-negative values and is skewed right. It is used to compare two variances (F=S_1^2/S_2^2) and in ANOVA (F=\text{MS}_{\text{between}}/\text{MS}_{\text{within}}).


The gamma distribution is a generalisation of the exponential (the exponential is gamma with \alpha=1), and the chi-square is gamma with \alpha=v/2 and \beta=2. This is mentioned in the lecture on other distributions for completeness.



                  
                  Self-check 
                  
                

1. Mean and variance of f(x)=\frac1{500}e^{-x/500}? 500 and 250,000.
2. State the memoryless property. P(X>s+t\mid X>s)=P(X>t).
3. Calls arrive at 2 per hour; probability of no call in 30 minutes? e^{-1}=0.3679.
4. Mean of U(2,10)? 6.
5. Which distribution compares two variances? The F distribution.

2-Statistics/S1-Introduction-to-Statisti.content:
S1 · Introduction to Statistics, Data and Sampling
Why this matters for the term final. This chapter is pure theory, and theory questions are “free marks” if you have the words ready. The 2022-23 term final asked (Q5a, 10 marks) “What do you mean by statistical data? How are they produced? Why do you need statistical data at all? What are the usual sources of statistical data in Bangladesh?” The 2023-24 term final asked (Q6c) you to “explain with an example, stratified random sampling”, and Q7a asked for “statistic and parameter” type short notes (also 2022-23 Q7a). Every one of those answers is written out below in exam-ready form. The full answers for those two papers are in TF 2022-23 Solutions and TF 2023-24 Solutions.

1. What is statistics?


                  
                  Memorize: Definition of Statistics 
                  
                

Statistics is the science of collecting, organizing, summarizing, analyzing and interpreting data, and of drawing conclusions (making decisions) from data in the presence of uncertainty.


The word “statistics” is used in two senses. In the plural sense, “statistics” means numerical facts themselves, for example the statistics of rice production in Bangladesh. In the singular sense, “statistics” means the subject, that is, the methods used to collect and analyze such numbers. In an exam, start your answer with the definition above and then add one line of example; that is enough for a 2–3 mark definition.
We study statistics because almost every engineering and computing decision is made with incomplete information. A software team does not know exactly how many users will log in tomorrow, a factory does not know the exact life of each bulb, and a network engineer does not know the exact delay of each packet. Statistics gives us a systematic way to describe what we have seen and to make reliable statements about what we have not seen.
2. Population, sample, census
A population is the complete collection of all individuals or objects that we are interested in. All the students of BUET, all the bulbs produced by a factory in one year, or all the packets passing through a router in a day are examples of populations.
A sample is a part (subset) of the population that we actually observe. If we test 50 bulbs out of the whole production, those 50 bulbs form a sample.
When we collect data from every member of the population, the study is called a census. Bangladesh’s Population and Housing Census is the classic example. A census is accurate but very expensive, slow and sometimes impossible (for example, you cannot test every bulb for its full life, because testing destroys the bulb). That is why we usually work with samples and use probability to generalize from the sample to the population.
A sample is called representative if it reflects the characteristics of the population well. A sample is biased if it systematically over-represents or under-represents some part of the population, for example, surveying only hall students to estimate the travel time of all BUET students.
3. Parameter versus statistic


                  
                  Memorize: Parameter vs Statistic (asked in 2022-23 Q7a) 
                  
                

A parameter is a numerical characteristic of a population, such as the population mean \mu, population variance \sigma^2 or population proportion P. It is a fixed constant, but usually unknown.
A statistic is a numerical characteristic computed from a sample, such as the sample mean \bar{x}, sample variance s^2 or sample proportion \hat{p}. It is known once the sample is drawn, but it changes from sample to sample, so it is itself a random variable.
We use statistics to estimate and test parameters. Example: the average GPA of all students of a college (\mu) is a parameter; the average GPA of 40 randomly selected students (\bar{x} = 2.8) is a statistic.


A simple memory trick: Parameter goes with Population, Statistic goes with Sample. Parameters are usually written with Greek letters (\mu, \sigma, \rho) and statistics with Latin letters (\bar{x}, s, r).
4. Descriptive and inferential statistics
Descriptive statistics consists of the collection, organization, summarization and presentation of data. When we make a frequency table, draw a histogram, or compute the mean and standard deviation of the marks of a class, we are doing descriptive statistics. We only describe the data we have; we do not go beyond it.
Inferential statistics consists of generalizing from samples to populations, performing estimation and hypothesis tests, determining relationships among variables, and making predictions. Inferential statistics uses probability, because a conclusion drawn from a sample is never 100% certain. When we use 40 students’ GPA to say something about all students of the college, or test whether a new machine has a lower defect rate, we are doing inferential statistics.


                  
                  Exam trick 
                  
                

If the question’s conclusion stays inside the observed data (“the average of these 30 values is 52”), it is descriptive. If the conclusion is about a larger group or the future (“all customers”, “the population”, “next year”), it is inferential.


5. Variables and types of data
A variable is a characteristic or attribute that can take different values for different individuals, for example height, gender, number of children, or blood group. The values we record are called data; each single value is a datum or observation. A collection of observations is a data set.
Qualitative (categorical) variables place individuals into categories that are not numbers in the usual sense, such as gender, religion, blood group or department. Quantitative variables are numerical and can be counted or measured, such as age, income or weight.
Quantitative variables are further divided into two kinds. A discrete variable takes values that can be counted, with gaps between them, such as the number of children in a family (0, 1, 2, …) or the number of calls received per hour. A continuous variable can take any value in an interval and is obtained by measuring, such as height, temperature, or time to failure. In practice continuous data are rounded (for example, height recorded to the nearest cm), but the underlying variable is still continuous.
graph TD
  V[Variables] --> QL[Qualitative / Categorical<br/>gender, blood group]
  V --> QN[Quantitative / Numerical]
  QN --> D[Discrete — counted<br/>no. of calls, no. of defects]
  QN --> C[Continuous — measured<br/>height, time, weight]

There are also four levels (scales) of measurement: nominal (names only, e.g. blood group), ordinal (ordered categories, e.g. grade A, B, C), interval (differences meaningful but no true zero, e.g. temperature in °C), and ratio (true zero exists, e.g. weight, income). Ranks used in Spearman’s rank correlation (S6 Correlation and Regression) are ordinal data.
6. What is statistical data? How is it produced? Why do we need it?
This section is written as a complete exam answer because 2022-23 Q5(a) asked exactly this.


                  
                  Memorize: Statistical data 
                  
                

Statistical data are aggregates of facts, expressed numerically (or classified into categories), collected in a systematic manner for a pre-determined purpose, and affected to a marked extent by a multiplicity of causes. A single isolated number (for example “Rahim is 170 cm tall”) is not statistics; the heights of 500 students collected to study the average height of students is statistical data. Statistical data must be numerically expressed, reasonably accurate, collected systematically, comparable, and placed in relation to each other.


How statistical data are produced. Data are produced in two main ways. Primary data are collected for the first time by the investigator himself or herself for a specific purpose, through methods such as direct personal interview, indirect oral investigation, mailed questionnaires, schedules filled by enumerators, observation and measurement, and designed experiments (for example, testing the life of bulbs in a laboratory). Secondary data are data that were already collected by someone else for some other purpose, and are taken from published or unpublished sources such as government reports, statistical yearbooks, research journals, company records and online databases. In addition, a large share of modern data is produced as a by-product of administration, called administrative records (birth and death registration, tax records, hospital records, school enrolment records, mobile phone and banking transaction logs). Data can be produced either by a census (every unit is covered) or by a sample survey (only a selected part is covered), and either by observation (we only record what happens) or by experiment (we control some factors and observe the effect).
Why do we need statistical data? We need data because sound decisions require facts rather than guesses. The government needs population and income data to plan schools, hospitals, roads and the national budget, and to measure poverty, inflation and unemployment. Businesses need data on sales, costs and customer behavior to forecast demand and control quality. Scientists and engineers need data to test theories, compare designs and measure reliability. In computer science, data are needed to measure system performance, to train and evaluate machine-learning models, and to detect anomalies. Without data, we cannot measure progress, compare alternatives or test claims; statistics turns data into information and information into decisions.
7. Sources of statistical data in Bangladesh


                  
                  Memorize: Main sources in Bangladesh (2022-23 Q5a) 
                  
                

The Bangladesh Bureau of Statistics (BBS), under the Statistics and Informatics Division of the Ministry of Planning, is the national statistical office and the most important source. It conducts the Population and Housing Census (every 10 years; the latest in 2022), the Household Income and Expenditure Survey (HIES) (poverty and income), the Labour Force Survey (LFS) (employment and unemployment), the Agriculture Census and crop estimates, the Economic Census, the Multiple Indicator Cluster Survey (MICS, with UNICEF), and publishes the Statistical Yearbook of Bangladesh, the Monthly Statistical Bulletin, national accounts (GDP) and the consumer price index (inflation).


Other important sources are the following. Bangladesh Bank (the central bank) publishes data on money supply, interest rates, exchange rates, remittances, foreign reserves and balance of payments in its Annual Report and Economic Trends. The Ministry of Finance publishes the Bangladesh Economic Review every year with the budget. The Directorate General of Health Services (DGHS) and its Management Information System (MIS) publish health statistics such as hospital data and disease surveillance; NIPORT conducts the Bangladesh Demographic and Health Survey (BDHS) on fertility, family planning and child health. BANBEIS (Bangladesh Bureau of Educational Information and Statistics) publishes education statistics such as enrolment and number of institutions. Research organizations such as icddr,b (health and population research) and BIDS (Bangladesh Institute of Development Studies) produce research data. Other sources include the Export Promotion Bureau (export data), the National Board of Revenue (tax data), the Bangladesh Telecommunication Regulatory Commission (mobile and internet subscribers), the Election Commission (voter data) and international organizations such as the World Bank, UNDP, WHO and UNICEF that publish data on Bangladesh.
In the exam, write the BBS paragraph in detail and then name at least four or five other organizations with one line each about what data they provide.
8. Sampling methods
Sampling is the process of selecting a sample from a population. The goal is a sample that is representative, so that conclusions about the population are reliable. Sampling methods are divided into probability sampling (every unit has a known, non-zero chance of selection) and non-probability sampling (selection by judgment or convenience). The course focuses on probability sampling.
Simple random sampling (SRS). Every possible sample of size n has the same chance of being selected, so every unit has an equal chance. In practice we number all N units of the population and select n numbers using a lottery or random number generator. Example: number all 500 students of a department and choose 50 using a random number generator. SRS is simple and unbiased, but it needs a complete list (sampling frame) and may, by chance, under-represent small groups.


                  
                  Memorize: Stratified random sampling (asked in 2023-24 Q6c) 
                  
                

In stratified random sampling, the population is first divided into non-overlapping, internally homogeneous groups called strata, based on a characteristic related to the study (for example gender, level, region or income group). Then a simple random sample is drawn from each stratum separately, usually in proportion to the stratum size (proportional allocation: n_h = n \times N_h/N). The samples from all strata are combined to form the full sample.


Example of stratified sampling. Suppose the CSE department has 600 students: 180 in Level 1, 160 in Level 2, 140 in Level 3 and 120 in Level 4. We want a sample of 60 students to estimate average daily screen time, and we believe screen time differs by level. Under proportional allocation we take 60 \times 180/600 = 18 students from Level 1, 60 \times 160/600 = 16 from Level 2, 60 \times 140/600 = 14 from Level 3 and 60 \times 120/600 = 12 from Level 4, each chosen by simple random sampling within its level. This guarantees that every level is represented in the correct proportion. Because each stratum is homogeneous, stratified sampling usually gives more precise estimates (smaller standard error) than SRS of the same size, and it also gives separate estimates for each stratum. Its disadvantage is that we must know the stratum of every unit and the stratum sizes in advance.
Systematic sampling. We arrange the population in some order, compute the sampling interval k = N/n, choose a random start between 1 and k, and then take every k-th unit. Example: from a list of 1000 customers we need 50, so k = 20; if the random start is 7, we choose customers 7, 27, 47, and so on. It is easy to carry out, but if the list has a periodic pattern matching k, the sample can be biased.
Cluster sampling. The population is divided into groups called clusters (for example villages, schools or city blocks) that are each like a mini-population (heterogeneous inside). A random sample of clusters is chosen, and all units (or a sample of units) inside the chosen clusters are studied. Example: to survey household internet use in Dhaka, randomly choose 20 wards and survey every household in those wards. It is cheap when the population is spread out, but usually less precise than SRS of the same size.


                  
                  Common mistake: strata vs clusters 
                  
                

In stratified sampling the groups (strata) are homogeneous inside and we sample from every stratum. In cluster sampling the groups (clusters) are heterogeneous inside and we sample only some clusters. Do not mix these up in a definition answer.


Non-probability methods (mention only briefly): convenience sampling (whoever is easy to reach), judgment or purposive sampling (expert chooses), quota sampling (fill fixed quotas of each group, but not randomly), and snowball sampling (existing subjects recruit others). These are quick and cheap but cannot support valid probability statements.



                  
                  Self-check 
                  
                

1. A survey of 400 voters finds 52% support a candidate. Identify the parameter and the statistic.
The parameter is the true proportion P of all voters who support the candidate (unknown). The statistic is the sample proportion \hat p = 0.52.
2. Classify: (a) number of bugs in a program, (b) CPU temperature, (c) blood group.
(a) quantitative discrete, (b) quantitative continuous, (c) qualitative (nominal).
3. A university has 3000 science, 2000 engineering and 1000 arts students. How many from each group in a stratified sample of 120 (proportional allocation)?
120 \times 3000/6000 = 60 science, 120 \times 2000/6000 = 40 engineering, 120 \times 1000/6000 = 20 arts.
4. Name the survey run by BBS that measures poverty.
The Household Income and Expenditure Survey (HIES).
5. Why is a census not used to estimate the mean life of bulbs?
Because testing life destroys the bulb; a census would destroy the whole production. A sample is used instead.

2-Statistics/S10-ANOVA-One-Way-and-Two-W.title: S10 · ANOVA: One-Way and Two-Way
2-Statistics/S10-ANOVA-One-Way-and-Two-W.content:
S10 · ANOVA: One-Way and Two-Way
Why this matters for the term final. ANOVA is a big-mark question that appears almost every year. 2021-22 Q8(b) (18 marks): one-way ANOVA with unequal group sizes (three salesmen) — solved below. 2022-23 Q8(b) (10 marks): one-way ANOVA for four brands of bulbs at 5% and 1%, and Q8(c) (15 marks): two-way ANOVA (corn types × soil blocks). 2023-24 Q8(b) (20 marks): one-way ANOVA for prices in three cities. The 2022-23 and 2023-24 solutions are in TF 2022-23 Solutions and TF 2023-24 Solutions; this note teaches the method and includes a fresh two-way practice. The calculation is completely mechanical: learn the five formulas and the table layout and you cannot lose these marks.

1. The idea of analysis of variance
Suppose we want to compare the means of three or more groups (three teaching methods, four bulb brands, three cities’ prices). Doing many separate two-sample t-tests would be tedious and would inflate the chance of a Type I error. Analysis of variance (ANOVA), developed by R. A. Fisher, tests all the means at once:
H_0: \mu_1 = \mu_2 = \dots = \mu_k \qquad\text{against}\qquad H_1: \text{at least two means are unequal}


                  
                  Memorize: The ANOVA idea 
                  
                

==ANOVA splits the total variation of all observations into parts due to identifiable sources (variation between groups, caused by differences among group means) and a part due to chance (variation within groups).== If the between-group variation is large compared with the within-group variation, the group means are significantly different. The comparison is made with the F ratio:
F = \frac{\text{mean square between groups}}{\text{mean square within groups (error)}}
If H_0 is true, both mean squares estimate the same \sigma^2 and F is close to 1. A large F leads to rejection. The test is always right-tailed.




                  
                  Memorize: Assumptions of ANOVA 
                  
                

The samples are drawn independently and at random; each population is normally distributed; all populations have the same variance \sigma^2 (homogeneity of variance); and the effects are additive.


2. F-test for two variances (brief)
To test H_0: \sigma_1^2 = \sigma_2^2, compute F = \dfrac{s_1^2}{s_2^2} with the larger sample variance in the numerator (so F \ge 1), and compare with F_{\alpha,(n_1 - 1),(n_2 - 1)} (for a two-tailed test use \alpha/2 in the table). Lecture example: route variances 8.9947^2 and 4.3753^2 give F = 4.23; with 6 and 7 df at \alpha/2 = 0.05, the critical value is 3.87, so the variances differ. This is the same F distribution that ANOVA uses (see S7 Sampling Distributions CLT and Confidence Intervals).
3. One-way ANOVA (completely randomized design)
We have k groups; group i has n_i observations with total T_i. Let N = \sum n_i and G = \sum T_i (grand total).


                  
                  Memorize: One-way ANOVA formulas 
                  
                

\text{Correction term: } CT = \frac{G^2}{N}
\text{Total SS: } S_T = \sum\sum x_{ij}^2 - CT
\text{Between-groups SS: } S_B = \sum_{i=1}^{k} \frac{T_i^2}{n_i} - CT
\text{Within-groups (error) SS: } S_W = S_T - S_B
F = \frac{S_B/(k - 1)}{S_W/(N - k)} \sim F_{(k-1),\,(N-k)}
Reject H_0 if F_{cal} > F_{\alpha,(k-1),(N-k)}.




                  
                  Memorize: One-way ANOVA table 
                  
                


































Source of variationdfSum of squaresMean squareFBetween groupsk - 1S_BMS_B = S_B/(k-1)MS_B/MS_WWithin groups (error)N - kS_WMS_W = S_W/(N-k)TotalN - 1S_T


Why it works. S_T measures how all N observations vary around the grand mean. S_B measures how the group means vary around the grand mean (weighted by group size). S_W is what is left: the scatter of observations around their own group mean, which can only be chance. Note that the formula \sum T_i^2/n_i handles unequal group sizes automatically; just divide each squared total by its own n_i.


                  
                  Exam trick: coding the data 
                  
                

Subtracting the same constant from every observation does not change S_T, S_B, S_W or F, and dividing every observation by the same constant c divides every sum of squares by c^2, so F is unchanged. So you may subtract a convenient number (e.g. 20) or divide by 100 to make the arithmetic small. State clearly that you coded the data. If you report sums of squares, convert back (multiply by c^2).




                  
                  Past TF 2021-22 Q8(b) (18 marks): Do three salesmen differ in average sales? 
                  
                

Data (weekly sales, Tk thousand). A (5 sales): 300, 400, 300, 500, 0. B (4 sales): 600, 300, 300, 400. C (5 sales): 700, 300, 400, 600, 500. Given F_{0.05,(2,11)} = 3.98.
Hypothesis: H_0: \mu_A = \mu_B = \mu_C (the salesmen’s average sales are equal) against H_1: at least two means differ.
Coding: divide every value by 100 (this does not change F).



























































ABC3674333345460–5n_i545T_i151625\sum x^25970135
N = 14, k = 3, G = 15 + 16 + 25 = 56.
CT = \frac{56^2}{14} = 224, \qquad S_T = (59 + 70 + 135) - 224 = 264 - 224 = 40
S_B = \frac{15^2}{5} + \frac{16^2}{4} + \frac{25^2}{5} - 224 = 45 + 64 + 125 - 224 = 10, \qquad S_W = 40 - 10 = 30

































SourcedfSSMSFBetween salesmen2105.0005/2.727 = 1.83Within (error)11302.727Total1340
(In original units every SS is multiplied by 100^2: S_B = 100{,}000, S_W = 300{,}000, S_T = 400{,}000; F is the same.)
Decision: F_{cal} = 1.83 < F_{0.05,(2,11)} = 3.98, so we do not reject H_0.
Comment: There is no significant difference among the average sales of the three salesmen at the 5% level; the observed differences (means 300, 400 and 500 thousand Tk) can be explained by chance variation.


Pairwise comparison (if H_0 is rejected). The lecture compares each pair with t = \dfrac{|\bar{x}_i - \bar{x}_j|}{\sqrt{MS_W\left(\frac{1}{n_i} + \frac{1}{n_j}\right)}} against t_{\alpha/2,(N-k)}, to find which particular means differ. Only do this when the overall F test is significant (or when asked).
4. Two-way ANOVA without replication (randomized block design)
Sometimes the observations are classified by two factors, with exactly one observation in each cell. A typical example: four types of corn (treatments, columns) are each planted in five blocks of land (rows), and the blocks may differ in soil fertility. Two-way ANOVA separates the variation due to rows, the variation due to columns, and the remaining random error, and tests both factors.
Let there be r rows and c columns, N = rc observations, row totals R_i, column totals C_j, grand total G.


                  
                  Memorize: Two-way ANOVA formulas (one observation per cell) 
                  
                

CT = \frac{G^2}{N}, \qquad S_T = \sum\sum x_{ij}^2 - CT
S_R = \frac{\sum R_i^2}{c} - CT \;(\text{rows / blocks}), \qquad S_C = \frac{\sum C_j^2}{r} - CT \;(\text{columns / treatments})
S_E = S_T - S_R - S_C















































SourcedfSSMSFRows (blocks)r - 1S_RMS_R = S_R/(r-1)F_R = MS_R/MS_EColumns (treatments)c - 1S_CMS_C = S_C/(c-1)F_C = MS_C/MS_EError(r-1)(c-1)S_EMS_E = S_E/[(r-1)(c-1)]Totalrc - 1S_T==Compare F_R with F_{\alpha,(r-1),(r-1)(c-1)} and F_C with F_{\alpha,(c-1),(r-1)(c-1)}.== Note: row totals are divided by the number of columns (each row total is a sum of c values), and column totals by the number of rows.


Two null hypotheses are tested: H_{01}: there is no difference among the row (block) means, and H_{02}: there is no difference among the column (treatment) means.
Fresh practice (two-way). Three fertilizers (columns) are tried on four plots of different soil (rows); yields (kg):















































Soil plotFertilizer F1F2F3Row total R_iP1454351139P2474652145P3485055153P4423749128Column total C_j182176207G = 565
Test at 5% whether yields differ (i) among soil plots and (ii) among fertilizers. Given F_{0.05,(3,6)} = 4.76 and F_{0.05,(2,6)} = 5.14.
r = 4, c = 3, N = 12. CT = 565^2/12 = 26602.08. \sum x^2 = 26867, so S_T = 26867 - 26602.08 = 264.92.
S_R = \dfrac{139^2 + 145^2 + 153^2 + 128^2}{3} - CT = \dfrac{80139}{3} - 26602.08 = 26713.00 - 26602.08 = 110.92.
S_C = \dfrac{182^2 + 176^2 + 207^2}{4} - CT = \dfrac{106949}{4} - 26602.08 = 26737.25 - 26602.08 = 135.17.
S_E = 264.92 - 110.92 - 135.17 = 18.83.








































SourcedfSSMSFSoil plots (rows)3110.9236.9711.78Fertilizers (columns)2135.1767.5821.53Error618.833.139Total11264.92
Decision. (i) F_R = 11.78 > 4.76: reject H_{01}; the soil plots differ significantly in yield. (ii) F_C = 21.53 > 5.14: reject H_{02}; the fertilizers differ significantly, F3 giving the highest total yield.


                  
                  Common mistakes in ANOVA 
                  
                

Forgetting to subtract CT; dividing row totals by the number of rows instead of the number of columns; using N instead of N - k for the error df; putting the smaller mean square in the numerator; and, with coded data, forgetting that F is unchanged but sums of squares scale by c^2. When a question asks for two significance levels (5% and 1%), compare the same F_{cal} with both critical values and write both decisions.


5. How the parts connect
S_T = S_B + S_W (one-way) and S_T = S_R + S_C + S_E (two-way) mirror the regression identity SST = SSR + SSE in S6 Correlation and Regression: in every case we split total variation into an explained part and an unexplained part, and the F ratio compares them after dividing each by its degrees of freedom. The degrees of freedom also add up: (k - 1) + (N - k) = N - 1.



                  
                  Self-check 
                  
                

1. Three groups of sizes 4, 5, 6. Degrees of freedom of F?
k - 1 = 2 and N - k = 15 - 3 = 12.
2. G = 120, N = 12, \sum x^2 = 1300. Find CT and S_T.
CT = 14400/12 = 1200; S_T = 100.
3. In a two-way table with 5 rows and 4 columns, what are the error df?
(5-1)(4-1) = 12.
4. MS_B = 12, MS_W = 3, critical F = 3.89. Decision?
F = 4 > 3.89: reject H_0, means differ.
5. Why can’t we just do several t-tests instead of ANOVA?
Many separate tests increase the overall chance of a Type I error and are tedious; ANOVA tests all means simultaneously at the chosen \alpha.

2-Statistics/S2-Frequency-Distributions-.title: S2 · Frequency Distributions and Graphs
2-Statistics/S2-Frequency-Distributions-.content:
S2 · Frequency Distributions and Graphs
Why this matters for the term final. Graph and table questions appear every year. In 2023-24, Q5(a) asked “What are stem-and-leaf plots and how do you create them?” and Q5(b) asked you to explain and interpret a scatter plot of price versus rating. In 2022-23, Q5(b) asked for a frequency table using Sturges’ rule, a histogram and a cumulative frequency graph from 60 raw values, and Q6(b) asked for a stem-and-leaf plot of pencil lengths with median, mode and range. In 2021-22, Q5(a) asked for an ogive to read the median and a count of workers in an interval, and Q5(b)(i) asked for class limits and class marks. The 2021-22 questions are fully solved here; the 2023-24 and 2022-23 ones are solved in TF 2023-24 Solutions and TF 2022-23 Solutions, and this note gives you fresh practice of exactly the same kind.

1. Frequency distribution: the vocabulary
When we have many raw observations, we organize them into a frequency distribution, which is a table showing each value or class of values together with the number of observations (the frequency, f) falling in it. If there are few distinct values we list each value separately (an ungrouped frequency distribution). If the values are many and spread out, we group them into classes (a grouped frequency distribution).


                  
                  Memorize: Class terminology 
                  
                

The class limits are the smallest and largest values that can actually be written in a class, for example 200–219. The class boundaries are the points halfway between the upper limit of one class and the lower limit of the next, for example 199.5–219.5; they remove the gaps between classes so that the classes touch each other. The class mark (mid-value) is the midpoint of the class: \text{class mark} = \dfrac{\text{lower limit} + \text{upper limit}}{2} (the same result is obtained from the boundaries). The class width h is the difference between two consecutive lower boundaries (or lower limits), equivalently upper boundary minus lower boundary.


If data are recorded to the nearest integer, boundaries are found by subtracting 0.5 from each lower limit and adding 0.5 to each upper limit. If data are recorded to one decimal place, subtract and add 0.05, and so on. When a table is written like “20–30, 30–40, …” the classes are already given by boundaries (the convention is that 30 goes into the class 30–40), and the class mark is simply (20+30)/2 = 25.
2. How many classes? Sturges’ rule


                  
                  Memorize: Sturges' rule (used in 2022-23 Q5b) 
                  
                

K = 1 + 3.322 \log_{10} N
where K is the number of classes and N is the total number of observations. Round K to a whole number. Then
\text{class width } h \approx \frac{\text{Largest value} - \text{Smallest value}}{K}
and round h up to a convenient number.


For example, with N = 50 observations, K = 1 + 3.322 \times \log_{10}50 = 1 + 3.322 \times 1.699 = 6.64 \approx 7 classes. If the data run from 12 to 75, the range is 63 and h = 63/7 = 9, so we could use classes 12–20, 21–29, 30–38 and so on (each containing 9 integers).
Step-by-step method to build a grouped frequency table. First find the largest and smallest values and the range. Second, decide the number of classes K (by Sturges’ rule if asked, otherwise usually 5 to 15). Third, compute the width h and round it up. Fourth, choose the first lower limit (the smallest value or a convenient number just below it) and write down all the classes by repeatedly adding h. Fifth, go through the raw data one by one and put a tally mark against the right class; this prevents missing values. Sixth, count the tallies to get the frequencies and check that the total equals N. Finally add columns for class boundaries, class marks and cumulative frequency, because the graphs and almost every later calculation need them.


                  
                  Common mistake 
                  
                

Always check that the frequencies add up to N. In a 60-value question one missed tally costs you the histogram, ogive and every number after it.




                  
                  Past TF 2021-22 Q5(b)(i): class limits and class marks 
                  
                

Problem: 34 observations recorded to the nearest integer range from 201 to 337. Seven classes of width 20 are to be used, beginning the first class at 199.5. Find the class limits and class marks.
Solution. Since the first class begins at 199.5 (a boundary) and the width is 20, the class boundaries are 199.5–219.5, 219.5–239.5, 239.5–259.5, 259.5–279.5, 279.5–299.5, 299.5–319.5 and 319.5–339.5. The data are integers, so each lower limit is the lower boundary plus 0.5 and each upper limit is the upper boundary minus 0.5. Hence the class limits are 200–219, 220–239, 240–259, 260–279, 280–299, 300–319, 320–339. The class marks are the midpoints: (200+219)/2 = 209.5, and each next one is 20 more, giving 209.5, 229.5, 249.5, 269.5, 289.5, 309.5, 329.5. Check: the seven classes cover 200 to 339, which contains the smallest value 201 and the largest value 337, so all 34 observations fit.


3. Histogram, frequency polygon and ogive
A histogram is a graph of a grouped frequency distribution in which the class boundaries are marked on the x-axis and a rectangle (bar) is drawn over each class with height equal to the frequency. The bars touch each other because the data are continuous (this is the difference from a bar chart). If class widths are unequal, the height must be the frequency per unit width (frequency density), otherwise wide classes look too important. The tallest bar marks the modal class.
A frequency polygon is drawn by plotting the frequency of each class against its class mark and joining the points with straight lines. To close the polygon, add one empty class at each end with zero frequency, so the polygon starts and ends on the x-axis.


                  
                  Memorize: Ogive (cumulative frequency graph) 
                  
                

An ogive is the graph of the cumulative frequency. For a “less-than” ogive, the cumulative frequency (number of observations less than a value) is plotted against the upper class boundary, starting from the point (first lower boundary, 0), and the points are joined by straight lines or a smooth curve. The ogive always rises from 0 to N. Its main use is to read the median, quartiles and percentiles graphically, and to count how many observations lie between two values.


To read the median from a less-than ogive, mark N/2 on the y-axis, draw a horizontal line to the ogive, then drop a vertical line to the x-axis; the x-value is the median. For Q_1 use N/4, for Q_3 use 3N/4, and for the k-th percentile use kN/100. To count values between a and b, read the ogive heights at a and b and subtract.
The median formula used to verify the graph is (see S3 Measures of Central Tendency):
\text{Median} = L + \frac{\frac{N}{2} - F}{f_m} \times h
where L is the lower boundary of the median class, F is the cumulative frequency before the median class, f_m is the frequency of the median class and h is its width.


                  
                  Past TF 2021-22 Q5(a) (18 marks): ogive, median, workers between 2000 and 2170 Tk 
                  
                

Data. Monthly wages and workers: 1900–1950: 6, 1950–2000: 10, 2000–2050: 22, 2050–2100: 30, 2100–2150: 16, 2150–2200: 12, 2200–2400: 15.
Choice of diagram. The last class (2200–2400) is four times wider than the others, so a plain histogram would be misleading. Since we must read the median and count workers in an interval, the suitable diagram is the less-than ogive.
Cumulative frequency table.



























Wages (less than)19001950200020502100215022002400Cumulative no. of workers061638688496111
Plot these eight points (upper boundary, cumulative frequency) and join them. N = 111.

Median from the graph. N/2 = 55.5. A horizontal line at 55.5 meets the ogive above about 2079 on the wage axis, so the median wage is about Tk 2079.
Verification by formula. The 55.5-th value lies in the class 2050–2100 (cumulative frequency goes from 38 to 68). So L = 2050, F = 38, f_m = 30, h = 50:
\text{Median} = 2050 + \frac{55.5 - 38}{30} \times 50 = 2050 + 29.17 = 2079.17 \text{ Tk}
which agrees with the graph.
Workers earning between 2000 and 2170 Tk. All workers of the classes 2000–2050, 2050–2100 and 2100–2150 are included: 22 + 30 + 16 = 68. From the class 2150–2200 (12 workers, width 50) we need the part from 2150 to 2170, which is 20 out of 50, so assuming uniform spread inside the class we take 12 \times \frac{20}{50} = 4.8. Total = 68 + 4.8 = 72.8 \approx 73 workers. From the ogive: height at 2170 is about 84 + 4.8 = 88.8, height at 2000 is 16, difference \approx 72.8.


4. Charts for qualitative data and time (brief)
A bar chart shows categories (qualitative data) with separated bars whose heights are the frequencies; bars do not touch. A compound (multiple) bar chart puts bars of two or more groups side by side for comparison. A Pareto chart is a bar chart for categorical data in which the bars are arranged from the highest frequency to the lowest, which quickly shows the most important categories. A pie chart divides a circle into sectors whose angles are proportional to the frequencies, with angle = \frac{f}{N} \times 360^\circ; it shows parts of a whole. A time series graph (line graph) plots values against time to show trends, such as yearly sales.
5. Stem-and-leaf plot


                  
                  Memorize: Stem-and-leaf plot (2023-24 Q5a, 10 marks) 
                  
                

A stem-and-leaf plot is a way of displaying quantitative data in which each value is split into a stem (the leading digit or digits) and a leaf (the last digit). The stems are written once in a vertical column in increasing order, and the leaves of all values with the same stem are written in a row to the right of that stem, in increasing order. It looks like a histogram turned on its side, but unlike a histogram it keeps every original data value, so we can still read the exact values, find the median, mode and range directly, and see the shape (symmetry, skewness, gaps, outliers) of the distribution.


How to create a stem-and-leaf plot. First decide how to split the numbers: for two-digit numbers the tens digit is the stem and the units digit is the leaf; for numbers like 17.4 the integer part is the stem and the decimal digit is the leaf. Second, write all possible stems from the smallest to the largest in a column, including stems with no leaves (so that gaps are visible). Third, go through the data and write each leaf next to its stem. Fourth, rewrite the plot with the leaves of each row arranged in increasing order (an ordered stem-and-leaf plot). Finally, always add a key such as “4 | 2 means 42”, so the reader knows the units.
Example (fresh). The scores of 20 students are: 42, 57, 38, 61, 45, 49, 53, 66, 71, 58, 44, 39, 62, 55, 47, 51, 68, 74, 59, 46.
Stem | Leaf           (Key: 4 | 2 means 42)
  3  | 8 9
  4  | 2 4 5 6 7 9
  5  | 1 3 5 7 8 9
  6  | 1 2 6 8
  7  | 1 4
From the plot we can read everything. There are n = 20 values, so the median is the average of the 10th and 11th ordered values. Counting leaves: stem 3 has 2 values, stem 4 has 6 (total 8), so the 9th, 10th and 11th values are 51, 53 and 55. The median is (53 + 55)/2 = 54. The range is 74 - 38 = 36. No value repeats, so there is no unique mode, but the modal rows (most leaves) are the 40s and 50s. The shape is roughly symmetric with a slight tail.
A decimal example (fresh, same style as the pencil question). Battery lives in hours: 4.2, 3.8, 4.5, 5.1, 4.2, 3.9, 4.7, 5.0, 4.2, 4.8, 3.6, 4.4. Use the integer part as stem and the first decimal as leaf.
Stem | Leaf           (Key: 4 | 2 means 4.2 hours)
  3  | 6 8 9
  4  | 2 2 2 4 5 7 8
  5  | 0 1
n = 12, so the median is the average of the 6th and 7th values: 4.2 and 4.4, giving median = 4.3 hours. The mode is the most repeated leaf: 4.2 appears three times, so mode = 4.2 hours. Range = 5.1 - 3.6 = 1.5 hours. If two values tie for the most repeats, the data are bimodal and you must report both modes.
6. Scatter plot


                  
                  Memorize: Scatter plot (2023-24 Q5b) 
                  
                

A scatter plot (scatter diagram) is a graph of paired data (x, y) in which each pair is plotted as one point, with the independent (explanatory) variable on the x-axis and the dependent (response) variable on the y-axis. It is the first step in correlation and regression analysis, because it shows whether a relationship exists, its direction (positive or negative), its form (linear or curved) and its strength (how tightly the points cluster), and it reveals outliers.



How to interpret a scatter plot. If the points rise from left to right, the relationship is positive (as x increases, y tends to increase). If they fall from left to right, it is negative. If the points lie close to a straight line, the linear relationship is strong; if they form a wide cloud, it is weak; if there is no pattern, there is no relationship. A curved pattern means a non-linear relationship, in which case Pearson’s r can be near zero even though x and y are strongly related (last panel above). In an exam answer, always draw the plot with labelled axes, describe direction, form and strength in words, and, if you can, support it with the value of r (see S6 Correlation and Regression).
Quick example. Hours studied (2, 4, 5, 7, 9) and marks (45, 55, 60, 72, 85): the points rise steadily and lie close to a line, so there is a strong positive linear relationship; more study hours go with higher marks.
7. Box plot (box-and-whisker plot)

A box plot displays the five-number summary: minimum, first quartile Q_1, median Q_2, third quartile Q_3 and maximum. A box is drawn from Q_1 to Q_3 with a line at the median, and “whiskers” extend from the box to the smallest and largest values that are not outliers. The length of the box is the interquartile range IQR = Q_3 - Q_1. A value is usually flagged as an outlier if it is below Q_1 - 1.5\,IQR or above Q_3 + 1.5\,IQR. If the median is in the middle of the box and the whiskers are equal, the distribution is symmetric; if the right whisker is longer and the median is nearer Q_1, the distribution is positively skewed. Box plots are excellent for comparing two or more groups side by side.


                  
                  Exam trick: which graph to draw? 
                  
                

For raw quantitative data with few values, use a stem-and-leaf plot. For grouped data, use a histogram (shape and mode) or an ogive (median, quartiles, “how many between”). For two related variables, use a scatter plot. For categories, use a bar, Pareto or pie chart. For data over time, use a time series graph. Write one sentence justifying your choice; examiners give a mark for it.





                  
                  Self-check 
                  
                

1. Classes 15–19, 20–24, 25–29 (integer data). Give the boundaries and class marks.
Boundaries 14.5–19.5, 19.5–24.5, 24.5–29.5; class marks 17, 22, 27; width 5.
2. Using Sturges’ rule, how many classes for N = 100?
K = 1 + 3.322 \times 2 = 7.644 \approx 8 classes.
3. In a less-than ogive, against what is the cumulative frequency plotted?
Against the upper class boundary (starting at the first lower boundary with 0).
4. Why is a stem-and-leaf plot sometimes preferred to a histogram?
It shows the distribution’s shape like a histogram but retains every original value, so exact median, mode and range can be read.
5. A scatter plot shows points forming a U shape. Will Pearson’s r be large?
No. r measures only linear association, so it can be close to 0 even though there is a strong curved relationship.

2-Statistics/S3-Measures-of-Central-Tend.title: S3 · Measures of Central Tendency
2-Statistics/S3-Measures-of-Central-Tend.content:
S3 · Measures of Central Tendency
Why this matters for the term final. The mean, median, mode and quartiles are the raw material for almost every statistics question. The 2020-21 term final Q5(a)(i) asked “which factory pays higher average wages?” (solved below). Every coefficient-of-variation question (S4 Measures of Dispersion), every skewness question (Pearson needs the mode, Bowley needs quartiles, Kelly needs percentiles; see S5 Moments Skewness and Kurtosis), the ogive median of 2021-22 Q5(a) (S2 Frequency Distributions and Graphs) and the corrected-mean question of 2023-24 Q5(c) (TF 2023-24 Solutions) all start here. The median and mode from a stem-and-leaf plot (2022-23 Q6b, in TF 2022-23 Solutions) also use these definitions.

1. What is a measure of central tendency?
A measure of central tendency (or measure of location, or average) is a single value that represents the centre of a data set, the value around which the observations tend to cluster. The three main ones are the mean, the median and the mode. A good average should be rigidly defined, easy to understand and compute, based on all observations, not too affected by extreme values, and suitable for further algebraic treatment. The arithmetic mean satisfies most of these, which is why it is the most used.
2. Arithmetic mean


                  
                  Memorize: Arithmetic mean formulas 
                  
                

Ungrouped data (n values): \bar{x} = \frac{\sum x_i}{n}
Grouped data (class marks x_i, frequencies f_i, N = \sum f_i): \bar{x} = \frac{\sum f_i x_i}{N}
Step-deviation (short-cut) method, with assumed mean A and class width h: u_i = \frac{x_i - A}{h}, \qquad \bar{x} = A + h \cdot \frac{\sum f_i u_i}{N}


The step-deviation method gives exactly the same answer as the direct method, but the numbers are tiny (−3, −2, −1, 0, 1, 2, 3), so arithmetic mistakes are far less likely. ==Choose A as the class mark in the middle of the table (preferably where the frequency is largest) and h as the common class width.== The same u-column is reused for variance and for moments, so one table answers the whole question.
Properties of the mean. The sum of deviations from the mean is zero: \sum (x_i - \bar{x}) = 0. The sum of squared deviations is smallest when taken about the mean: \sum (x_i - A)^2 is minimum at A = \bar{x}. If every value is changed as y = a + bx, then \bar{y} = a + b\bar{x} (change of origin and scale). The mean uses all observations and is the basis of variance, but it is strongly affected by extreme values (outliers) and cannot be found for open-ended classes without assumptions.
Weighted mean. When values have different importance w_i: \bar{x}_w = \dfrac{\sum w_i x_i}{\sum w_i}. Example: a CGPA is a weighted mean of grade points with credit hours as weights. Grades 4.00 (3 credits), 3.50 (4 credits), 3.00 (2 credits) give \bar{x}_w = (12 + 14 + 6)/9 = 3.56.


                  
                  Memorize: Combined mean of two groups 
                  
                

\bar{x}_c = \frac{n_1 \bar{x}_1 + n_2 \bar{x}_2}{n_1 + n_2}
Example: 40 workers with mean wage 50 and 60 workers with mean wage 45 have combined mean (40\times50 + 60\times45)/100 = (2000+2700)/100 = 47.




                  
                  Past TF 2020-21 Q5(a)(i): Which factory pays higher average wages? 
                  
                

Data. Daily wages 20–30, 30–40, …, 80–90. Factory A frequencies: 15, 30, 44, 60, 30, 14, 7. Factory B frequencies: 25, 40, 60, 35, 20, 15, 5. Take A = 55, h = 10, so u = (x - 55)/10.






















































































Wagesxuf_Af_A uf_Bf_B u20–3025−315−4525−7530–4035−230−6040−8040–5045−144−4460−6050–6055060035060–706513030202070–807521428153080–90853721515Total200−70200−150
\bar{x}_A = 55 + 10 \times \frac{-70}{200} = 55 - 3.5 = 51.5 \text{ Tk}, \qquad \bar{x}_B = 55 + 10 \times \frac{-150}{200} = 55 - 7.5 = 47.5 \text{ Tk}
Conclusion. Since 51.5 > 47.5, Factory A pays higher average daily wages. (Part (ii), the variability comparison, is solved in S4 Measures of Dispersion.)


3. Median
The median is the middle value of the data when they are arranged in increasing order, so that half of the observations are below it and half above it. For ungrouped data with n values arranged in order, the median is the \left(\frac{n+1}{2}\right)-th value; if n is even, it is the average of the \frac{n}{2}-th and \left(\frac{n}{2}+1\right)-th values.


                  
                  Memorize: Median of grouped data 
                  
                

\text{Median} = L + \frac{\frac{N}{2} - F}{f_m} \times h
L = lower boundary of the median class, N = total frequency, F = cumulative frequency of the class before the median class, f_m = frequency of the median class, h = width of the median class. ==The median class is the first class whose cumulative frequency is at least N/2.==


The logic of the formula is linear interpolation: we need N/2 - F more observations after reaching the start of the median class; the class contains f_m observations spread evenly over width h, so we move a fraction \frac{N/2 - F}{f_m} of the width into the class.
Example (Factory A data). Cumulative frequencies: 15, 45, 89, 149, 179, 193, 200. N/2 = 100. The first cumulative frequency that reaches 100 is 149, so the median class is 50–60, with L = 50, F = 89, f_m = 60, h = 10:
\text{Median} = 50 + \frac{100 - 89}{60} \times 10 = 50 + 1.83 = 51.83.
The median is not affected by extreme values, can be found for open-ended classes and can be read from an ogive, so it is the better average for skewed data such as incomes. Its weakness is that it does not use the actual size of every observation and is less suitable for algebra.
4. Mode
The mode is the value that occurs most often. Data can have one mode (unimodal), two modes (bimodal), more, or none (if every value occurs once).


                  
                  Memorize: Mode of grouped data 
                  
                

\text{Mode} = L + \frac{\Delta_1}{\Delta_1 + \Delta_2} \times h, \qquad \Delta_1 = f_m - f_1,\; \Delta_2 = f_m - f_2
L = lower boundary of the modal class (the class with the highest frequency), f_m = its frequency, f_1 = frequency of the class before it, f_2 = frequency of the class after it, h = class width.


Example (Factory A data). The highest frequency is 60, in class 50–60. So L = 50, \Delta_1 = 60 - 44 = 16, \Delta_2 = 60 - 30 = 30, h = 10:
\text{Mode} = 50 + \frac{16}{16 + 30} \times 10 = 50 + 3.48 = 53.48.
The mode is easy to understand and is the only average for qualitative data (e.g. the most popular programming language), but it may not exist or may not be unique, and it is not based on all observations.


                  
                  Memorize: Empirical relation (moderately skewed data) 
                  
                

\text{Mean} - \text{Mode} \approx 3(\text{Mean} - \text{Median}) \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \text{Mode} \approx 3\,\text{Median} - 2\,\text{Mean}
For a symmetric distribution, Mean = Median = Mode. For positive skew, Mode < Median < Mean. For negative skew, Mean < Median < Mode. (Diagram in S5 Moments Skewness and Kurtosis.)


For Factory A: Mean 51.5, Median 51.83, Mode 53.48, so Mean < Median < Mode, suggesting a slight negative skew. The empirical formula would give Mode \approx 3(51.83) - 2(51.5) = 52.5, close to the formula value; the relation is only approximate.
5. Quartiles, deciles and percentiles (partition values)
Quartiles divide ordered data into four equal parts: Q_1 has 25% of observations below it, Q_2 is the median, and Q_3 has 75% below it. Deciles D_1, \dots, D_9 divide into ten parts, and percentiles P_1, \dots, P_{99} divide into a hundred parts. Note that Q_2 = D_5 = P_{50} = \text{Median}, D_1 = P_{10} and D_9 = P_{90}.


                  
                  Memorize: Partition values for grouped data (needed for Bowley and Kelly skewness) 
                  
                

Q_j = L + \frac{\frac{jN}{4} - F}{f} \times h, \qquad D_j = L + \frac{\frac{jN}{10} - F}{f} \times h, \qquad P_j = L + \frac{\frac{jN}{100} - F}{f} \times h
It is the median formula with N/2 replaced by the required position. L, F, f, h refer to the class that contains that position (the first class whose cumulative frequency reaches it).


Example (Factory A). For Q_1: N/4 = 50. Cumulative frequencies 15, 45, 89 → the class 40–50 contains the 50th value (F = 45, f = 44): Q_1 = 40 + \frac{50 - 45}{44}\times 10 = 41.14. For Q_3: 3N/4 = 150. The cumulative frequency up to 60 is 149, which is less than 150, so Q_3 is in 60–70 (F = 149, f = 30): Q_3 = 60 + \frac{150 - 149}{30}\times 10 = 60.33.


                  
                  Common mistake 
                  
                

When the required position exactly equals or just exceeds a cumulative frequency, read carefully: the class containing the position is the first one whose cumulative frequency is greater than or equal to the position. Using the class before it gives a value outside its own class, which is a sure sign of error.


For ungrouped data, the j-th quartile is the value at position \frac{j(n+1)}{4} in the ordered list (interpolate if it is not a whole number).
6. Geometric and harmonic means (brief)
The geometric mean of n positive values is GM = (x_1 x_2 \cdots x_n)^{1/n}, equivalently \log GM = \frac{1}{n}\sum \log x_i. It is used for averaging rates of growth and ratios, for example average yearly growth of users. The harmonic mean is HM = \dfrac{n}{\sum (1/x_i)} and is used for averaging rates such as speeds over equal distances. For positive data, AM \ge GM \ge HM, with equality only when all values are equal. Example: speeds 40 and 60 km/h over equal distances give average speed HM = 2/(1/40 + 1/60) = 48 km/h, not 50.
7. Which average to use?
Use the mean when the data are roughly symmetric and further calculations (variance, tests) will follow. Use the median when the data are skewed or have outliers, or classes are open-ended (incomes, house prices, response times). Use the mode for qualitative data or when the “most typical” value is needed (most common shoe size). In an exam comparison question like “which pays higher on average”, compute the means unless told otherwise.



                  
                  Self-check 
                  
                

1. Find the mean, median and mode of 4, 7, 7, 9, 13.
Mean = 40/5 = 8; median = 3rd value = 7; mode = 7.
2. Two sections have 30 students (mean 60) and 50 students (mean 68). Combined mean?
(30\times60 + 50\times68)/80 = (1800+3400)/80 = 65.
3. In a grouped table with N = 80, cumulative frequencies are 10, 25, 47, 70, 80 for classes 0–10, …, 40–50. Find the median.
N/2 = 40 lies in 20–30 (F = 25, f = 22): 20 + \frac{40-25}{22}\times10 = 26.82.
4. Which average is not affected by extreme values and can be read from an ogive?
The median.
5. If mean = 30 and median = 28, estimate the mode.
Mode \approx 3(28) - 2(30) = 24.
