S9 · Chi-Square Tests
Why this matters for the term final. The contingency-table \chi^2 test appeared in both of the latest papers. 2023-24 Q8(a) (15 marks) gave a 3×3 table of job performance against educational attainment (this is exactly the lecture’s Problem 1), and 2022-23 Q8(a) (10 marks) gave a 2×2 table of drug versus typhoid. Goodness of fit appeared as a short note in 2023-24 Q7(a). Both full solutions are in TF 2023-24 Solutions and TF 2022-23 Solutions; this note teaches the method with fresh practice of each type. The general testing steps are in S8 Hypothesis Testing Concepts and z t Tests.

1. The chi-square statistic
All chi-square tests compare observed frequencies O (what we counted) with expected frequencies E (what we would expect if H_0 were true):


                  
                  Memorize: The chi-square statistic 
                  
                

\chi^2 = \sum \frac{(O_i - E_i)^2}{E_i} \qquad\left(\text{equivalently } \chi^2 = \sum \frac{O_i^2}{E_i} - N\right)
It follows (approximately) a chi-square distribution with \nu degrees of freedom. ==If O and E agree closely, \chi^2 is small and we accept H_0; if they disagree a lot, \chi^2 is large and we reject H_0.== The test is always right-tailed: reject H_0 if \chi^2_{cal} \ge \chi^2_{\alpha,\nu}.


Why square and divide by E? Squaring stops positive and negative differences cancelling, and dividing by E makes a difference of 10 count more when we expected 15 than when we expected 1000.


                  
                  Memorize: Conditions for a valid chi-square test 
                  
                

The observations must be independent and counted (frequencies, not percentages or measurements). The total N should be reasonably large (at least 50). Every expected frequency should be at least 5; if some are smaller, merge neighbouring classes and reduce the degrees of freedom accordingly. The sum of the expected frequencies must equal the sum of the observed frequencies.


Useful critical values: \chi^2_{0.05} with 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 df is 3.84, 5.99, 7.81, 9.49, 11.07, 12.59; \chi^2_{0.01} with 1, 2, 3, 4 df is 6.63, 9.21, 11.34, 13.28.
2. Goodness-of-fit test


                  
                  Memorize: Goodness of fit 
                  
                

A goodness-of-fit test checks whether an observed frequency distribution agrees with a hypothesized theoretical distribution (uniform, a given ratio, binomial, Poisson, normal, …). H_0: the data follow the stated distribution; H_1: they do not.
\nu = k - 1 - m
where k is the number of classes (after merging small ones) and m is the number of parameters estimated from the data to compute the expected frequencies (e.g. m = 1 when \lambda of a Poisson is estimated by \bar{x}; m = 0 when all probabilities are given).


Fresh practice 1 (is a die fair?). A die is rolled 120 times: faces 1 to 6 appear 22, 17, 20, 26, 18, 17 times. Test at 5% whether the die is fair.
H_0: the die is fair, so each face has probability 1/6 and expected frequency E = 120/6 = 20. H_1: the die is not fair.













































Face123456TotalO221720261817120E202020202020120(O-E)^2/E0.200.450.001.800.200.453.10
\nu = 6 - 1 = 5, critical value \chi^2_{0.05,5} = 11.07. Since 3.10 < 11.07, we do not reject H_0: the die may be regarded as fair; the differences are due to chance.
Fresh practice 2 (given ratio). In a genetics experiment 556 seeds are classified into four types with observed counts 315, 108, 101, 32. Theory predicts the ratio 9:3:3:1. Expected frequencies: 556 \times 9/16 = 312.75, 556 \times 3/16 = 104.25, 104.25, 556 \times 1/16 = 34.75. Then \chi^2 = \frac{2.25^2}{312.75} + \frac{3.75^2}{104.25} + \frac{(-3.25)^2}{104.25} + \frac{(-2.75)^2}{34.75} = 0.016 + 0.135 + 0.101 + 0.218 = 0.47. With \nu = 3, \chi^2_{0.05,3} = 7.81; 0.47 < 7.81, so the data fit the 9:3:3:1 theory very well.
3. Contingency table: test of independence (association)
A contingency table is a two-way table of frequencies in which individuals are classified by two qualitative attributes A (with r categories, the rows) and B (with c categories, the columns). The categories of each attribute must be mutually exclusive and exhaustive.


                  
                  Memorize: Test of independence in an r \times c table
                  
                

H_0: there is no association between A and B (they are independent). H_1: there is an association.
E_{ij} = \frac{R_i \times C_j}{N} = \frac{(\text{row total}) \times (\text{column total})}{\text{grand total}}
\chi^2 = \sum_i \sum_j \frac{(O_{ij} - E_{ij})^2}{E_{ij}}, \qquad \nu = (r - 1)(c - 1)
Reject H_0 if \chi^2 \ge \chi^2_{\alpha,(r-1)(c-1)}.


Where the expected frequency formula comes from. If A and B are independent, P(A_i \cap B_j) = P(A_i)P(B_j) = \frac{R_i}{N}\cdot\frac{C_j}{N}, so the expected count in cell (i,j) is N \cdot \frac{R_i}{N}\cdot\frac{C_j}{N} = \frac{R_iC_j}{N}. Why (r - 1)(c - 1) degrees of freedom? With all row and column totals fixed, once we fill in (r - 1)(c - 1) cells, the remaining cells are forced by the totals.
Fresh practice 3 (2×3 table). 200 students are classified by gender and preferred study mode.

































OnlineOfflineHybridTotalMale253540100Female352540100Total606080200
Test at 5% whether study preference depends on gender.
H_0: preference is independent of gender; H_1: there is an association. Expected frequencies: E_{11} = 100 \times 60/200 = 30, E_{12} = 30, E_{13} = 100 \times 80/200 = 40, and the same for the second row.





























































CellOEO - E(O-E)^2/E(1,1)2530−50.833(1,2)353050.833(1,3)404000(2,1)353050.833(2,2)2530−50.833(2,3)404000Total20020003.333
\nu = (2 - 1)(3 - 1) = 2, critical value \chi^2_{0.05,2} = 5.99. Since 3.33 < 5.99, we do not reject H_0: there is no significant association between gender and preferred study mode.


                  
                  Exam trick: layout 
                  
                

Write the expected frequency in brackets under each observed frequency inside the original table (exactly as in the lecture), then make the (O - E)^2/E column table. Check that \sum O = \sum E and \sum(O - E) = 0. Keep two or three decimal places in each term.


4. The 2×2 table and Yates’ correction


                  
                  Memorize: 2×2 contingency table shortcut (lecture formula, with Yates' correction) 
                  
                










































B_1B_2TotalA_1aba+bA_2cdc+dTotala+cb+dN$$\chi^2 = \frac{N\left(\leftad - bc\right- \frac{N}{2}\right)^2}{(a+b)(c+d)(a+c)(b+d)} \sim \chi^2_1$$Without the correction the formula is \chi^2 = \dfrac{N(ad - bc)^2}{(a+b)(c+d)(a+c)(b+d)}. Critical value at 5% with 1 df: 3.84.


Yates’ correction for continuity. The chi-square distribution is continuous but frequencies are discrete; with only 1 degree of freedom this makes the uncorrected \chi^2 slightly too large. Yates suggested reducing |ad - bc| by N/2 (equivalently reducing each |O - E| by 0.5). It is especially important when some expected frequencies are small (between 5 and 10). The course’s lecture formula includes the correction, so use it, and you may mention the uncorrected value as well.
Fresh practice 4 (lecture Problem 1: smoking and lung disease).





























Lung diseaseNo lung diseaseTotalSmoker361450Non-smoker183250Total5446100
H_0: lung disease is independent of smoking. a = 36, b = 14, c = 18, d = 32, N = 100. ad - bc = 1152 - 252 = 900.
\chi^2 = \frac{100\,(900 - 50)^2}{50 \times 50 \times 54 \times 46} = \frac{100 \times 722500}{6210000} = 11.63
(Without correction: 100 \times 900^2/6210000 = 13.04.) Since 11.63 > 3.84 (1 df, 5%), reject H_0: lung disease is associated with smoking.


                  
                  Common mistake: "effective" questions 
                  
                

A question like “can it be concluded that the drug is effective?” is answered with this test of independence. If H_0 (independence) is rejected, look at the table to decide the direction of the association (e.g. the typhoid rate is much lower in the drug group), and only then say “the drug is effective”. Rejecting independence by itself only shows that there is an association.





                  
                  Self-check 
                  
                

1. In a 4×3 table, how many degrees of freedom?
(4-1)(3-1) = 6.
2. Row total 60, column total 50, grand total 200. Expected frequency?
60 \times 50/200 = 15.
3. A goodness-of-fit test to a Poisson distribution uses 6 classes and estimates \lambda from the data. df?
6 - 1 - 1 = 4.
4. Why is the chi-square test right-tailed only?
Because \chi^2 is a sum of non-negative terms; only large values indicate disagreement with H_0.
5. What should you do if an expected frequency is 3?
Merge that class with a neighbouring class (and reduce the degrees of freedom), or use Yates’ correction in a 2×2 table.

Exam Answer Templates and Strategy
This page is about how to write answers so that you collect full marks, and how to decide quickly which method a question wants. Most marks in MATH 243 are lost not because a student does not know the formula, but because they pick the wrong distribution or test, skip a step the examiner expects, or forget to write a conclusion in words. Read this page once at the start of your preparation and once again just before the exam.
Time and question choice
The paper carries 210 marks in 3 hours. You answer three questions from Section A and three from Section B, so each full question is worth 35 marks and you have about 28 minutes per question, leaving roughly 10 minutes to read the paper and check. When you first open the paper, spend two or three minutes marking every part you can do with confidence. Choose questions where the big-mark parts are ones you are sure of, because a 15 or 20-mark calculation question that you know is safer than three small theory parts you half remember. In Section B the ANOVA, chi-square and moments questions are long but completely mechanical, which makes them excellent choices if you have practised them, since there is no guesswork involved.


                  
                  Use separate scripts 
                  
                

The paper says “use separate scripts for each section”. Section A answers go in one answer script and Section B answers in another. Mixing them can cost you marks.


Choosing the right distribution
Most probability questions are a short story, and the first job is to recognise which model the story describes. The flowchart below captures the decision. The key questions are: is the variable a count or a measurement, is the number of trials fixed, and are we sampling with or without replacement?
flowchart TD
    A[Read the story] --> B{Is X a count<br/>or a measurement?}
    B -->|Measurement: time, length, weight| C{What is given?}
    C -->|mean and SD, bell shape| N[Normal: use Z = X - μ / σ]
    C -->|waiting time between events, rate λ| E[Exponential: P X > x = e^-λx]
    C -->|a formula f x is given| D[Integrate the given pdf]
    B -->|Count| F{Fixed number of trials n?}
    F -->|Yes, with replacement or independent, constant p| G{Two outcomes?}
    G -->|Yes| BI[Binomial]
    G -->|More than two| MU[Multinomial]
    F -->|Yes, without replacement from a small lot| H[Hypergeometric]
    F -->|No: wait until a success| I{First success or k-th?}
    I -->|First| GE[Geometric]
    I -->|k-th| NB[Negative binomial]
    F -->|No: events in time or space, average rate| P[Poisson]
    BI -->|n large, p small| P



                  
                  Signal words 
                  
                

“On average … per minute / per day / per page” means Poisson. “Time between calls” or “time to failure” with a mean means exponential. “Probability of … is 0.4, if 15 people …” means binomial. “Lot of 5 contains 2 defective, choose 3” means hypergeometric. “The fifth prescription is the first/third …” means geometric/negative binomial. “Normally distributed with mean … and SD …” means normal.


Choosing the right test
flowchart TD
    A[What is being compared?] --> B{Means?}
    B -->|One mean vs a claimed value| C{σ known or n ≥ 30?}
    C -->|Yes| Z1[z-test]
    C -->|No, small sample| T1[t-test, df = n-1]
    B -->|Two independent means| D{Both samples large?}
    D -->|Yes| Z2[two-sample z-test]
    D -->|No| T2[pooled t-test, df = n1+n2-2]
    B -->|Same subjects measured twice| T3[paired t-test]
    B -->|Three or more means| AN[ANOVA F-test]
    A --> P{Proportions?}
    P -->|one or two proportions| ZP[z-test for proportions]
    A --> Q{Frequencies in categories?}
    Q -->|Fit to a model| GF[chi-square goodness of fit]
    Q -->|Two attributes in a table| CT[chi-square contingency test]
    A --> V{Two variances?}
    V --> FT[F = larger s² / smaller s²]

Template 1: any hypothesis test
The course lectures always use the same layout, and examiners expect it. Write every heading, even when the step is obvious, because each line carries marks.


                  
                  Memorize this layout 
                  
                

Hypothesis. H_0:\ \mu=\mu_0 against H_1:\ \mu\ne\mu_0 (or > or <, read the question’s wording).
Level of significance. \alpha=0.05 (or as given).
Test statistic. Write the general formula and state its distribution, for example t=\frac{\bar x-\mu_0}{s/\sqrt n}\sim t_{n-1}.
Critical region. For example, reject H_0 if t<-t_{0.05,11}=-1.796.
Calculated value. Substitute the numbers and compute.
Decision. “Since the calculated value falls in the critical region, we reject H_0 at 5% level of significance” (or “falls in the acceptance region, so we do not reject H_0”).
Comment. Translate back into the story in plain words, for example “the new procedure has reduced the mean waiting time”.


The direction of H_1 comes from the question’s words. “Has the machine improved”, “is it less than”, “is there reason to believe \mu<40”, “greater than 220 mg” are one-tailed. “Is the difference significant”, “does it differ”, “can it be regarded as coming from a population with mean …” are two-tailed.


                  
                  P-value questions 
                  
                

If the question says “use a P-value”, compute it: for a left-tailed test, p=\Phi(z_{cal}); for a right-tailed test, p=1-\Phi(z_{cal}); for a two-tailed test, p=2[1-\Phi(|z_{cal}|)]. Then reject H_0 if p\le\alpha. If no \alpha is given, say “the P-value is very small (less than 0.01), so the evidence against H_0 is strong”.


Template 2: total probability and Bayes
Start by naming the events in words, because half the marks are for setting up the problem correctly. For example: “Let B_1, B_2, B_3 be the events that the product is made by machine 1, 2, 3 and let D be the event that it is defective.” Write the given probabilities with symbols, P(B_1)=0.30 and P(D\mid B_1)=0.02, and so on. A tree diagram earns marks and prevents mistakes. Then compute P(D) by total probability, and finally each P(B_i\mid D) by Bayes, checking that the posterior probabilities add up to 1.
Template 3: a grouped-data statistics question
Always present a full calculation table with these columns: class, mid value x, frequency f, u=\frac{x-A}{h}, fu, fu^2, fu^3, fu^4 (and cumulative frequency if medians or quantiles are needed). Choose A as the mid value of the class with the highest frequency or near the middle, because this keeps the numbers small. Write the totals in the last row. Then write each formula, substitute, and give the result with units. Finish with an interpretation sentence about the shape (skewness and kurtosis) or the comparison (which group is more consistent).
Template 4: interpretation sentences
Interpretation lines are short but carry real marks. For correlation, say whether r is positive or negative and whether it is weak (about 0 to 0.3), moderate (0.3 to 0.7) or strong (above 0.7), and what that means in the story. For CV, say “the group with the smaller CV is more consistent (less variable)“. For skewness, say “since \gamma_1>0 the distribution is positively skewed, meaning a longer tail to the right and mean greater than mode”. For kurtosis, say “since \beta_2<3 the distribution is platykurtic, flatter than the normal curve”. For R^2, say “about 93% of the variation in yield is explained by the fitted model”.
Reading the statistical tables
The normal table in your exam gives \Phi(z)=P(Z\le z), the area to the left of z. For a right tail use 1-\Phi(z), and for a negative z use \Phi(-z)=1-\Phi(z). For a reverse question such as “find the time above which the slowest 15% of trips lie”, look inside the table for 0.85 and read off z\approx1.04. The t-table is read with degrees of freedom on the left and the tail area at the top; for a two-tailed 5% test you need the column for 0.025. The chi-square and F tables are always used as one-tailed (right tail). For F_{\alpha}(\nu_1,\nu_2), \nu_1 is the numerator df (between groups) and \nu_2 is the denominator df (within groups or error). In many questions the examiner simply gives you the critical value, so read the question carefully before looking for a table.


                  
                  Critical values that appeared in past papers 
                  
                

\chi^2_{0.05,4}=9.49, \chi^2_{0.05,1}=3.84, t_{0.05}(13)=2.16 (two-tailed), t_{0.05}(11)=1.796 (one-tailed), t_{0.05}(9)=2.262 (two-tailed), t_{0.05}(19)=1.729 (one-tailed), F_{0.05}(2,9)=4.26, F_{0.05}(2,11)=3.98, F_{0.05}(3,8)=4.07, F_{0.01}(3,8)=7.59, F_{0.05}(4,12)=3.26, F_{0.05}(3,12)=3.49.


Final-week plan
In the first pass, read the probability notes P1 to P9 and the statistics notes S1 to S10 in order, solving every “Past TF” example yourself before reading its solution. In the second pass, use the TF Question Map to attempt every 2019-20, 2020-21 and 2021-22 question under time pressure. In the third pass, sit the 2022-23 and 2023-24 papers as mock exams with a timer, and only then compare with TF 2022-23 Solutions and TF 2023-24 Solutions. Read the Formula Sheet every day.

3-Exam-Toolkit/Formula-Sheet.title: Formula Sheet (memorize everything here)
3-Exam-Toolkit/Formula-Sheet.content:
Formula Sheet
This is the page to read on the last evening and on the morning of the exam. Every formula here has been used in at least one of the last five term finals or is needed to reach one. Each block says in one line when you use the formula, because knowing when is just as important as knowing the formula. If a formula here feels unfamiliar, click the linked note and read the explanation again.


                  
                  The five things students most often forget 
                  
                

First, \gamma_1=\mu_3/\mu_2^{3/2} is positive for positive (right) skew. Second, when you use step deviations u=(x-A)/h, the r-th moment must be multiplied by h^r. Third, the sample variance in tests uses n-1: s^2=\frac{\sum (x-\bar x)^2}{n-1}. Fourth, the normal table gives the left area \Phi(z)=P(Z\le z). Fifth, in rank correlation with ties, add \frac{m^3-m}{12} for every tied group in both variables.



1. Basic probability — P1 Probability Basics and Counting
Use these whenever you count outcomes or combine events.
P(A\cup B)=P(A)+P(B)-P(A\cap B),\qquad P(A^c)=1-P(A)
P(A\cup B\cup C)=P(A)+P(B)+P(C)-P(AB)-P(AC)-P(BC)+P(ABC)
{}^nP_r=\frac{n!}{(n-r)!}\ (\text{order matters}),\qquad {}^nC_r=\binom{n}{r}=\frac{n!}{r!\,(n-r)!}\ (\text{order does not matter})
De Morgan: (A\cup B)^c=A^c\cap B^c and (A\cap B)^c=A^c\cup B^c. Odds in favour of A are a:b means P(A)=\frac{a}{a+b}.
2. Conditional probability and Bayes — P2 Conditional Probability Independence and Bayes
Use the multiplication law when events happen one after another; use total probability when the final event can happen through several routes; use Bayes when you are asked “given the result, what is the probability of the cause”.
P(A\mid B)=\frac{P(A\cap B)}{P(B)},\qquad P(A\cap B)=P(A)\,P(B\mid A)
\text{Independent}\iff P(A\cap B)=P(A)P(B)
P(B)=\sum_i P(A_i)\,P(B\mid A_i)\qquad\text{(total probability)}
P(A_k\mid B)=\frac{P(A_k)\,P(B\mid A_k)}{\sum_i P(A_i)\,P(B\mid A_i)}\qquad\text{(Bayes)}


                  
                  Mutually exclusive is not independent 
                  
                

If P(A)>0 and P(B)>0 and A\cap B=\varnothing, then P(A\cap B)=0\ne P(A)P(B), so the events are dependent. Two events can be both mutually exclusive and independent only if one of them has probability zero.


3. Random variables — P3 Random Variables PMF PDF CDF and P4 Joint Marginal and Conditional Distributions
Use \sum f(x)=1 or \int f(x)\,dx=1 to find an unknown constant k.
\text{Discrete: } P(X=x)=f(x),\ \sum_x f(x)=1;\qquad \text{Continuous: } P(a<X<b)=\int_a^b f(x)\,dx,\ \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f(x)\,dx=1
F(x)=P(X\le x)=\int_{-\infty}^{x} f(t)\,dt,\qquad f(x)=F'(x),\qquad P(a<X\le b)=F(b)-F(a)
g(x)=\int f(x,y)\,dy,\quad h(y)=\int f(x,y)\,dx,\quad f(y\mid x)=\frac{f(x,y)}{g(x)},\quad \text{independent}\iff f(x,y)=g(x)h(y)
4. Expectation — P5 Expectation Variance Covariance and Chebyshev
E(X)=\sum x f(x)\ \text{or}\ \int x f(x)\,dx,\qquad E[g(X)]=\sum g(x)f(x)\ \text{or}\ \int g(x)f(x)\,dx
\operatorname{Var}(X)=E(X^2)-[E(X)]^2,\qquad E(aX+b)=aE(X)+b,\qquad \operatorname{Var}(aX+b)=a^2\operatorname{Var}(X)
\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)=E(XY)-E(X)E(Y),\qquad \operatorname{Var}(aX+bY)=a^2\sigma_X^2+b^2\sigma_Y^2+2ab\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)


                  
                  Chebyshev's theorem 
                  
                

For any distribution with mean \mu and standard deviation \sigma,
P(\mu-k\sigma<X<\mu+k\sigma)\ \ge\ 1-\frac{1}{k^2},\qquad P(|X-\mu|\ge k\sigma)\ \le\ \frac{1}{k^2}.
With k=2 at least 75% lies within two SDs; with k=3 at least 88.9%. If the distribution is symmetric, each tail gets at most half: P(X\ge \mu+k\sigma)\le \frac{1}{2k^2}.


5. Discrete distributions — P6 Bernoulli Binomial Multinomial Hypergeometric Geometric and P7 Poisson Distribution and Poisson Process





























































DistributionpmfMeanVarianceUse it whenBernoullip^x q^{1-x},\ x=0,1ppqone trial, success or failureBinomial\binom{n}{x}p^x q^{n-x}npnpqfixed n independent trials, constant pMultinomial\frac{n!}{x_1!\cdots x_k!}p_1^{x_1}\cdots p_k^{x_k}np_inp_i(1-p_i)each trial has k outcomesHypergeometric\frac{\binom{k}{x}\binom{N-k}{n-x}}{\binom{N}{n}}\frac{nk}{N}\frac{N-n}{N-1}\,n\frac{k}{N}\left(1-\frac{k}{N}\right)sampling without replacementGeometricq^{x-1}p,\ x=1,2,\dots\frac1p\frac{q}{p^2}trial on which the first success occursNegative binomial\binom{x-1}{k-1}p^k q^{x-k}\frac kp\frac{kq}{p^2}trial on which the k-th success occursPoisson\frac{e^{-\lambda}\lambda^x}{x!}\lambda\lambdacounts in time/space; or binomial with large n, small p (\lambda=np)
6. Continuous distributions — P8 Normal Distribution and P9 Uniform Exponential and Other Continuous Distributions
\text{Uniform }(A,B):\ f(x)=\frac{1}{B-A},\quad \mu=\frac{A+B}{2},\quad \sigma^2=\frac{(B-A)^2}{12}
\text{Exponential (mean }\beta=1/\lambda):\ f(x)=\lambda e^{-\lambda x},\ F(x)=1-e^{-\lambda x},\ P(X>x)=e^{-\lambda x},\ \mu=\frac1\lambda,\ \sigma^2=\frac1{\lambda^2}
Memoryless property: P(X>s+t\mid X>s)=P(X>t).
\text{Normal: } f(x)=\frac{1}{\sigma\sqrt{2\pi}}\,e^{-\frac{(x-\mu)^2}{2\sigma^2}},\qquad Z=\frac{X-\mu}{\sigma}\sim N(0,1)
P(a<X<b)=\Phi\!\left(\frac{b-\mu}{\sigma}\right)-\Phi\!\left(\frac{a-\mu}{\sigma}\right),\qquad \Phi(-z)=1-\Phi(z)
Normal approximation to binomial (when np\ge5 and nq\ge5): use \mu=np, \sigma=\sqrt{npq} and a continuity correction of \pm0.5.


                  
                  Normal-table values to know by heart 
                  
                

\Phi(1)=0.8413, \Phi(1.645)=0.95, \Phi(1.96)=0.975, \Phi(2)=0.9772, \Phi(2.33)=0.99, \Phi(2.58)=0.995, \Phi(3)=0.9987. Within 1\sigma, 2\sigma, 3\sigma: 68.27%, 95.45%, 99.73%.



7. Frequency tables — S2 Frequency Distributions and Graphs
\text{Sturges: } K=1+3.322\log_{10}N,\qquad \text{class width}\approx\frac{\text{Largest}-\text{Smallest}}{K}
Class mark = (lower limit + upper limit)/2. Class boundaries are halfway between the upper limit of one class and the lower limit of the next.
8. Central tendency — S3 Measures of Central Tendency
\bar x=\frac{\sum fx}{N}=A+\frac{\sum fu}{N}\times h,\quad u=\frac{x-A}{h}
\text{Median}=L+\frac{\frac N2-F}{f_m}\times h,\qquad \text{Mode}=L+\frac{\Delta_1}{\Delta_1+\Delta_2}\times h
Q_i=L+\frac{\frac{iN}{4}-F}{f}\times h,\qquad D_i=L+\frac{\frac{iN}{10}-F}{f}\times h,\qquad P_i=L+\frac{\frac{iN}{100}-F}{f}\times h
Here L is the lower boundary of the class containing the position, F is the cumulative frequency before that class, f is its frequency, and h is its width. For the mode, \Delta_1=f_m-f_{m-1} and \Delta_2=f_m-f_{m+1}. Combined mean: \bar x=\frac{n_1\bar x_1+n_2\bar x_2}{n_1+n_2}.
9. Dispersion — S4 Measures of Dispersion
\sigma^2=\frac{\sum f x^2}{N}-\bar x^2=h^2\left[\frac{\sum fu^2}{N}-\left(\frac{\sum fu}{N}\right)^2\right],\qquad CV=\frac{\sigma}{\bar x}\times100\%
Larger CV means more variable (less consistent). For a corrected mean and SD, first rebuild \sum x=N\bar x and \sum x^2=N(\sigma^2+\bar x^2), then subtract the wrong values and add the right ones.
10. Moments, skewness, kurtosis — S5 Moments Skewness and Kurtosis
\mu_r'=\frac{\sum f u^r}{N}\times h^r\quad(\text{about }A)
\mu_2=\mu_2'-\mu_1'^2,\qquad \mu_3=\mu_3'-3\mu_2'\mu_1'+2\mu_1'^3,\qquad \mu_4=\mu_4'-4\mu_3'\mu_1'+6\mu_2'\mu_1'^2-3\mu_1'^4
\beta_1=\frac{\mu_3^2}{\mu_2^3},\quad \gamma_1=\frac{\mu_3}{\mu_2^{3/2}},\quad \beta_2=\frac{\mu_4}{\mu_2^2},\quad \gamma_2=\beta_2-3
SK_P=\frac{\text{Mean}-\text{Mode}}{\sigma},\qquad SK_B=\frac{Q_3+Q_1-2Q_2}{Q_3-Q_1},\qquad SK_K=\frac{P_{90}-2P_{50}+P_{10}}{P_{90}-P_{10}}
\beta_2>3 leptokurtic (peaked), =3 mesokurtic (normal), <3 platykurtic (flat).
11. Correlation and regression — S6 Correlation and Regression
S_{xx}=\sum x^2-\frac{(\sum x)^2}{n},\quad S_{yy}=\sum y^2-\frac{(\sum y)^2}{n},\quad S_{xy}=\sum xy-\frac{\sum x\sum y}{n}
r=\frac{S_{xy}}{\sqrt{S_{xx}S_{yy}}},\qquad b_{yx}=\frac{S_{xy}}{S_{xx}},\qquad b_{xy}=\frac{S_{xy}}{S_{yy}},\qquad r=\pm\sqrt{b_{yx}\,b_{xy}}
Y\text{ on }X:\ y-\bar y=b_{yx}(x-\bar x),\qquad X\text{ on }Y:\ x-\bar x=b_{xy}(y-\bar y)
SST=S_{yy},\quad SSR=b_{yx}S_{xy},\quad SSE=SST-SSR,\quad R^2=\frac{SSR}{SST}=r^2\ (\text{linear case})
r_s=1-\frac{6\left[\sum D^2+\sum\frac{m^3-m}{12}\right]}{n(n^2-1)}
Second-degree fit y=a+bx+cx^2: solve \sum y=na+b\sum x+c\sum x^2, \sum xy=a\sum x+b\sum x^2+c\sum x^3, \sum x^2y=a\sum x^2+b\sum x^3+c\sum x^4.
12. Sampling and estimation — S7 Sampling Distributions CLT and Confidence Intervals
\bar X\approx N\!\left(\mu,\ \frac{\sigma^2}{n}\right)\ (\text{CLT, large }n),\qquad SE(\bar x)=\frac{\sigma}{\sqrt n}
\text{CI: }\ \bar x\pm z_{\alpha/2}\frac{\sigma}{\sqrt n}\ \ (\sigma\text{ known or }n\ge30),\qquad \bar x\pm t_{\alpha/2,\,n-1}\frac{s}{\sqrt n}\ \ (\text{small }n)
13. Hypothesis tests — S8 Hypothesis Testing Concepts and z t Tests, S9 Chi-Square Tests, S10 ANOVA One-Way and Two-Way




























































SituationTest statisticDistributionOne mean, \sigma known or n\ge30z=\frac{\bar x-\mu_0}{\sigma/\sqrt n}N(0,1)One mean, small n, \sigma unknownt=\frac{\bar x-\mu_0}{s/\sqrt n}t_{n-1}Two means, large samplesz=\frac{\bar x_1-\bar x_2}{\sqrt{s_1^2/n_1+s_2^2/n_2}}N(0,1)Two means, small samples, equal variancest=\frac{\bar x_1-\bar x_2}{s_p\sqrt{1/n_1+1/n_2}},\ s_p^2=\frac{(n_1-1)s_1^2+(n_2-1)s_2^2}{n_1+n_2-2}t_{n_1+n_2-2}Paired samplest=\frac{\bar d}{s_d/\sqrt n}t_{n-1}One proportionz=\frac{\hat p-p_0}{\sqrt{p_0q_0/n}}N(0,1)Two proportionsz=\frac{\hat p_1-\hat p_2}{\sqrt{\hat p\hat q(1/n_1+1/n_2)}},\ \hat p=\frac{x_1+x_2}{n_1+n_2}N(0,1)Goodness of fit / contingency\chi^2=\sum\frac{(O-E)^2}{E},\ E=\frac{R\times C}{N}\chi^2_{k-1} or \chi^2_{(r-1)(c-1)}2×2 table (Yates)\chi^2=\frac{N(\lvert ad-bc\rvert-N/2)^2}{(a+b)(c+d)(a+c)(b+d)}\chi^2_1Two variancesF=\frac{s_1^2}{s_2^2} (larger on top)F_{n_1-1,\,n_2-1}


                  
                  Critical values of z
                  
                

Two-tailed: 1.96 at 5%, 2.58 at 1%. One-tailed: 1.645 at 5%, 2.33 at 1%. A left-tailed test uses the negative value.




                  
                  One-way ANOVA 
                  
                

CT=\frac{G^2}{N},\quad SST=\sum\sum x^2-CT,\quad SSB=\sum\frac{T_i^2}{n_i}-CT,\quad SSW=SST-SSB
F=\frac{SSB/(k-1)}{SSW/(N-k)}\sim F_{k-1,\ N-k}
Two-way (r blocks, c treatments): SSR=\sum\frac{R_i^2}{c}-CT, SSC=\sum\frac{C_j^2}{r}-CT, SSE=SST-SSR-SSC, with error df (r-1)(c-1).

TF Question Map (2019-20 to 2023-24)
This page maps every probability and statistics question from the last five term finals to the note where the concept is taught and, for the older papers, where the question is solved in full. Use it in two ways. Before studying a topic, look at how it has been asked so you know what to focus on. After studying a topic, come back here and make sure you can solve every question listed for it without looking.


                  
                  Read this first: what the papers look like 
                  
                

The 2022-23 and 2023-24 papers are MATH 243 (Probability and Statistics). Both sections (A and B) are probability and statistics, 8 questions in total, and you answer any three from each section. The 2019-20, 2020-21 and 2021-22 papers are MATH 245 (Complex Variable and Statistics). In those papers Section A was complex variables, which is not in your syllabus, so only their Section B (Q5 to Q8) matters for you. That is why the newest two papers are solved separately in TF 2023-24 Solutions and TF 2022-23 Solutions, while the Section B questions of the older three papers are solved inside the topic notes as worked “Past TF” examples.

What keeps coming back
Looking across all five papers, some question types appear almost every year, so they deserve the most practice. Bayes' theorem and total probability appears in four of the five papers (truth serum, machines, party supporters, ball transfer). Binomial, Poisson and normal probability calculations appear in every paper, usually with a real-life story, so you must be fast at choosing the right distribution and reading the normal table. Joint and continuous densities (finding k, marginals, conditional density, expected values) appear in every MATH 243 paper and in 2020-21.
On the statistics side, ==moments about an assumed mean with \beta_1,\beta_2 or \gamma_1,\gamma_2 appears in 2019-20, 2022-23 and 2023-24, and two of those are the exact examples from the lecture slides. Regression lines and correlation (including rank correlation with ties and a second-degree polynomial fit) appear every single year. Hypothesis testing is guaranteed: a z-test or t-test for a mean every year, plus a chi-square contingency test and a one-way ANOVA== in both MATH 243 papers. Finally, the newest papers have started asking short theory questions (CLT and its use in computer science, stratified sampling, stem-and-leaf plots, sources of statistical data in Bangladesh, differences between testing concepts), so do not skip the theory paragraphs in S1 Introduction to Statistics Data and Sampling, S2 Frequency Distributions and Graphs, S7 Sampling Distributions CLT and Confidence Intervals and S8 Hypothesis Testing Concepts and z t Tests.


                  
                  Lecture examples come back word for word 
                  
                

2023-24 Q4(c) (nitrogen dose and rice yield), 2023-24 Q8(a) (job performance vs education), 2022-23 Q4(b) (Bangla and English marks) and 2022-23 Q6(c) and 2019-20 Q5(b) (moments) are copied directly from the lecture slides. Practising the lecture examples is therefore directly practising the exam.

4-TF-Solutions/TF-2022-23-Solutions.content:
Term Final 2022-23 — Complete Solutions
This file contains the full solution of every part of the MATH 243 (Probability and Statistics) term final of 2022-23. The questions are not repeated, so keep your printed paper beside you. Try each part on your own first, then check your work against the steps here. Notice how each answer is presented: what is given, the formula, the substitution, and then a clear one-line conclusion. Copy that habit on your own script.

Q3(a) — Bernoulli and Poisson processes; deriving the Poisson distribution (10 marks)
Bernoulli process. A Bernoulli process is a sequence of repeated trials with these properties: the experiment consists of n repeated trials; each trial results in only two outcomes, called success and failure; the probability of success p stays the same from trial to trial; and the trials are independent. The number of successes X in n Bernoulli trials is a binomial random variable, b(x;n,p)=\binom nx p^xq^{n-x}. Example: tossing a coin 10 times and counting heads.
Poisson process. Experiments that count the number of events occurring in a given interval of time (or region of space) form a Poisson process if: the numbers of events in non-overlapping intervals are independent (no memory); the probability of exactly one event in a very short interval of length \Delta t is proportional to its length, about \lambda\Delta t, and does not depend on events outside it; and the probability of more than one event in such a short interval is negligible. The number of events X in an interval of length t is then a Poisson random variable with mean \lambda t. Examples: calls arriving at a switchboard per hour, typing errors per page, accidents per month.
Derivation of the Poisson distribution (as a limit of the binomial). Divide the interval into n tiny sub-intervals, each of which is a Bernoulli trial with success probability p=\lambda/n, where \lambda is the mean number of events in the interval. Then
P(X=x)=\binom nx\left(\frac\lambda n\right)^x\left(1-\frac\lambda n\right)^{n-x}=\frac{\lambda^x}{x!}\cdot\frac{n(n-1)\cdots(n-x+1)}{n^x}\cdot\left(1-\frac\lambda n\right)^n\left(1-\frac\lambda n\right)^{-x}.
As n\to\infty: \frac{n(n-1)\cdots(n-x+1)}{n^x}=1\left(1-\frac1n\right)\cdots\left(1-\frac{x-1}n\right)\to1, \left(1-\frac\lambda n\right)^{-x}\to1, and \left(1-\frac\lambda n\right)^n\to e^{-\lambda}. Hence
p(x;\lambda)=\frac{e^{-\lambda}\lambda^x}{x!},\qquad x=0,1,2,\dots
which is the Poisson distribution. It is a valid pmf since \sum_{x=0}^\infty\frac{e^{-\lambda}\lambda^x}{x!}=e^{-\lambda}e^{\lambda}=1.

Q3(b) — Variance of Poisson, and income-tax errors (12 marks)
Variance. First, E(X)=\sum_{x=0}^\infty x\frac{e^{-\lambda}\lambda^x}{x!}=\lambda e^{-\lambda}\sum_{x=1}^\infty\frac{\lambda^{x-1}}{(x-1)!}=\lambda e^{-\lambda}e^\lambda=\lambda.
Next compute E[X(X-1)]:
E[X(X-1)]=\sum_{x=0}^\infty x(x-1)\frac{e^{-\lambda}\lambda^x}{x!}=\lambda^2e^{-\lambda}\sum_{x=2}^\infty\frac{\lambda^{x-2}}{(x-2)!}=\lambda^2e^{-\lambda}e^{\lambda}=\lambda^2.
So E(X^2)=E[X(X-1)]+E(X)=\lambda^2+\lambda, and
\operatorname{Var}(X)=E(X^2)-[E(X)]^2=\lambda^2+\lambda-\lambda^2=\lambda.
For a Poisson variable the mean and the variance are equal, both \lambda.

Q4(a) — Properties of the normal curve; mean, mode and SD (10 marks)
The normal density is f(x)=\frac1{\sigma\sqrt{2\pi}}e^{-\frac{(x-\mu)^2}{2\sigma^2}}, -\infty<x<\infty.
Properties of the normal curve. The curve is bell-shaped and symmetric about the vertical line x=\mu. Its mean, median and mode are all equal to \mu, and the maximum height \frac1{\sigma\sqrt{2\pi}} occurs at x=\mu. The curve approaches the horizontal axis asymptotically on both sides but never touches it. It has points of inflection at x=\mu\pm\sigma, being concave downward between them and concave upward outside. The total area under the curve is 1, and about 68.27%, 95.45% and 99.73% of the area lies within \mu\pm\sigma, \mu\pm2\sigma and \mu\pm3\sigma respectively. Its skewness is 0 and \beta_2=3 (mesokurtic). Changing \mu shifts the curve left or right; a larger \sigma makes it flatter and wider.
Mean. Put z=\frac{x-\mu}{\sigma}, so x=\mu+\sigma z and dx=\sigma dz:
E(X)=\int_{-\infty}^\infty x f(x)\,dx=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}(\mu+\sigma z)\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}e^{-z^2/2}dz=\mu\underbrace{\int\frac{e^{-z^2/2}}{\sqrt{2\pi}}dz}_{=1}+\sigma\underbrace{\int z\frac{e^{-z^2/2}}{\sqrt{2\pi}}dz}_{=0\ (\text{odd})}=\mu.
Mode. f'(x)=-\frac{x-\mu}{\sigma^2}f(x)=0 gives x=\mu, and f''(\mu)=-\frac{f(\mu)}{\sigma^2}<0, so f is maximum at x=\mu: mode =\mu.
Standard deviation.
\operatorname{Var}(X)=E(X-\mu)^2=\int_{-\infty}^\infty \sigma^2z^2\frac{e^{-z^2/2}}{\sqrt{2\pi}}dz=\sigma^2\cdot\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}\left\{\Big[-ze^{-z^2/2}\Big]_{-\infty}^{\infty}+\int_{-\infty}^\infty e^{-z^2/2}dz\right\}=\sigma^2(0+1)=\sigma^2,
using integration by parts with u=z, dv=ze^{-z^2/2}dz. So the SD is \sigma.
Standard normal variable. If Z=\frac{X-\mu}{\sigma}, then E(Z)=\frac{E(X)-\mu}{\sigma}=0 and \operatorname{Var}(Z)=\frac{\operatorname{Var}(X)}{\sigma^2}=1. So the standard normal variable always has mean 0 and variance 1, Z\sim N(0,1), which is why a single table of \Phi(z) serves all normal distributions.

Correlation vs regression. Correlation analysis measures the degree and direction of the relationship between two variables using a single number (such as r, between −1 and +1); both variables are treated alike as random, and r_{xy}=r_{yx}. Regression analysis finds the actual average functional relationship (an equation such as y=a+bx) between a dependent variable and an independent variable, so that the dependent variable can be predicted from the independent one; the two variables play different roles, and the regression of Y on X is different from that of X on Y. Correlation is a pure number without units, while regression coefficients have units. Correlation does not imply cause and effect, whereas regression is generally used where one variable is considered to influence the other.

Q5(a) — Statistical data, how produced, why needed, and sources in Bangladesh (10 marks)
Statistical data. Statistical data are numerical facts (measurements or counts) about a group of individuals or items, collected in a systematic way for a definite purpose, which can be compared and analysed. A single number is not statistical data; an aggregate of related facts is. For example, the monthly incomes of 500 households of Dhaka, or the yearly rice production of each district, are statistical data.
How they are produced. Data are produced either as primary data, collected first-hand by the investigator for the specific purpose through a census (complete enumeration of every unit), a sample survey, direct observation, interviews, questionnaires or experiments; or as secondary data, which are data already collected by some other agency and taken from published or unpublished records, reports, journals, websites and administrative registers. Data are also produced continuously as administrative records (birth and death registrations, tax returns, customs records, hospital records) and automatically by digital systems (sensors, transactions, web logs).
Why we need them. Without data we cannot describe a situation accurately or make objective decisions. Government needs data for planning (budgets, schools, hospitals, food and energy supply) and for measuring progress such as GDP growth, inflation, poverty and literacy. Businesses need data for market research, production planning, quality control and forecasting demand. Researchers need data to test hypotheses and build models. In short, statistical data turn guesswork into evidence-based decision-making.
Usual sources of statistical data in Bangladesh. The main official source is the Bangladesh Bureau of Statistics (BBS), which conducts the Population and Housing Census, the Agriculture Census, the Economic Census, the Household Income and Expenditure Survey (HIES), the Labour Force Survey, and publishes the Statistical Yearbook of Bangladesh, national accounts (GDP) and consumer price index (inflation). Other sources are Bangladesh Bank (money, banking, exchange rate, remittance, balance of payments), the Ministry of Finance (Bangladesh Economic Review, budget documents), the Export Promotion Bureau and National Board of Revenue (trade and tax data), the Directorate General of Health Services and NIPORT (health data and the Bangladesh Demographic and Health Survey), the Bangladesh Election Commission (voter data), BANBEIS (education statistics), research institutes such as BIDS and icddr,b, and international organizations such as the World Bank, UNDP, UNICEF and WHO.

For the examples below take the small data set 2, 4, 6, 8 with mean \bar x=5.
(i) Standard deviation. The standard deviation is the positive square root of the mean of the squared deviations of the observations from their arithmetic mean: \sigma=\sqrt{\frac{\sum(x-\bar x)^2}{n}}. It measures, in the same units as the data, how far the observations typically lie from the mean. For the example, the deviations are −3, −1, 1, 3, their squares add to 20, so \sigma=\sqrt{20/4}=\sqrt5=2.236.
(ii) Variance. The variance is the mean of the squared deviations from the mean, i.e. the square of the standard deviation: \sigma^2=\frac{\sum(x-\bar x)^2}{n} (the sample variance uses divisor n-1: s^2=\frac{\sum(x-\bar x)^2}{n-1}). For the example, \sigma^2=20/4=5 and s^2=20/3=6.67. A larger variance means the data are more spread out.
(iii) Skewness. Skewness means lack of symmetry in a distribution. If the longer tail is on the right, the distribution is positively skewed and mean > median > mode (e.g. income of people in a country); if the longer tail is on the left, it is negatively skewed and mean < median < mode (e.g. marks in an easy exam). It is measured by Karl Pearson’s coefficient Sk_p=\frac{\text{Mean}-\text{Mode}}{\sigma}, Bowley’s coefficient \frac{Q_3+Q_1-2Q_2}{Q_3-Q_1}, or by \gamma_1=\frac{\mu_3}{\mu_2^{3/2}}. The example 2, 4, 6, 8 is symmetric, so its skewness is 0.
(iv) Kurtosis. Kurtosis is the degree of peakedness or flatness of a frequency curve compared with the normal curve. It is measured by \beta_2=\frac{\mu_4}{\mu_2^2} (or \gamma_2=\beta_2-3). If \beta_2=3 the curve is mesokurtic (normal), if \beta_2>3 it is leptokurtic (more peaked, e.g. daily stock returns), and if \beta_2<3 it is platykurtic (flatter, e.g. a uniform distribution, which has \beta_2=1.8).
(v) Moments. The r-th moment is the average of the r-th powers of the deviations of the observations from a fixed point. Moments about an arbitrary point A are raw moments, \mu'_r=\frac{\sum f(x-A)^r}{N}; moments about the mean are central moments, \mu_r=\frac{\sum f(x-\bar x)^r}{N}. The first raw moment about zero is the mean, the second central moment is the variance, the third central moment measures skewness and the fourth measures kurtosis. For the example, \mu_2=5, \mu_3=\frac{(-27-1+1+27)}{4}=0 and \mu_4=\frac{81+1+1+81}{4}=41.
Concept: S4 Measures of Dispersion · S5 Moments Skewness and Kurtosis
Q6(b) — Stem-and-leaf plot of pencil lengths (10 marks)
Use the whole-number part as the stem and the first decimal digit as the leaf. Ordered data: 16.4, 16.8, 17.2, 17.4, 17.4, 17.5, 17.8, 18.6, 18.7, 18.8, 19.0, 19.0.
 16 | 4 8
 17 | 2 4 4 5 8
 18 | 6 7 8
 19 | 0 0            Key: 17 | 4 means 17.4 cm

Median. n=12 is even, so the median is the average of the 6th and 7th ordered values: \frac{17.5+17.8}{2}=17.65 cm.
Mode. The leaves show that 17.4 (twice) and 19.0 (twice) occur most often, so the data are bimodal with modes 17.4 cm and 19.0 cm.
Range. 19.0-16.4=2.6 cm.


                  
                  Answer 
                  
                

Median =17.65 cm, modes =17.4 and 19.0 cm, range =2.6 cm.


Concept: S2 Frequency Distributions and Graphs · S3 Measures of Central Tendency

A=35, h=10, u=\frac{m-35}{10}, N=100.

\mu'_1=\frac{-14}{100}(10)=-1.4,\quad \mu'_2=\frac{154}{100}(10^2)=154,\quad \mu'_3=\frac{-62}{100}(10^3)=-620,\quad \mu'_4=\frac{490}{100}(10^4)=49000.

Concept: S5 Moments Skewness and Kurtosis

Q7(a) — Differentiate the pairs of concepts (10 marks)
(i) Statistic and parameter. A parameter is a numerical characteristic of a population, such as the population mean \mu, variance \sigma^2 or proportion P; it is usually fixed but unknown. A statistic is a numerical characteristic computed from a sample, such as \bar x, s^2 or p; it is known once the sample is drawn but varies from sample to sample, and it is used to estimate the parameter.
(ii) Critical region and acceptance region. The set of possible values of the test statistic is divided into two parts. The critical (rejection) region is the part for which the null hypothesis is rejected; its probability under H_0 equals the level of significance \alpha. The acceptance region is the complementary part, for which H_0 is not rejected; its probability under H_0 is 1-\alpha. For a two-tailed z-test at 5%, the critical region is |z|>1.96 and the acceptance region is -1.96\le z\le1.96.
(iii) Exact and inexact hypothesis. An exact (simple) hypothesis specifies the parameter as a single exact value and so completely specifies the distribution, e.g. H:\mu=50. An inexact (composite) hypothesis specifies a range of values for the parameter, e.g. H:\mu>50 or \mu\neq50. The null hypothesis is usually exact, while the alternative is usually inexact.
(iv) Unidirectional and non-directional test. A unidirectional (one-tailed) test is one where the alternative hypothesis specifies a direction (H_1:\mu>\mu_0 or \mu<\mu_0), so the whole critical region lies in one tail. A non-directional (two-tailed) test is one where the alternative is H_1:\mu\neq\mu_0, so the critical region is divided equally between the two tails, \alpha/2 in each.
(v) Level of significance and p-value. The level of significance \alpha is the maximum probability of a Type I error (rejecting a true H_0) that we are willing to accept; it is fixed before the test (commonly 0.05 or 0.01). The p-value is the probability, computed from the sample assuming H_0 is true, of getting a test statistic as extreme as or more extreme than the one observed. We reject H_0 when p-value \le\alpha.
Concept: S8 Hypothesis Testing Concepts and z t Tests
Q7(b) — Large-sample z-test for GPA and 99% confidence interval (12 marks)
Given n=40, \bar x=2.8, s=0.35, \mu_0=2.4.
Hypothesis: H_0:\mu=2.4 against H_1:\mu\neq2.4 (two-tailed).
Level of significance: \alpha=0.01. Critical region: |z|>2.58.
Test statistic (large sample, \sigma estimated by s): z=\dfrac{\bar x-\mu_0}{s/\sqrt n}.
Calculated value:
z=\frac{2.8-2.4}{0.35/\sqrt{40}}=\frac{0.4}{0.05534}=7.23.
Decision: z=7.23>2.58, so we reject H_0.
Comment: The sample cannot be regarded as coming from a group of students whose mean GPA is 2.4.
99% confidence interval for \mu:
\bar x\pm z_{0.005}\frac{s}{\sqrt n}=2.8\pm2.58(0.05534)=2.8\pm0.1428\ \Rightarrow\ 2.657<\mu<2.943.
Notice that 2.4 lies outside this interval, which agrees with the rejection of H_0.


                  
                  Answer 
                  
                

z=7.23>2.58 ⇒ reject H_0; 99% CI: 2.657\le\mu\le2.943.


Concept: S8 Hypothesis Testing Concepts and z t Tests · S7 Sampling Distributions CLT and Confidence Intervals
Q7(c) — Small-sample t-test for the bank waiting time (13 marks)
Given n=12, \bar x=42, s=11.9, \mu_0=50, population normal, \sigma unknown, small sample → t-test.
Hypothesis: H_0:\mu=50 against H_1:\mu<50 (left-tailed).
Level of significance: \alpha=0.05, d.f. =n-1=11. Critical region: t<-t_{0.05,11}=-1.796.
Test statistic: t=\dfrac{\bar x-\mu_0}{s/\sqrt n}\sim t_{n-1}.
Calculated value:
t=\frac{42-50}{11.9/\sqrt{12}}=\frac{-8}{3.435}=-2.33.
Decision: t=-2.33<-1.796, so it falls in the critical region; we reject H_0.
Comment: At the 5% level, the population mean waiting time under the new computerised system is less than 50 minutes — the new procedure reduces waiting time.


                  
                  Answer 
                  
                

t=-2.33<-1.796 ⇒ reject H_0; the mean waiting time is now less than 50 minutes.


Concept: S8 Hypothesis Testing Concepts and z t Tests

\chi^2=\frac{N\left(|ad-bc|-\frac N2\right)^2}{(a+b)(c+d)(a+c)(b+d)}.

\chi^2\approx220>3.84 ⇒ significant association; the drug is effective against typhoid.

Term Final 2023-24 — Complete Solutions
This file contains the full solution of every part of the MATH 243 (Probability and Statistics) term final of 2023-24. The questions are not repeated here, so keep your printed question paper next to you. The best way to use this file is simple: try each part yourself on paper first, then come here and compare step by step. Pay attention not only to the final number but also to how the answer is written, because the presentation shown here (definitions first, then formula, then substitution, then a clear conclusion) is exactly what earns full marks.


                  
                  Final answers at a glance 
                  
                

Q1(a) No — two events with non-zero probabilities cannot be both mutually exclusive and independent. Q1(b) P(\text{red}) = 103/144 = 0.7153. Q1(c) P(A\mid \bar V)=0.504,\ P(B\mid \bar V)=0.256,\ P(C\mid \bar V)=0.240.
Q2(a) P(X<0.2) = 1-e^{-1.6} = 0.7981. Q2(b) P[(X,Y)\in A]=9/14, \operatorname{Var}(X)=45/112=0.4018, \operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)=-9/56=-0.1607.
Q3(a) At most about 31 applicants can score 84 or more, so yes, the person can count on a job. Q3(b) P(X=2)=0.2565. Q3(c) 0.0338,\ 0.8778,\ 0.0245.
Q4(a) P(778<X<834)=0.5111. Q4(b) r_s = 0.679. Q4(c) \hat y = 11.536 + 21.654x - 2.982x^2, R^2 = 0.931.
Q5(b) Moderate positive relationship (r\approx 0.60). Q5(c) Mean =59.8, SD =20.09, CV =33.60\%.
Q6(a) \mu_2=236.76,\ \mu_3=264.34,\ \mu_4=141290.1,\ \beta_1=0.0053,\ \beta_2=2.52 (nearly symmetric, platykurtic). Q6(c) z=-4.67, reject H_0, claim supported.
Q7(b) z=0.104, not significant, machine not improved. Q7(c) t=1.217<2.16, difference not significant.
Q8(a) \chi^2=17.5>9.49, association exists. Q8(b) F=0.175<4.26, no significant difference among cities.



SECTION A
Q1(a) — Can events be mutually exclusive and independent at the same time? (6 marks)
Two events A and B are called mutually exclusive when they cannot occur together, that is A\cap B=\varnothing, so P(A\cap B)=0. Two events are called independent when the occurrence of one does not change the probability of the other, which means P(A\cap B)=P(A)\,P(B).
Suppose A and B are both mutually exclusive and independent. Then from the first property P(A\cap B)=0, and from the second property P(A\cap B)=P(A)P(B). Putting these together we get P(A)P(B)=0, which is only possible when P(A)=0 or P(B)=0.
So if both events have positive probability, they cannot be mutually exclusive and independent simultaneously. In fact mutually exclusive events are strongly dependent: if A happens, we know for certain that B did not happen, so P(B\mid A)=0\neq P(B). The only exception is the trivial case where at least one of the events is impossible (probability zero).
Example: in one toss of a die let A=\{1\} and B=\{2\}. They are mutually exclusive, P(A\cap B)=0, but P(A)P(B)=\tfrac1{36}\neq 0, so they are not independent.


                  
                  Answer 
                  
                

No. Mutually exclusive means P(A\cap B)=0, independence means P(A\cap B)=P(A)P(B). Both can hold only if P(A)=0 or P(B)=0. For events with non-zero probability, it is impossible.


Concept: P2 Conditional Probability Independence and Bayes
Q1(b) — Multiplication law and the ball-transfer problem (12 marks)
Multiplication law of probability. For any two events A and B, the probability that both occur equals the probability of one of them multiplied by the conditional probability of the other given that the first has occurred:
P(A\cap B)=P(A)\,P(B\mid A)=P(B)\,P(A\mid B).
If A and B are independent, this reduces to P(A\cap B)=P(A)P(B). For three events, P(A_1\cap A_2\cap A_3)=P(A_1)P(A_2\mid A_1)P(A_3\mid A_1\cap A_2).
Problem. Box A has 5 white and 7 red balls (12 in total). Box B has 3 white and 8 red balls (11 in total). One ball is moved from A to B, so B will then have 12 balls.
Let W_1 be the event that the transferred ball is white and R_1 that it is red. Let R be the event that the ball finally drawn from box B is red.
P(W_1)=\frac{5}{12},\qquad P(R_1)=\frac{7}{12}.
If a white ball is transferred, box B has 4 white and 8 red, so P(R\mid W_1)=\frac{8}{12}. If a red ball is transferred, box B has 3 white and 9 red, so P(R\mid R_1)=\frac{9}{12}.
Since W_1 and R_1 are mutually exclusive and exhaustive, using the multiplication law for each path and then adding (total probability):
P(R)=P(W_1)P(R\mid W_1)+P(R_1)P(R\mid R_1)=\frac{5}{12}\cdot\frac{8}{12}+\frac{7}{12}\cdot\frac{9}{12}=\frac{40+63}{144}=\frac{103}{144}.


                  
                  Answer 
                  
                

P(\text{red ball from box } B)=\dfrac{103}{144}\approx 0.7153


Concept: P2 Conditional Probability Independence and Bayes
Q1(c) — Bayes’ theorem: who is the non-voter? (17 marks)
Let A, B, C be the events that a randomly chosen city dweller supports party A, B or the other parties. Let V be the event that the person voted, and \bar V that the person did not vote. The given information is:
P(A)=0.45,\quad P(B)=0.40,\quad P(C)=0.15.
The turn-out rates are 65%, 80% and 50%, so the probabilities of not voting are:
P(\bar V\mid A)=0.35,\quad P(\bar V\mid B)=0.20,\quad P(\bar V\mid C)=0.50.
By the theorem of total probability:
P(\bar V)=P(A)P(\bar V\mid A)+P(B)P(\bar V\mid B)+P(C)P(\bar V\mid C)
=0.45(0.35)+0.40(0.20)+0.15(0.50)=0.1575+0.0800+0.0750=0.3125.
By Bayes’ theorem, P(A\mid\bar V)=\dfrac{P(A)P(\bar V\mid A)}{P(\bar V)}, and similarly for B and C:
P(A\mid\bar V)=\frac{0.1575}{0.3125}=0.504,\qquad P(B\mid\bar V)=\frac{0.0800}{0.3125}=0.256,\qquad P(C\mid\bar V)=\frac{0.0750}{0.3125}=0.240.
Check: 0.504+0.256+0.240=1. ✓


                  
                  Answer 
                  
                

Given that the person did not vote: P(A)=0.504, P(B)=0.256, P(C)=0.240. The non-voter is most likely a supporter of party A.


Concept: P2 Conditional Probability Independence and Bayes

Q2(a) — Waiting time between speeders (15 marks)
The CDF is F(x)=1-e^{-8x} for x\ge 0 and 0 otherwise, where x is in hours. Since 12 minutes =\frac{12}{60}=0.2 hour, we need P(X<0.2).
Using the CDF. For a continuous random variable P(X<a)=F(a), so
P(X<0.2)=F(0.2)=1-e^{-8(0.2)}=1-e^{-1.6}=1-0.2019=0.7981.
Using the PDF. The density is the derivative of the CDF:
f(x)=\frac{d}{dx}F(x)=\frac{d}{dx}\left(1-e^{-8x}\right)=8e^{-8x},\quad x\ge 0\quad(\text{and } 0 \text{ otherwise}).
Then
P(X<0.2)=\int_0^{0.2}8e^{-8x}\,dx=\Big[-e^{-8x}\Big]_0^{0.2}=1-e^{-1.6}=0.7981.
Both methods give the same answer, as they must. (This X is exponential with rate \lambda=8 per hour, mean 1/8 hour =7.5 minutes.)


                  
                  Answer 
                  
                

f(x)=8e^{-8x} for x\ge0; \;P(\text{wait} < 12\text{ min})=1-e^{-1.6}\approx 0.7981


Concept: P3 Random Variables PMF PDF CDF · P9 Uniform Exponential and Other Continuous Distributions
Q2(b) — Joint distribution of red and blue pens (20 marks)
The bag has 3 red, 2 blue and 3 black pens, 8 pens in total. Two pens are selected, so the total number of equally likely samples is \binom{8}{2}=28. With X = number of red and Y = number of blue pens, the joint pmf is the multivariate hypergeometric:
f(x,y)=\frac{\binom{3}{x}\binom{2}{y}\binom{3}{2-x-y}}{\binom{8}{2}},\qquad x=0,1,2;\ y=0,1,2;\ 0\le x+y\le 2.
For example f(0,0)=\frac{\binom30\binom20\binom32}{28}=\frac{3}{28}, f(1,0)=\frac{\binom31\binom20\binom31}{28}=\frac{9}{28}, f(1,1)=\frac{3\cdot2\cdot1}{28}=\frac{6}{28}, and so on. The full table is:








































f(x,y)y=0y=1y=2g(x)x=03/286/281/2810/28x=19/286/28015/28x=23/28003/28h(y)15/2812/281/281
(i) Plot of f(x,y) against (x,y). Since X and Y are discrete, the plot is a three-dimensional “stick” (or bar) diagram. Draw the x-axis and y-axis on the floor, and at each point (x,y) raise a vertical stick whose height equals f(x,y). The tallest stick is at (1,0) with height 9/28; sticks of height 6/28 stand at (0,1) and (1,1); sticks of height 3/28 stand at (0,0) and (2,0); the shortest stick of height 1/28 stands at (0,2). No sticks are drawn at (1,2),(2,1),(2,2) because those points have zero probability. A top view, with the heights written in units of 1/28, looks like this:
 y=2 |  1
 y=1 |  6    6
 y=0 |  3    9    3
     +---------------
       x=0  x=1  x=2      (heights in 1/28)

(ii) A=\{(x,y): x+y\le 1\} contains (0,0),(0,1),(1,0):
P[(X,Y)\in A]=\frac{3}{28}+\frac{6}{28}+\frac{9}{28}=\frac{18}{28}=\frac{9}{14}.
(iii) Marginal distributions. Add along rows and columns of the table:
g(x)=\sum_y f(x,y):\quad g(0)=\tfrac{10}{28}=\tfrac{5}{14},\ g(1)=\tfrac{15}{28},\ g(2)=\tfrac{3}{28}.
h(y)=\sum_x f(x,y):\quad h(0)=\tfrac{15}{28},\ h(1)=\tfrac{12}{28}=\tfrac{3}{7},\ h(2)=\tfrac{1}{28}.
(iv) Variance of X.
E(X)=0\cdot\tfrac{10}{28}+1\cdot\tfrac{15}{28}+2\cdot\tfrac{3}{28}=\tfrac{21}{28}=\tfrac34,\qquad E(X^2)=0+1\cdot\tfrac{15}{28}+4\cdot\tfrac{3}{28}=\tfrac{27}{28}.
\operatorname{Var}(X)=E(X^2)-[E(X)]^2=\frac{27}{28}-\frac{9}{16}=\frac{108-63}{112}=\frac{45}{112}\approx 0.4018.
(v) Covariance.
E(Y)=0\cdot\tfrac{15}{28}+1\cdot\tfrac{12}{28}+2\cdot\tfrac{1}{28}=\tfrac{14}{28}=\tfrac12.
E(XY)=\sum\sum xy\,f(x,y); the only non-zero product term is at (1,1): E(XY)=1\cdot1\cdot\frac{6}{28}=\frac{3}{14}.
\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)=E(XY)-E(X)E(Y)=\frac{3}{14}-\frac34\cdot\frac12=\frac{3}{14}-\frac38=\frac{12-21}{56}=-\frac{9}{56}\approx-0.1607.

Q3(a) — Chebyshev’s theorem and the job applicants (11 marks)
Chebyshev’s theorem. For any random variable X (any distribution) with mean \mu and standard deviation \sigma, the probability that X lies within k standard deviations of the mean is at least 1-\frac{1}{k^2}:
P(\mu-k\sigma<X<\mu+k\sigma)\ \ge\ 1-\frac1{k^2},\qquad\text{equivalently}\qquad P(|X-\mu|\ge k\sigma)\le\frac1{k^2},\quad k>1.
Problem. \mu=60, \sigma=6, 1000 applicants, 70 jobs. A score of 84 is
k=\frac{84-60}{6}=4
standard deviations above the mean. By Chebyshev,
P(|X-60|\ge 24)\le\frac{1}{4^2}=\frac{1}{16}.
The event |X-60|\ge 24 means X\le 36 or X\ge 84. Since the distribution is symmetric about the mean, these two tails have equal probability, so
P(X\ge 84)\le\frac12\cdot\frac1{16}=\frac1{32}.
So the number of applicants scoring 84 or more is at most 1000\times\frac1{32}=31.25, i.e. at most about 31 people. Since 70 jobs are available and at most 31 people can score as high as (or higher than) 84, a person scoring 84 is certainly among the top 70.


                  
                  Answer 
                  
                

At most 1000/32\approx31 applicants can score \ge 84. Since there are 70 positions, the person scoring 84 can count on getting a job.

Q3(b) — Binomial to Poisson, and calls at a switchboard (12 marks)
Relation between binomial and Poisson. The Poisson distribution is the limiting form of the binomial distribution when the number of trials n is very large, the probability of success p is very small, and the mean np=\lambda stays fixed.
Start from the binomial pmf and put p=\lambda/n:
b(x;n,p)=\binom nx p^x(1-p)^{n-x}=\frac{n(n-1)\cdots(n-x+1)}{x!}\left(\frac{\lambda}{n}\right)^x\left(1-\frac{\lambda}{n}\right)^{n-x}
=\frac{\lambda^x}{x!}\cdot\underbrace{1\left(1-\frac1n\right)\left(1-\frac2n\right)\cdots\left(1-\frac{x-1}{n}\right)}_{\to\,1}\cdot\underbrace{\left(1-\frac{\lambda}{n}\right)^{n}}_{\to\,e^{-\lambda}}\cdot\underbrace{\left(1-\frac{\lambda}{n}\right)^{-x}}_{\to\,1}.
As n\to\infty (with \lambda=np fixed), using \lim_{n\to\infty}\left(1-\frac{\lambda}{n}\right)^n=e^{-\lambda}, we get
\lim_{n\to\infty}b(x;n,p)=\frac{e^{-\lambda}\lambda^x}{x!},\qquad x=0,1,2,\dots
which is the Poisson pmf. Both distributions then have mean \lambda=np; the binomial variance np(1-p) also tends to \lambda because 1-p\to 1. In practice the approximation is good when n\ge 20 and p\le 0.05 (or n\ge100, np\le 10).
Problem. Calls arrive at a mean rate of 0.5 per minute, so in a 5-minute period the mean is \lambda=0.5\times5=2.5. With X\sim\text{Poisson}(2.5):
P(X=2)=\frac{e^{-2.5}(2.5)^2}{2!}=\frac{0.082085\times6.25}{2}=0.2565.


                  
                  Answer 
                  
                

Poisson is the limit of binomial as n\to\infty,\ p\to0,\ np=\lambda. \;P(\text{2 calls in 5 min})=\dfrac{e^{-2.5}2.5^2}{2!}\approx0.2565

Q4(a) — Mode of the normal distribution, and the light bulbs (11 marks)
Mode =\mu. The normal density is
f(x)=\frac{1}{\sigma\sqrt{2\pi}}\,e^{-\frac{(x-\mu)^2}{2\sigma^2}},\qquad -\infty<x<\infty.
The mode is the value of x where f(x) is maximum. Differentiating,
f'(x)=\frac{1}{\sigma\sqrt{2\pi}}\,e^{-\frac{(x-\mu)^2}{2\sigma^2}}\cdot\left(-\frac{x-\mu}{\sigma^2}\right)=-\frac{x-\mu}{\sigma^2}\,f(x).
Since f(x)>0 for all x, f'(x)=0 only when x-\mu=0, i.e. x=\mu. For the second derivative,
f''(x)=-\frac{1}{\sigma^2}f(x)-\frac{x-\mu}{\sigma^2}f'(x)=\frac{f(x)}{\sigma^2}\left[\frac{(x-\mu)^2}{\sigma^2}-1\right],\qquad f''(\mu)=-\frac{f(\mu)}{\sigma^2}<0.
So f has its maximum at x=\mu; the mode of the normal distribution is \mu, the same as its mean.
Light bulbs. X\sim N(\mu=800,\ \sigma=40). Standardise with z=\frac{x-\mu}{\sigma}:
z_1=\frac{778-800}{40}=-0.55,\qquad z_2=\frac{834-800}{40}=0.85.
P(778<X<834)=P(-0.55<Z<0.85)=\Phi(0.85)-\Phi(-0.55)=0.8023-0.2912=0.5111.


                  
                  Answer 
                  
                

Mode =\mu (shown by f'(\mu)=0, f''(\mu)<0). \;P(778<X<834)\approx0.5111, i.e. about 51% of bulbs.

Pearson’s correlation coefficient measures the strength and direction of the linear relationship between two quantitative variables X and Y:

Q5(a) — Stem-and-leaf plots (10 marks)
A stem-and-leaf plot is a way of organising quantitative data that shows the shape of the distribution like a histogram, while still keeping every original data value visible. Each number is split into two parts: the stem, which is the leading digit or digits, and the leaf, which is the last digit. All values sharing the same stem are written on one row.
To create one: first decide how to split the numbers (for two-digit data, the tens digit is the stem and the units digit the leaf). Second, write the stems in a vertical column in increasing order, with a vertical line to their right. Third, write the leaf of each data value on the row of its stem. Fourth, arrange the leaves in each row in increasing order, and add a key such as “3 | 2 means 32”.
Example: data 12, 15, 21, 24, 24, 27, 30, 33, 38, 41.
 1 | 2 5
 2 | 1 4 4 7
 3 | 0 3 8
 4 | 1          Key: 2 | 4 means 24

From this plot we can directly see that most values lie in the twenties, we can read the minimum (12), maximum (41), mode (24) and median (average of 5th and 6th values =\frac{24+27}{2}=25.5), and turning the plot sideways shows the shape of the distribution.


                  
                  Answer 
                  
                

Split each value into stem (leading digits) and leaf (last digit), list stems vertically, write ordered leaves beside them, and add a key. It shows the distribution shape while keeping the raw data.

Q6(b) — Central Limit Theorem, algorithm and applications (10 marks)
Statement. If \bar X is the mean of a random sample of size n taken from a population (of any shape) with mean \mu and finite variance \sigma^2, then as n becomes large the sampling distribution of \bar X approaches a normal distribution with mean \mu and variance \sigma^2/n. In other words,
Z=\frac{\bar X-\mu}{\sigma/\sqrt n}\ \longrightarrow\ N(0,1)\quad\text{as } n\to\infty.
The approximation is generally good when n\ge30, whatever the shape of the population. If the population itself is normal, \bar X is exactly normal for every n. The importance of the theorem is that it lets us use the normal table for problems about averages (and sums) even when the original population is not normal.
Algorithm for solving CLT problems. Step 1: identify the population mean \mu, population SD \sigma and the sample size n, and check that n is large (at least about 30) or that the population is normal. Step 2: write the mean and standard error of the sample mean, \mu_{\bar X}=\mu and \sigma_{\bar X}=\sigma/\sqrt n (for a sum T=n\bar X, use mean n\mu and SD \sigma\sqrt n). Step 3: convert the required value(s) of \bar x into z=\frac{\bar x-\mu}{\sigma/\sqrt n}. Step 4: read the probability from the standard normal table, using P(Z<z)=\Phi(z), P(Z>z)=1-\Phi(z) and P(a<Z<b)=\Phi(b)-\Phi(a). Step 5: state the answer in the words of the problem.
Applications in Computer Science. In performance analysis, the average response time of a server measured over many requests is approximately normal, so confidence intervals and service-level guarantees can be computed even though individual response times are highly skewed. In A/B testing of websites and apps, CLT justifies the z-test on average click rates or conversion rates. In networking, the total number of packets or bytes arriving in a time window (a sum of many independent contributions) is modelled as normal for buffer sizing. In machine learning, the error of an average over mini-batches (stochastic gradient) and the accuracy measured on a large test set are approximately normal, which allows error bars and significance tests. In simulation and randomized algorithms (Monte Carlo methods), the average of many random runs is approximately normal, which gives the error of the estimate as \sigma/\sqrt n.

Q6(c) — Stratified sampling, and testing the delivery-time claim (12 marks)
Stratified random sampling. In stratified random sampling the population is first divided into non-overlapping groups called strata, such that units inside each stratum are similar (homogeneous) while the strata differ from each other. Then a simple random sample is drawn independently from every stratum, usually with sample size proportional to the stratum size, and these samples are combined. This gives more precise estimates than simple random sampling and guarantees that every important subgroup is represented. Example: to estimate the average CGPA of a university of 10,000 students, where 4,000 are in engineering, 3,500 in science and 2,500 in arts, a stratified sample of 200 would take 80 engineering, 70 science and 50 arts students, each chosen at random within their faculty.

Calculated value:

Decision: z=-4.67<-1.645, so it falls in the critical region; we reject H_0.

Q7(a) — Short notes (10 marks)
Goodness of fit. A goodness-of-fit test checks whether an observed frequency distribution agrees with a theoretical (expected) distribution such as binomial, Poisson, normal or uniform. If O_i and E_i are the observed and expected frequencies of the k classes, the test statistic is \chi^2=\sum\frac{(O_i-E_i)^2}{E_i} with k-1-m degrees of freedom, where m is the number of parameters estimated from the data. A small \chi^2 means a good fit; if \chi^2 exceeds the table value, we conclude that the assumed distribution does not fit the data. Each expected frequency should be at least 5.
One-tailed and two-tailed test. A test whose critical (rejection) region lies in only one tail of the sampling distribution is a one-tailed test; it is used when the alternative hypothesis has a direction, such as H_1:\mu>\mu_0 (right-tailed) or H_1:\mu<\mu_0 (left-tailed). A test whose critical region is split between both tails, with area \alpha/2 in each, is a two-tailed test; it is used when H_1:\mu\neq\mu_0. At \alpha=0.05 the critical value is 1.645 for a one-tailed z-test and \pm1.96 for a two-tailed z-test.
Degrees of freedom. The degrees of freedom of a statistic is the number of values in its calculation that are free to vary independently, which equals the number of observations minus the number of restrictions (parameters estimated) imposed on them. For example, the sample variance uses \sum(x_i-\bar x)=0, so only n-1 deviations are free, and the one-sample t test has n-1 degrees of freedom; an r\times c contingency table has (r-1)(c-1) degrees of freedom.
Null and alternative hypothesis. The null hypothesis H_0 is the statement of “no difference” or “no effect” about a population parameter, which is assumed true and tested for possible rejection, e.g. H_0:\mu=50. The alternative hypothesis H_1 is the statement that we accept if H_0 is rejected; it is contrary to H_0, e.g. H_1:\mu\ne50, \mu>50 or \mu<50. The form of H_1 decides whether the test is one-tailed or two-tailed.

t=\frac{\bar x_1-\bar x_2}{s_p\sqrt{\frac1{n_1}+\frac1{n_2}}},\qquad s_p^2=\frac{\sum(x_1-\bar x_1)^2+\sum(x_2-\bar x_2)^2}{n_1+n_2-2}.
Calculated value:
s_p^2=\frac{33.5+23.7143}{13}=4.401,\qquad s_p=2.098,
t=\frac{11.75-10.4286}{2.098\sqrt{\frac18+\frac17}}=\frac{1.3214}{2.098\times0.5175}=\frac{1.3214}{1.0858}=1.217.
Decision: |t|=1.217<2.16, so we do not reject H_0.
Comment: The difference between the two sample means is not significant at the 5% level; both samples may be regarded as coming from populations with the same mean weight.


                  
                  Answer 
                  
                

t=1.217<2.16 ⇒ the difference between the means is not significant.


Concept: S8 Hypothesis Testing Concepts and z t Tests

Q8(a) — χ² test of independence: education vs job performance (15 marks)
Hypothesis: H_0: There is no association between educational attainment and job performance (they are independent), against H_1: there is an association.

MATH 243 — Probability and Statistics: Term Final Guide
Welcome. This vault is a complete, exam-focused course for the MATH 243 (L-2/T-2, CSE) term final. It was built from the course lecture slides in the resources folder and from a careful study of the last five term finals (2019-20 to 2023-24). The goal is simple: by the time you finish these notes you should be able to solve any question from those five papers on your own, and the solutions of the two newest papers are kept for the very end as a final check.


                  
                  How this guide is organised 
                  
                

The notes follow the order of the course: probability first, then statistics. Every topic note begins by telling you which past term-final questions use it, explains the ideas in plain language, marks the formulas and definitions you must memorize, and then works through real past questions (2019-20, 2020-21, 2021-22) in full exam style. The 2022-23 and 2023-24 papers are solved separately in the last folder so that you can use them as mock exams.


Part 1 — Probability
Start here. Probability is the language of the whole course, and Section A of the MATH 243 paper is mostly probability.

P1 Probability Basics and Counting — sample spaces, events, counting, the addition rule, odds.
P2 Conditional Probability Independence and Bayes — the multiplication law, independence, total probability and Bayes' theorem (asked almost every year).
P3 Random Variables PMF PDF CDF — discrete and continuous random variables, finding k, cumulative distribution functions.
P4 Joint Marginal and Conditional Distributions — joint tables and joint densities, marginals, conditionals, independence.
P5 Expectation Variance Covariance and Chebyshev — mean, variance, covariance, rules for aX+b, Chebyshev’s theorem.
P6 Bernoulli Binomial Multinomial Hypergeometric Geometric — the counting distributions.
P7 Poisson Distribution and Poisson Process — Poisson, its derivation, and the Poisson approximation.
P8 Normal Distribution — the normal curve, the Z table, and the normal approximation.
P9 Uniform Exponential and Other Continuous Distributions — exponential waiting times and the memoryless property.

Part 2 — Statistics

S1 Introduction to Statistics Data and Sampling — what statistics is, types of data, sources in Bangladesh, sampling methods.
S2 Frequency Distributions and Graphs — Sturges’ rule, histograms, ogives, stem-and-leaf plots, scatter and box plots.
S3 Measures of Central Tendency — mean, median, mode, quartiles and percentiles.
S4 Measures of Dispersion — variance, standard deviation, coefficient of variation, corrected values.
S5 Moments Skewness and Kurtosis — moments, Pearson, Bowley and Kelly skewness, \beta_1,\beta_2,\gamma_1,\gamma_2.
S6 Correlation and Regression — Pearson and rank correlation, regression lines, R^2, second-degree fitting.
S7 Sampling Distributions CLT and Confidence Intervals — the central limit theorem and confidence intervals.
S8 Hypothesis Testing Concepts and z t Tests — all testing concepts plus z, t and proportion tests.
S9 Chi-Square Tests — goodness of fit and contingency tables.
S10 ANOVA One-Way and Two-Way — analysis of variance.

Part 3 — Exam toolkit
Formula Sheet collects every formula you need on one page. TF Question Map lists every question from the five papers with the note that teaches it. Exam Answer Templates and Strategy shows how to choose a method quickly and how to lay out answers for full marks.
Part 4 — Term final solutions (read last)
TF 2023-24 Solutions and TF 2022-23 Solutions contain complete solutions to every part of both MATH 243 papers. Try each paper under timed conditions first, and only then compare.
How to read the highlights
Throughout the notes, a red Important / Memorize box contains a formula or definition you must know exactly. A green Tip box gives an exam shortcut. A yellow Warning box points out a common mistake. A Past TF example box contains a real past question solved in full, and highlighted text marks phrases worth remembering word for word. Each note ends with a collapsed self-check; click it open only after you have tried the questions.


                  
                  Suggested schedule 
                  
                

Spend roughly 60% of your time on Part 1 and Part 2, working every past example by hand, 20% on practising past papers from the TF Question Map, and the last 20% on sitting the 2022-23 and 2023-24 papers as timed mock exams.


The original lecture slides and the past-paper PDF are in the resources folder if you want to look at the source material.
